YEARNING FOR THE END. Breathe soft and low. 0 whispering wind, At.we the tangled grasses deep, Where those who loved me long ago Forgot the world and fell asleep.
o toirering shaft, or sculptured urn, _ Or mausoleum's empty pride, Tells to the curious passer-by.. Their virtues or the time they diect I count the old; familiar names,

Crergrown with moss and lichen gray, Where tangled brier and creeping vine Across the creeping tablets stray. The summer sky is softly blue; LIN t The birds still sing the sweet, old strain; But something from the summer time Is gone, that will not come again. 4 So many voices hate been hushed, • So many songs have ceased for aye, So many hands I used VI touch Are folded over hearts of clay. The noisy world recedes from me: I cease to hear its praise or blame, -; The mossy marbles echo back liro hollow sound of empty fame. • I only know that calm and still They sleep beyon..l life's woe and wail, Beyend the fleet of Sailing clouds, Beyond the shadow of the vale, I only feel that, tired and worn, I halt upon the highway bare, . And gazoiwith yearning eyes beyond, On fields that shine supremely fair. .—Pligadelphia Record,

SOMEONE. Talk of blue Italian skies— Ah, the deeper blue that lies ' In the depth of Woman's eyes! sever coral from the South Like the coral of her mouth, IS'hen the woman comes to Youth. Ah, the dainty chin whose curve With a delicate reserve Tells of rule that waits to serve! And the ripple of the ear n • That takes in the meaning clear .1. Of the tides that tend more near. Her's a voice as soft and low As the silver over flow: Where the slender streamlets go. Never yet across the brink-r Of the Day did Morn, I think, ."• - Fingers lift so dainty pink. Never Mountain cut the Dawn With a brow so deftly drawn As those o'er her eyelids borne. Talk of form.—as grand and calm • - Stands the Queen—Areca Palm r In a breath of Southern balm! a - Talk of soul,—Ah ! turn and mark 'Vega's bright fetherial spark Glittering on the breast of Dark— Vera of the Heavenly Lyre, Would my lips could touch its fire- - Lend thine Eagle wings Altair !I JAMES CAMERON GRANT.

In the quiet of the early morning we should laden oar our hearts with kindness and goodwill for use during the day. A man should never be ashamed to own he has been in the wrong, which is but saying, in other words, that he -is wiser to-day than he was yesterday. Not a day passes but men and women of note do great deeds, speak great words, suffer noble sorrows. Of these obscure heroes, philosophers, and martyrs, the greater part will never be known till that hour when many that are great shall be small and the small great. 'People are always talking about originality; but what do they mean? As soon as we are born the worldbegins to work upon us; and this goes on to the end. And, after all, what can we call our own except energy, strength, and will? If we could give an account of all that we owe to great predecessors and contemporaries, there would be but a small balance in our favour. A YOUNG LADY'S IDEA OF MARRIAGE.—Here is an ex- tract from the writings of Charles Reade, which will doubtless be read with general interest :—So she was going to be married! to be mistress of a house, settle in London; to be able to go out in the streets all alone, to shop or visit; have a gentleman all her own, whom she could put her finger on any moment, and make him take her about, bven to the opera and the theatre; to give dinner parties her own self, and even a little ball once in a way; to buy whatever dresses she thought proper, in- stead of being crippled by an allowance; have the legal right f speaking first in society, instead of sitting mum- chance and mock-modest; to be mistress instead of miss —contemptible title; to be a woman instead of a girl, and all this rational liberty, domestic power, and social dignity were to be obtained by merely wedding a dear fellow who loved her, and who was so nice; and the bright-career to be ushered in with several delights; each of them dear to a very soul; presents from all our friends, as many new dresses as if one was changing her body, or her hemisphere, instead of her name; going to church, which is a good English girl's theatre of display and temple of vanity, and there tasting delightful pub- licity and whispered admiration, in a heavenly long veil, which she could not wear even once if she remain' single." Menicar. OPINION or Atconer..—The British 'Medical -Journal has undertaken to tell "The Truth about Alco- hol." The Journal says that the medical profession. "cannot be indifferent to a great moral movement," nor eau it "sanction the employment even for the noblest ends of a single questionable statement or argument, nee sacrifice a vestige of truth even at the holiest of shrines." The writer, whilst claiming that alcohol pos- sesses value as a medicinal agent, says :—" We take it as conclusively proved, in the first place, that alcohol is not a necessary food, and that the most perfect physical and intellectual vigour is compatible with total abstinence. We may go a step further, and confidently assert that people in perfect health are as a rule better without alcohol." The fear hinted rather than expressed by Sir William Roberts that the race may be injured by two or three generations of abstinence is put aside as ground- less. and against it is cited the excellent health of tee- totallers as evidenced by the returns of insurance and benefit societies. The "truth about alcohol" is thus summarised :—" Alcohol may be accorded a place as a luxury; it certainly has a definite value as a medicine ; but we think it most desirable, in the interests alike of truth and of national morality, that the medical profes- sion should authoritatively and unambiguously cleclare that it is in no sense a necessity. It is on this point that the controversy really hinges, and we think that the evidence regarding it is perfectly conclusive." The specie,l responsibility which attaches to medical men'as to the "temperance question's-is insisted upon. "They must refose," it is observed, "to be coerced into abating one jot of their deliberate convictions at the bidding of an,y orgarfisation ; but they will, we think, learn to look with a more favourable eye upoa a great moral move- ment which will not in all cases gain their adhesion, but which has a powerful claim upon their sympathy and respect.", MANNERS AND CUSTOMS OF TEE OMAHA INDIANS.— Writing on the work of the Bureau of Ethnology at- tached to the Smithsonian Institution at Washington, the Times gives some extracts from the last report of the director. Mr. J. C. Dorsey, it says, is responsible for an elaborate dissertation on Omaha sociology; and it is, on the whole, the most interesting portion of the volume. The Omahas, though not numerous, at least do not diminish. In 1876 they were 1,076, and in 1882 1,100. Few or many, they form a nation with a considerable body of ordinances, which Mr. Dorsey has punctiliously recorded. Their supreme chief is the " sacred pole." It is a cotton-tree which, wanting a ruler, they two hun- dred years ago felled, and having put hair on its head, invested with authority. It is regularly greased. A prominent warrior is believed to have lost his leg from Scalps are offered to it. omitting to grease the pole. Omahas are imaginative in their names. Among them " are "Rusty-yellow Corn-husk," "Stomach Fat, "Forked Lightning Walks," "She who is Returning Bellowing," and "She who is made Muddy as she Moves." Omaha matrimonial law is based, like that of most primitive clans, on the view that the community has all the same ancestors. An Omaha may not wed his deceased wife's sister, unless the dying wife should have said to her brother, "Pity your brother-in-law. ...het him:marry my sister." Polygamy, within limits, is lawful with the original wife's consent. Though she have given it, human 'nature is weak, and she may turn resticle at signs of her husband's affection for his second choice. Authorities differ on the mode in which she betrays her feelings. One declares that thereupon she strikes the dog, beats her child, and kicks the fire about. A man may not lawfully speak to his wire's grandmother. So strict is the Omaha etiquette about mothers-in-raw, that a son-in-law will fly from the room, in which his mother-in-law happens to be. Omahas are cleanly in their habits. They bathe daily. An untidy man or woman is nicknamed "the _ man who does not wash his hands," or "the woman who does not comb her hair." They are not cannibals, like the old lowa chief commemorated in the report as fond of roast Osage ribs.. They are so redoubtable as archers that they can send an arrow sight through a buffalo. ' They are as skilfulin games, one of _which, described as shooting at the rolling wheel, might be popular in Europe. Dancing, however, is their favourite pastime, and they have a variety_ of societies or clubs, each of which owns a characteristic dance. One society has a dance which "tends to pride and temptation." In this dance not over five are permitted to .carry otter skin- bags ; the rest wave fans of eagles' wings. There is the rtrie Buffalo dance, danced after the recovery of a patient bir doctors, who may invite members of the Horsedance, aid not of the Wolf dance. The Grizzly Bear dance has not been danced for ten years. Its dancers paint their bodies yellow, and one wears a grizzly bear's skin. The Ssalp dance is a woman's dance. In the Ghost dance no woman may join. Public Analysts have submitted CADstrity'S COCOA to close tests, sad the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining and nourishing beverage. Beware of Imitations.- 4th;.

I know dat eberY ting in his home is on de same scale—a gallon of miry to ebery half-pound of comfort." _ ______ _ __ _ _ -- POWER OF A Sorr Assswe.a.—" I have been about a great deal," said an old gentleman, "and I believe that nearly all, if not all, the bickerings, the qu.arrelsaend disa , putes which arise among -men - women, or children, in families. neiehbourhoods, churclee,ear even`nations, can be cured by the mighty moral pee* of a eat answer; for the Scripture has it, 1 A soft' answefttdineth away wrath." A bear broke into the house of a Nevada miner the other night He was away, and his Wife thought he had come home inebriated. She did not wait to light a lamp, but began operation!, at once. -When the bear finally got away, it is said that he did not stop running till he had travelled eight 'miles into thei heart 'of the mountains, and heaves such a sight, that the other bears would not associate with hide A very learned judge•Wis'asked what he -would do if a man owed him 'ten pounds and refused to pay. His reply was worth remembering by those who are quick to take offence an begin a quarrel. He said: "Rather than bring an action against him, with its costs and un- certainty, I would give him a receipt in full of all de- mands; yes, and I would send him five pounds over to cover all" possible expenses." That Was his conclusion after extensive observation on the matter of going to law. Many persons think that in Order to' enjoy perfect liberty it is necessary only td be free from the control of other people, If no one exacts obedience, regulates their lives. or interferes with their will, they triumphantly call themselves free. Yet there is a bondage which is -not the less slavishsbecause-they forge the chains them- selves. There are iyranf a that -hold Men in unflinching servitude, and burdens under which they bend without thinking it possible to rebel against the one or to east off the other. -Somebody a %id Rothschild had grown weary of whist. " I can believe it;' remarked W. S. Gilbert. "He is too rich to enjoy the piquancy and excitement of gambling. He doesn't care whether he wins, and he can't feel what he Loses." he author of The Mikado is also credited with having slid that "a husband can hope to be a hero in his wife's eyes only ON months—the month before he is married and the month after his death." To a well-known actress be is reported to have replied, when she playfully asked; "What age am I ?"—" I really can't say; but you don't look IL" "Did yeti see anything of a pocket book that I dropped Somewhere in the bedroom that I occupied last night, landlord?" "Any money in it ?" "About £50." "Yea, sir. Here is your pocket book, with the money. The maid was honest enough to bring it to me, and I locked it up in the safe." ft-Ithl very correct proceedings— very. I had intended placing the money in a et)vings bank this morning, where it would have been drawing four per cent. As a reward for your honesty I will say nothing about the interest for the time it has been in your possession, and you can make it., square with the chamber-maid. There is nething mean about me when I run across a; man who seems to be trying to do_ what's right." WANTED, A WirE.—lt was frequently Caroline Chis- holm's custom to escort large parties of young woman emigrants to the interior, in company with families, find- ing them situations as she went along, and receiving the blessings of those whom- shd- had assisted in the same manner previously. On such excursions she was ac- customed td depend for food supplies upon the grateful generosity of the settlers. During one of these journeys sire was accosted by a bushman as follows :—" Are you Mrs. Chisholm? "- "Yes," wee the reply, "what do you want ?" " Want! what every man like_me wants when he sees Mrs. Chisholm. Come now; look up that hill, and see that nice cottage, and forty acres under crop; and I have in the cottage twenty hams and flitches of bacon, and a chest of tea, and a bag of sugar. The land is paid for, and the three cows; it would no you good "to see my three cows." Then, pulling out a roll of papers, he continued, "See what a character I have got from the magistrate in charge of the district; and, look here, ma'am; at this roll of notes! Now, Mrs. Chisholm, do be a mother to me, and give me a- wife. The smile. of a woman has never welcomed me home after a day's hard. work. Never mind the breakfast! I could keep all Yeiir party-Int 1-week reinly- give-me olie or your nice Irish girls for a wife." A FRIENDLY ROBIN.—Whr is it we all love the robins so? Many would, answer this question quickly enough, and with no attempt at analysis, and their reply. Would be, "Oh, because he deserves to be loved." Thie ie true enough; but let me tell you why I love him.. Though I never had a caged robin, thinking it cruel to deprive a dear bird- of its liberty, I always do all I can to make friends with it wherever we meet. I was very young when I made my first acquaintance with Master Robin. We lived in the country, and one time there was a' veryhard winter indeed; the birds came to the lawn to be fed, but one was not to be content with simple feedine, and so one colder day tin usual he kept throwing :himself againet a lower pane in the parlour window--thnright, cheerful fire, I suppose, attracted his notice. "You do look So easy and comfortable in that nice room," he seemed to say; " thieds of my cold feet out in this dreary weather." My dear mother—she who first taught Inc to love birds and beasts, and all created things—did think of his cold feet. She opened the window, and by-and-by he came in. He would have preferred the windo* left open, but being given to understand that this would in- terfere materially with family arrangements, he sub nutted to his semi-imprisonment with charming grace, and perched himself on top of a picture-frame, which became his resting-place when not busy picking up crumbs, or drinking water or milk, through all the live- long winter. We were all greatly pleased when one day he threw back his pert wee head and treated ue to a song. And it was always while we were at dinner that he sang. "I suppose,' he seemed to say, "you won't object to a little music, will you?" Then he Would strike up. But when the winter wore away he gage us to understand he had an appointment somewhere; and so he was allowed to go about his business. . : Tire ROSE AND TEE BEE.—The poor rose was very sad; for, like many Others, she did wish to be of some ' little good in the world. Presently the bee came hum- ming by, and gathered the honey from the rose; and as he gathered it he whispered in the rose tree's ear, and told her that not the cornfield nor the stateliest tree could give the sweet gifts which she gave him. So When he went humming merrily away to the hive the rose tree felt less sad, for she knew that she was not wholly use- less in the worfel ; but still she tonged to be of service to the men and women and children. And soon all her roses were phicke-d, and the bee came in vain, humming over the leaves; there was no sweet store left for him, and the rose tree-felt she was indeed of no use at all. So' she said to the bee, "Poor friend, I have no sweetness left for you. lam but a useless thing." "No, no," said 1 the bee; "you stay here, and you know -little of what I goes on in-the great big world; but I move about, and I see plenty; I know that you are not useless, but that you have made glad the hearts of many. Why, this morning I flew through a pleasant room where I saw bright-faced children were at breakfast; they were very happy, and I saw them eating the honey that you helped me to make; and I saw, too, in a vase in the middle of the table one of your roses smiling it the children; and as they cameinto the room one by one they'said, ' Oh, , what a lovely rose 1' And I saw more than that," said , the little bee.-"I saw a man in the churchyard, and he I had a handful of per roses in his hand; and he went to a little grass-covered grave, and lie tenderly placed the roses upon the soft turf; his face was very sad, but I think, when he saw your rotes smiling 'over the grave, that his heart was a little less sad." So the bee tried to comfort.the rose tree, and to show her that her flowers had done some good. And it'si-as quitelrue, the flowers had done good; and far more geed than either the bee or the rose tree ever knew.--From" Truth in-Tale," by tit, Bishop of Ripon (Macmillan and Co.): ---- ' FELLING A FOREST GIANT.—:One of the most remark- able forests in the world is the Redwood Forest of Cali- fornia. It extends several hundred biles up anddown the coast, and is from five to twenty miles wide. The redwood trees grow from two hundred to two hundred and fifty feet in height, and are eight or ten feet in diameter. At the east it is a productive forest thatyieldS one hundred cords of wood to the acre. But Dr. Dio Lewis while gipsying in the Sierras, camped in a spot of the Redwood Forest whe.re it was estimated that the trees, if cut into cord-wood, would produce fifteen hun- dred cords to the acre. Dr. Lewis describes the falling of an enormous 'redwood tree, which he witnessed :—lt was well up on the side of a mountain, in the midst of magnificent scenery. The tree was two hundred and fifty feet high and twelve feet in diameter. I climbed to the spot, and found the men arranging the bed on which the tree was to fall. The boss stood near the tree, sighted down the mountain side, and directed the rolling away of a boulder, or the placing of a mass of large limbs, to save She body of the tree from being broken. "Suppose the tree should take a n'otion to fall in some other direction ?" I asked. " Trees " replied the boss, "fall where they are told to fall. They have no kinks of their awn about it." div.p: TIM MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. DEAD POULTRY AT THE PARIS SHOW.

This year the bead Poultry Show at the Palais de Phi- • dustrie, Paris, has been by far the best that we remem- ber to have seen for several years, if, in fact, it has ever been.equailed before. Last year there was a very marked decline both in the quality and number exhibited. The number this year was just about .the same as in 1884, • but the merit of the specimens was, infinitely superior. There were altogether 322 pairs of raivu,-geese, turkeys, ducks, pigeons, guinea fowls, and rabbits, or above 600 specimens in all. This show is ivorth a very long journey to see, and it is unequalled elsewhere. Several causes conauce to its success. In the first place, the French poultry breeders of the La Bresse, La Fleche,and adjacent districts have brought the system of fattening poultry to a 'wonderful degree 'of perfection. This is evinced by what can be seen regularly in the Paris markets. Second, the French Government have en- couraged the fatteners by offering very liberal prizes every year to dead poultry at the annual Mardi Gras Show. As no charge is 'made for the exhibition of the fowls; and the Slow, is a splendid market for the sale thereof, it is not to be wondered at that large numbers are exhibited. The third cause at work is equally powerful, namely, that high prices are obtained for the prize birds at the show, given chiefly by the proprietors Of Alia great cafés, restaurants, and clubs. We have , known as much as 125 francs (f.. 5 given for the winning I pair of La Fleche, and 8044100 francs is -no uncommon price even for those which are not, so high in the prize list. These are of course merely abnormal figures, given so that the prize specimens may appear on the menu at these cafés, &c:, on Shrove Tuesday. But it will be seen that .the feeders of the birds stand to gain a great deal. Apart from the pril d'honneur, which is a valuable; trophy, the first prize in each of the classes is 30 francs,' and if 100 francs can be: obtained for the birds ,that ' means about five guineas for two fowls. But, whilst the very best specimens are undoubtedly kept fop this show, , they are not so very much above what regularly appearl in the Paris markets. We have gone into the Halles Centrales of Paris at various seasons of the year, and. I seen on the stalls specimens which were not at all in- ferierin qualityi though perhaps .a little/ smaller; and we- have just seen - several dead 'fowls -sent over fromi Paris bought in the usual way in the Market,- Which ..for fineness of flesh and skin could not be surpassed.

The fowls at the show are divided injo= their various sections and not all put together, ;leis too often the case in this country._ At the head stood the La Bresse, which are regarded as the most delicate -of all. These never reach the Size of some other breeds-, and are pre- pared in a peen/jai. manner. When killed and plucked, and whilst yet warra, they-ate tightly rolled in cloths so made as to give them a cylindrical shape. They are then dipped in milk, and allowed to remain in the cloths for twenty-four hours. When opened out the wings and legs are found to be tightly pressed into the sides. At the show were 18 pairs of capons and 21 pairs of pou- lardes in the La Bresse classes, and the quality was simply magnificent. One of the winning capons weighed 81bs. lloz., and one of the winning poulardes 7lbs. In both these birds the colour of skin and flesh was exqui- site, and from the weights just given it will be seen that they were very large for what can only be regarded as a small race of fowls. The La Fleche were not so nume- rous, there being sixteen pairs of capons and the same number of poulardes. Here the quality was eqnally good and the weights' great. One of the -winning capons weighed nibs. lioz., but this was considerably I exceeded by one of the pair which obtained the third I prize, for this turned the scale at 12/-lbs.; but it was not nearly so good in quality and was rightly put down on that account. Of the pair of first prize La Fleche poulardes one weighed 81bs. 141 oz. It is customary in France to only caponise La Bresse and the La Fleche, but the reason of this we have not , yet learned, for all table fowls aKe the better for being 1 subjected to this process. We suppose that there is some reason for the arrangement. Only the La Bresse variety are trussed in the peculiar manner already de- scribed. All the others are laid upon shaping boards Iwith their backs upwards. The advantages of this method have often been stated, both so far as they refer to the appearance and to the carving. For this purpose Ishaping boards are used, and damp eloths are tied;ovei. ithe backs of the birds. The Houdan is not regarded as 1 a first class table fowl in France, though it is not in any way a bad one. At the show were thirteen pairs, for they were shown in pairs, the cook of the first prize pair weighed - ?lbs. 2iozs. Houdans haveinot the fine' skin and shape of some other breeds, but ace larger and ; make a good dish. The Crevecceurs were simply magni- ficent, though not very numerous. But for quality they could not be beaten, considering, that the specimens were not capons or poulardes. The cock in the winning pair weighed 91bs. 14ioz. -"and the pullet was a very grand one, fine in skin, and lovely in,colo#r of flesh. It anay here be renierked that the female is regarded as the finer and better of -the two, that is, when she has not laid, for, once having produced an egg, a pullet is thought to have lot the delicate flavour present before. One of the most delicate French poultry dishes, regarded as even a greater 'dainty than the La Bresse, the " Poules de Mans" has for its basis a young pullet...4,.,There were , seventy other pairs of fowls shown in two classes, but unfortunately these had nothing to show of what breeds they where, and it was in many instances almost ire-, possible to tell the variety. The minor French breeds I are in many cases very nearly allied, and with all the , feathers gone the slight distinctive features were absent. Of these we noticed a very nice pair of Courtes Pattes, which though small appear to make a 'Very nice table fowl. There was also a good lot of Du Mans, first rate in colour, both of skidand flesh. Forty-nine lots of turkeys made a remarkably good show, but, whilst perhaps better in colour and style of preparation, the weighta4ere not heaVier than are often found*in England. The winning pair were magnificent in colour, with beautifully distributed flesh. One of these weighed 231bs. 14oz. The largest of the turkey hens was just half this weight, but was very coarse in skin and flesh. :The third-prize pair was a very much better one in all points excepts that -of. size. The prix d'houneur . was given to the first pair of turkey cocks. Ducks were the only classes which we thought were below the average, for, though they,were very numer- rous, and one or two lots showed very high merit, yet the majority were decidedly poor. The winners were Rouens, one of which weighed 81bs. Bozs. Geese were better, but-not wonderfully large. We did not, however, obtain the weights, and cannot therefore give them. There was the usual display of ducks and geese with the enormous livers, fed for the production of fries gras. These may be wonderful, for the livers are enormous, sometimes weighing a couple of pounds, but they are rather disgusting, and certainly not such as would tempt anyone to relish this supposed dainty. The Guinea fowls were a very, fine collection, and very plump in- deed. Rabbits we have seen better at Paris before: The size to which these are bred and fed, for both these have a share in the result, is remarkable. They are usually trussed in the way sheep and calves are hung. The winners were large, and very fat, and one weighed 91bs. I 110 ZS. • It will be interesting here t 6 mention the lines upon which the French go in selecting table fowl. There can be no doubt that shape and size have their due influence, but between specimens of one variety the thing looked for first of all is a fine comb—a comb tine in quality,and small. Nearly all the best egg-laying breeds have large combs, and there seems some reason for this theory, that

The chief difficulty in teaching calves to drink from the pail arises from too great haste. Let the animal be- come hungry; give it the finger to suck, at the same time lowering the hand into the pail of milk, and the lesson will soon be learned.

The number of sheep and lambs received in the United Kingdom during the past month was 28,434, against 27,202, Germany sending 9,058, against 15,332; Holland 15,505, against 5,759; and Belgium 861, against 3,459, the number landed in London being 24,705, as compared with 23,254. Oscar Willey, of Davenport., lowa, is, according to an American paper, the possessor of a horse of excellent build and good gait, with five legs, and ovary time it is shod five shoes are required. The horse is six years old, and was raised on a farm near Moline, Illinois. It runs as well as a four-legged animal, and to all appearances' finds no inconvenience in using the fifth member.. Mr. Rigby, the Secretary of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society has just issued the prize list for 1886. The show will be held on the Roodee, Chaster, on the Bth, 9th, 10th, and 11th of September next. Entries for Implements and Machinery, horses, cattle, sheep, pigs, cheese, and butter close on the Ist of August; for poultry and dogs, on the 20th of that month. WINDOALLS.—" Glenderg " thys shall be glad to know the best remedy for windgalls without blistering or stopping a horse in his work.—The best non-blister- ing application to " windgalLs " is a mercurial charge. This is made by melting together Burgundy pitch and beeswax, and, when this is cooling, add ordinary mer- curial ointment in the proportion of one part of oint- ment to six parts of the pitch and beeswax mixture. When thoroughly mixed, apply with a fiat stick, and before it is too cold put on some tow cut in short pieces. This sticks to the charge, and prevents dirt, &c., adher- ing. The animal may continue his work regularly. CROSS-BRED HERHFORD SHORTHORN STRER.—A few ' enterprising breeders of Herefords are doing very useful work in bringing to notice the claims of white faces for crossing purposes with other breeds or descriptions of cow stock. There is no doubt a strong.disinclination exhibited by many to cross established herds of pure bred cattle. In the majority of herds it would evidently be unwise to do so, but where the cow stock is of an or- dinary kind that never rises above the level of what is known as market value, there need be no hesitation to cross-breed. Fashion has much influence on value, par- ticularly amongst Shorthorns, more so perhaps than in the case of Herefords, and it is quite necessary that there should be always such an article for • the investment of money in as fashion, though at times it is an unseen quality, judging from the style of the eeiMel itself, and frequently a most expensive thing to acquire for mode- rate value in money. Some of the best paying steers and dairy cows we have ever seen have been produced by crossing high-class Hereford sires on pure-bred Short- horn dams. The offspring of such stock invariably possess top value in the market, for the reason that the cross-bred steer is worth fully as much per stone as a , pure bred Hereford, whilst he realises more by quite a lhalfpenny per pound than a pure Shorthorn. When this' "can be effected not only without loss but actually with increase in weight an gain in early maturing for mar- ket, it should at once banish mere sentiment from the breeding of dairy herds.

MILK FOODS.—At a recent conference of dairy farmers in America, Professor G. C. Caldwell, of Cornell, delivered a lecture on the "Effect of Food on the Composition of Milk," of which the following is a brief summary :—Milk, he said, is tho result of two operations—the breaking down of the tissues of the milk glands, and the diffusion of matter from the blood. According to this theory, the blood will receive no more water than it needs from the use of succulent food, or fro.m water drunk by the ani- mal, all above that need being carried off by the kidneys. Nor are there any figures to show that water affects the milk unfavourably. Succulent food increases the flow of milk, but does not materially increase the proportion of water in it. The flow is undoubtedly greater in June than at any other time of the year, but the milk is no poorer. This subject, however, needs further investiga- tion. But feed does make a change in the dry substance of the milk. The fact is well established that. a ration rich in albuminoids will make a richer milk. The rela- tive proportions of fat and casein are changed in a marked manner by a change in the ratic,n. For instance, if oilcake be added to the feed, I have known the butter Product to be raised from 6 lb. per week to 8 lb. An extra yield of butter will naturally follow the use of richer feed, if the cow has been well selected; but a simi- lar result may not follow in the case of an ordinary cow. Another lesson to be learned is that certain kinds of food will produce changes in the composition of milk not in- dicated by their chemical analysis. Palm nut meal is known to increase the amount of butter, although no chemist can tell exactly why. The effect produced on milk by substances that pass into it directly from the blood has been well established by experiment. Thus, when drugs are given to a cow, their effect is seen in the milk in an exceedingly short time. For this reason it might be well to pay some attention to the use of aro- matic grasses ps food, such as sweet clover and sweet vernal grass. Strange to say, howexer, when alcohol is administered to a cow, it can never be detected in the milk, and this is regarded as a point in favour of fer- mented ensilage. Mouldy grain has caused the death of many cattle, and it has .now been traced to the presence of alkaloids in the grain. PRICES IN IRELAND FOR 35 YEARS.—At the present time, When the Irish question is occupying such pro- minent attention, the following tables of prices in Ire- land during the last 35 years will be of special interest. The averages are taken from the files of the Farmers' Gazette for the past forty years, and are based, as regards grain, beef, mutton, pork, and wool, also lambs, on the quotations of Dublin market: the item butter on the prices of "firsts," "seconds," and "thirds" (but not lower qualities) in Cork market; and store cattle on the reports of the most important country fairs. Prices current in 1885 are .added, and also the quotations on which the surveyors and valuers employed in making the tenement valuation of Ireland were instructed by Sir Richard Griffith to base their estimates:— QUINQUENNIAL AVRILLGE.3, 1850-85.

ROASTBD TO DEATH—On Saturday Mrs. Scott, aged 50 wife of a porter, living in Victoria-street, Glasgow, fell into the kitchen fire while suffering from giddiness. Two lodgers rushed into the room and attempted to extinguish the flames, but before they had succeeded she had succumbed. --Charles Thomas, aged 12 years, the son of a working- man residing at Cumberla. near Swansea, was missed on Friday. On Saturday morning his corpee, terribly charred, was found on the burning refuse tips near Cumfelyn Tin- works. it is supposed that thefttad had fallen aeleep there, and becoming stupefied by the fumes had been roasted to death.

FOG IN THE ENGLISII CHANNEL —A. dense fog prevailed ! in the English Channel on Saturday, and proved most dis- astrous to vessels near the coast. Three steamers went ! ashore near Dover, and three others had narrow escapes, one running stem-on into the Admiralty Pier, and doing great ' damage. The large Monarch liner Persian Monarch, which left Lcralon for New York on Thursday with a large num- ber of passengers, stranded on the Devon coast during the leg. Assistance was procured, and on Saturday afternoon ; the st:!amer was towed off and proceeded for Plymouth, but little damaged. The Glasgow steamer City of Venice was also unlucky enough to run ashore near the Lizard. After ! some hours" work she was got afloat, and steamed to Fal- mouth leaky. More serious results attended the strand- ing ef the full-rigged ship Port Chalmers, which left Fal- mouth for Glasgow on Saturday with a valuable cargo of sugar. In the fog she approached too closely to the land, and ran on the " Manacles " rocks, half-way between Fal- mouth and the Lizard- The ship remained fast on the rock, ailed with water as the tide rose, and is expected to become t total wreck.'

may be , of an width should be that is intended 4, there is no better oi , litter, thrown into a heap, and two or thred.times in order to free it of some of its ammonia, which proves destructive to plants when in excess. Where leavee:are plentiful the hot-bed may be composed of these and manure in equal parts, and after the bed is of no furthe*se its oontents,will be valuable as Manure, though not so stimulating as that which is fresh and possessed ofj ammonia. If a barrow-load of soil is placed in the centre of the frame a cucumber plant might be introduced into it, and the space sur- rounding can be Wised to raise seedlings. The strongest growing vanities of some sections are frequently trained on the walls, and in that ease their pruning would be similar to the recognised climbers. One of the objects'oVpruning is to reduce the number of shoots; in order to allow more space for the proper development of those that are retained. Here the pruning novice con- fronts a difficulty, and is bewildered as to which he shall cut and :which shall be spared. The weakly shoots should be removed first, and at the same time an eye should be kept on wood of two or more years' growth that may not have thrown out strong shoots during the past: year,"and lent it out, and' continue this process of I selection till they are reduced to the number required. Some of the varieties throw out shoots from six to eight feet long, which frequently produce laterals the whole of their length, and flowers appear at the point of each. These long growths may be reduced to any length, but if there is room to lay them in, all wood the thickness of an ordinary lead pencil may be depended upon to flower, and should, therefore, be retained. It is a mis- take to lay the shoots in too thick, and the distance , between those made last year should not be less than from six to eight inches, and those that proceed from the , bottom should have preference. THB GICHENHOUSE.—In consequence of the dulness and severity of the weather, there is still a paucity of flowers in the greenhouse; and the following are what we may , expect to see in those structures that are in possession I of the cottager :—Most varieties of Camelias may be had in flower now. and Chinese Primulas may be kept in good order for two or three weeks yet. Now and then a cottager tries his hand at Heath growing, and he is tempted to buy an Erica Hyemales or E. Wilmmeana, which are so beautiful, and offeted so cheap in the markets at this season of the year, but ere the last flower has developed the plants are all but dead. The fact is the plants are not easily managed, and if their requirements are well understood the money spent on them had better be laid out on other plants that will bear more hardship. =Once a Heath gets dry, it might as well be thrown away at once. They will bear cold even to freezing point, and they enjoy the hottest sum- mers, but extremes in the application of water will des- troy them in a few days. They also require the pots to be carefully drained, and they will not grow in any soil but good peat, with about one-eighth of coarse silver sand, which must be well rammed round the ball when the plant is introduced into a larger pot. Epacris are as handsome as the Erica, and perhaps not quite so fas- tidious as to water, though anything like a sodden state would in a short time prove inimical. We are now in the midst of their flowering season, and any one wishing tp try their hand with them should select Eclipse and Grandi Flora in preference to the upright growing ones; not that they are the handsomest, but they maintain a better habit as they grow older. The Cineraria is the gayest flower in the majority of greenhouses at the present time. Seeds of these sown now would flower before Christmas, and another sowing made in May or June would come in useful this time next year. The pot in which the seed are to be sown should be half-filled with broken crocks for drainage, and over these an inch or two of rough material out of the potting compost. The remaining space should be filled within a quarter of an inch from the top with soil that has been passed through a quarter-inch seine and pressed with the bottom of another pot, or a round flat piece of wood may be made for the purpose with an upright handle about four inches long in the centre of it. Then sow the seed thinly, and cover it over the eighth of an inch with finer soil still, and instead of watering in the usual way, dip the pot up to the rim in a pail of water till the moisture appears on the surface.

div.head: SENSATION IN CHELMSFORD,
div.p: SENSATION IN CHELMSFORD,

The Chelmsford 2rCiC3, the leading paper of Essex, fur nisbes the following facts :—The family of Mr. George Les- ter, who have resided in Marriages-square. Chelmsford, for twenty-three years, have just met with a thrilling experi- ence. ahe particulars of the event are so remarkable that they have created nothinv short kf a downright sensation in our usually quiet town. The facts as given below have been duly verified by us and are of such general interest that they should be made public everywhere, inasmuch as there are, no doubt, thousands of families who can profit by the intelligence thus conveyed. About eighteen months ago the son of Mr. Lester, a youth of seventeen, was attacked with a peculiar and painful ail- ment of his ankles and muscles, which so disabled him that he was obliged to stop working at his trade, that of a baker. He was placed under the treatment of a skilful physician, and notwithstanding every attention he received no bent fit, but speedily grew worse. His condition became so alarm- ing that further medical aid was called in, but he still failed to obtain relief. The raalady of the youth had now assumed such a violent form that hie condition was pitiable. He had completely lost the use of his ankles and was unable to walk. It was only with the aid of crutches that hecould move about at all, and even thea not without experiencing the most intense pain. In the language of his parents, he was completely crippled. He was then sent to one of the leading London hospitals, but there also big sufferings were not in the slightest relieved. He had now been crip- pled for nearly a year, and every treatment having utterly felled, he and his parents were almost in despair. His friends, and all who knew him, believed that he would never be able to walk again._

Havioi read in a Chelmlford paper of some remarkable cures wrought by a remedy recently introduced for the cure of pain, the young man was led, as a last resort, to make a trial of one bottle of the same. To use his own words' he was greatly relieved after having applied the article but once, and he was able to walk without his crutches in ten days from the time he purchased the first bottle. After using three bottles he was, strange as it may seem, actually able to resume his work, and is now free from pain and leading his former active life. His cure seems almost miraculous to those who are familiar with his long, agoniz- ing sufferings and his previous helpless condition, and St. Jacobs Oil, which is the remedy he used, is certainly entitled to the credit of having accomplished a wonderful cure under our very eyes.

When irepresentative of this paper called on Lester, in order to see for himself what this magical remedy had done for him, the young man could scarcely find words with which to express his gratitude at his recovery. He remarked that St. Jacobs Oil had transferred him from agony and misery to joy. Mr. James Tomlinson, the well-known dispensing chemist of Tindal-square, from whom Young Lester purchased this wonderful oil, and who is thoroughly familiar with his case, stated to our reporter that while this was a most astonish- ing recovery, numerous other cures, which had resulted from its use and which had come to his notice, were almost as remarkable. In consequence of the surprising power which the remedy possesses to relieve pain and strengthen and restore the muscles and joints to their normal condition, such extraordinary demand had, Mr. Tomlinson said, sprung up that he found it difficult to keep a sufficient stock on hand. In fact, instead of getting his supplies from the wholesale houses, as is usual, be is ordering hundreds of bottles at a time, direct from the Great Britain Branch of the proprietors. _ _

While on the subject of this medical discovery, we may mention that several cures very much like this of young Lester's, and likewise duly certified to by responsible parties, have come te our notice. Space will admit of our mention- ing only one of these. It is the case of Mrs. Mary Ann Hills, of \Yardley, Uppingbain, whose husband has been a resident of Butland County for over forty years. His call- ing is that of a shepherd, and it is safe to say that no one is better known in all the country about WardlGy than John Halls. He is universally respect-al as an industrious and honest man, and what he says may be relied upon. Mr. Halls writes that while he does not seek notoriety, he feels that the following facts should be made public for the benefit of others. What he states is well-known to his neighbours, among whom the almost miraculous recovery of his wife has caused no little excitement. This Case is so remarkable that one lady who had heard of it came all the way from London to satisfy herself by a personal visit of the truth of the astoniebirg reports which had reached her. In reciting the particulars of the case, we can do no better than use Mr. 11-Ms' own statement made to our renorter. He says : " For over eighteen years my wife was an intense sufferer from rheumatism. Much of the time her hands, elbows, knees, and feet were swollen to two or three time their usual size, so that she was unable to walk or dress herself. bhe was in fact absolutely helpless. Her joints became so stiff at times that she could not move them. During these periods she saffered the most intense agony, and in all these long years she was never entirely free from pain, either day or night. Different remedies were recommended to her, all of which she used but got no relief. Our family doctor said there was no help for her and that her case was incurable. She and I bad given tap all hope of her ever recovering her heahh or being again free from pain. She had suffered so long that he had become thoroughly disheartened. Just before last Christmaa we read in a newspaper an ' article copied from the "London Magazine of Chemistry and Medicine," which gave particulars ' of the wonderful cure, by St. Jacobs Oil, of Edward Evans, whose case was similar to my wife's. As we had for years tried everything we had heard of, she concluded to try this remedy also, and I sent to the Great Britain Branch of the prietors, The Charles A. Vogeler Co., 45, Farringdon Road, London, for a bottle of it. The Oil was first applied to her hands, which had for many years been so fearfully deformed as to be almost without shape. Before she had used the con- tents of one bottle, to our amazement and joy the swelling disappeared, and her crippled bands once more assumed their natural shape. You may well look astonished at what I say, but I am relating facts to you," remarked Mr. Halls. "She then applied the remedy to the joints of her limbs and , feet, and, marvellous it may seem, the swelling and pain which had withstood all treatment, began to disappear, and before the contents of this one bottle had been used, the swelling, stiffness, and pain with which she had been

'afflicted for nearly twenty years, vanished as if by magic. She recovered the full use of her limbs, hands, and feet. She tHn walk as well as ever she could in her life. She now at. fends to. her household duties regularly and sleeps soundly at night, while for years and years she had not known what it was to have a good night's rest. She is free from pain, and is completely cured, and all this was brought about by a single bottle of St. Jacobs Oil. I tell you frankly that I believe this remedy has no equal in the world. It has brought oomfort and happiness to my home, and I advise everyone suffering from pain to try it. The 2s. 9d. I spent for a bottle was the best investment I ever made in My life." Mrs. Halls personally confirmed everything her husband had said, and °sold scarcely say enough in praise of this re- markable agency of healing which had rescued her from her sufferings Facts like the foregoing certainly appeal most strongly to all reasonable men, and should convince everyone of the ex- traordinary efficacy of the remedy referred to.

THE STATE OF IRELAND. 1'
I disguised party attacked the members of the Doyle famitY. of Glencar, returning from:Killorglin on Saturday, and beat them unmercifully. One is not expected to recover. A horse was killed.

A girl named Doyle, aged 19 years, has died in the Lock Hospital, Dublin, from the effects of an outrage perpetrated upon her, as she alleged, by some soldiers, who aesaul.ed her in the presence of her sister. REPIZINYED.—The Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland has granted a reprieve to Thomas Crezier, who was sentenced to death at the Enniskillen Assizes for the murder ef his wife on the 2nd of January last near Newtownbutler. LOYALTY !—Major Sanderson, M.P., speaking at an Orange dinner in London, on Wednesday evening, said the Orange- men were right loyal subjwcts of the Crown, and would take up arms rather than submit to the 'terms which were being proposed.

A man named Pat Doyle, who lives at Laura Bridge, near Tralee, was attacked on Saturday night by a party of four men and severely beaten. Doyle is related to a man who suc- cessfully prosecuted a moonlight captain who was sent to penal servitude.

THE SEED FAMlNE.—Practical steps are being taken to avert the calamity of a seed famine in the West of Ireland. On Wednesday the ocean tug Seahorse was ordered to sail from Portsmouth to Queenstown, whence she will proceed along the south-west coast with reed potatoes for the suffer- ing population.

. --- A man named Lynch, a patient in Steven's Hospital, Dublin, tied a rope round his neck, fastened the end to a washhand stand, and then jumped out of the window. A convalescent patient discovered his position, and Lynch was hoisted up in an unconscious states. Faint hopes are enter- tained of his recovery. MR. TIME ON DISTRESS IN THE WEST OF IRELAND.— Mr. Tuke arrived at Clifden, county Gslway, on Monday, and after making inquiries telegraphed to Mr. Morley that most acute distress prevailed in the district. Mr. Tuke added that the best means of affording assistance would be providing work in connection with the erection of piers, &c., all along the coast.

_ SERIOUS FORGERIES.—A well-known professional athlete has been arrested for forgery and other offences. Letters were found on him purporting to be from Mr. Gladstone, Lord Salisbury, Mr. Parnell, Mr. Davitt, dia. He collected large stnas for the Curtin family. Whilst in the police lock-up he severed an artery with a piece of glass, and al- most bled to death before being discovered. He is in a very critical condition. FURTHER OUTRAGES.—Edward Spring was remanded at Milltown, county Kerry, on Monday, charged with firing into the dwelling of Darby Clifford. The police were close to the house when the shot was fired, and they saw two men whom they identified and watched. A piece of gun wad- ding was found near the house. It was a portion of the lining of a coat fitted into the place where a piece of lining had been torn out of the prisoner's coat. The second man disappeared from the district. LIBERAL CONVENTION IN IRELAND.—At a Liberal Con- vention at Belfast, attended by delegates from all parts of Ulster, resolutions were passed disapproving of coercive legislation as a remedy for social disorder in Ireland, de- claring that the conflict of interests between the owners and occupiers of land was the main cause of the disorder, dis- content, and distress that prevailed, declaring determined opposition to a separate Irish Parliament, but advocating the abolition of the Viceroyalty and tee establishment of an expensive system of local government. TERRORISM IN COUNTY GALWAY.—lntelligence from county Galway shows that at Woodford, where the bailiff Finlay was recently shot, the system of terrorism continues on the large properties of Lord Clanricarde and other land- bids. Not one tenant bus paid his rent without being im- mediately boycotted. Several other employs of the land- lords have resigned their situations to save their lives. Mr. Joyce, agent to Lord Clanricarde, drives about with a load:d gun across his knees, cars containing armed police going be- fore and after him Lord Huntingdon's bailiff has been frightened into throwing up his situation and joining the League. A MAGISTRATE'S WIFE COMMITTED rola ARSON.—The trial of Mrs. Alice Lucas for setting fire to Richfordstown House, the residence of her husband, John Lucas, magis- trate, was concluded at Cork AeSiZ9S on Saturday. Some malicious burnings having taken place on Mr. Lucas's pro- perty, protection police were stationed in the house, and they discovered the parlour on fire, all means of access from the outside being cut off at the time. The motive of the crime was allegcl to be to obtain compensation for malicious burning, thus taking advantage of the disturbed state of the country. The jury found her guilty. Judge O'Brien sentenced her to twelve months' imprison- ment.

THE Inisw CHURCH AND HOME RULE.—On Tuesday the Church of Ireland Synod met in Dublin under the presi- dency of Lord Bunker, Archbishop of Dublin, who called the meeting to express an opinion on the policy of Home Rule.—The Bislaop of Limerick moved—" That we, the bishops, clergy, and laity of the Church of Ireland assem- bled in this general synod from all parts of Ireland, repre- senting more than 600,000 of the Irisk people, consider it a duty at the present crisis to affirm our constant allegiance to the Throne and our unswerving at'achment to the legis- lative union now subsisting between Great Britain and Ireland, an we make this declaration, not as party ad- herents or for a class, but as a body of Irishmen holding various political opinion., following different callings, re- presenting many separate interests, and sharing at the same time a common desire for the honour and welfare of our native land.'—Sir FREDIC. HEYGATE, Bart., seconded the resolution.—The Bishop of Down supported the resolu- tion, viewing the prospect of Home Rule with the greatest alarm. Mr. Parnell would not be content with Home Rule, for he had said he would destroy the last link which bound Ireland to England.—The resolution was adopted.

NORWICH ELECTION PETITION.—This peiition was con- tinued on Saturday.—Edward Crane deposed to seeing a re- tired grocer named Bankara give a voter named Wigger either a florin or half-a-crown, and enjoin him to plump for "Old Harry. '—On Monday Mr. Bullard, the respondent, stated that he did not knosv anything about getting up the requisition to himself, nor that men had been paid to can- vass for signatures. A witness named Parker said aMr Kemp paid for the beer served out. PARLIAMENTARY PROCEDURE.--The Select Committee on Procedure met on Monday in private, Lord Elartingtou presiding. It was agreed that, as the committee included so many members themselves authorities on the subject, it was unnecessary to call veitneeses on the general principle of the proposed scheme. No evidence will therefore be taken unless it is found desirable to throw further light on special branches of the subject. The draft rules submitted by the Goverment were considered, and the principle of Standing Committees was approved. SIR HENRY JAMES, M.P., ON THE SITUATION.-0/1 Sat- urday night, Sir Henry James, ALP., formally opened the Cobden. Liberal Club, at Bury. In response to a vote of thanks, Sir H. James said that to his mind there never was a time when political education was more desirable or neces- sary for the safety of the commonwealth, and when more advantage could be obtained by every man who acquired that education for his own benefit. 'there was a dark sha- dow, as it seemed to him, over us. We had to meet a diffi- culty which was paralysing the action of all men desirous of progress—a difficulty which all ought by every precept of moderation to try to get to the root of. These were partly the reasons why he would avoid political discussion that night. Tali Horns or SHOPMEN.—On Monday the Select Com- mittee of the House of Commons on the Shop Hours Regulation Bill sat to take further evidence, Sir John Lub- bock presiding. A new clause, which runs as follows, has been added to the bill, namely :—" A. Every Town Council, Local Board, or ether rural or urban authority shall, upon receiving a requisition desiring the local adop- tion of compulsory early closing, and signed by two-thirds of the shopkeepers who are employers of one or more assis- tants within the district, making by-laws compelling all shops, excepting chemists' shops, coffee-houses, confec- tioners, eating-houses, fish and oyster shops, fruit and vegetable shops, restaurants, tobacconists' shops, booksel- lers' and newsagente' shops, to close at the hour specified in the requisition, provided that no shop (except those ex- empted above) shall be open after eight of the clock on five days of the week and ten (if the clock on the Bth day of the week, or on any day preceding a public holiday. B. In the excepted shops above mentioned, and in bookstalls and public-houses, no young person shall be employed for a longer period than twelve hours a day."

ENGLAND AND BURMAH. CALCUTTA, SUNDAY.—It has been decided to raise in India two levies of military police for service in Upper Bur- nish. Each levy will consist of four hundred privates, one being recruited from Punjabis and the other from Hindu- etinis. Each will be commended by a European military officer. THE EASTERN QUESTION.—THE ATTITUDE OF GREECE. CONSTANTINOPLE, SAIURDAY.—The negotiations in the Turco-Bulgarian Convention still continue. Prince Alex- ander's objection to his re-appointment every five years requiring the sanction of the Power is looked upon as quite reasonable by all the Powers with the exception ot Russia. SOFIA, SUNDAY.—In consequence of the assimilation of the Roumelian Budget with that of the Principality, many Roumelian functionaries basica been dismissed, their services being no longer required. VIENNA., SUNDAY.—An Athens telegram announces that a decree is about to be issued calling out four additional classes of reserves. Large numbers of volunteers from Thrace, Macedonia, and Reumelia are said to be joining the Greek army. ST. PETErtsBURG, MONDAY.—The Velomosti learne to- day on good authority that Russia would perhaps have no ebjections to assent to the conditions of Prince Alex- ander, but it seems to fear that the European Cabinets might think it incompatible with their dignity to give way. VrEavete, MONDAY.—The Sultan has to the present time flatly refused to appoint the Prince of Bulgaria to the Go- vernorship of Eastern:Roumelia for life. Not from England alone, but from several countries, has the advice been given to his Majesty to reconsider this decision. BERLIN. THURSDAT.—AII the Powers exeept Russia have accepted the Italian amendment to the Turco-Bulgarian agreement, to the effect that the governor generalship of Eastern Roumelia be vested indefinitely in the Prince go- verning Routnelia for the time being. EGYPT. CAIRO, MONDAY.—There is not the slightest doubt of in- structions having been received regarding the withdrawal of the frontier troops and the immediate retirement from Egypt of four regiments. The civil and military authorities refuse, however, to giye any information on the subject. THE GERMAN EMPEROR. BERLIN, MONDAY.—The eighty-ninth anniversary of the Emperor William's birth was celebrated here to-day amid general rejoicing. His Majesty, who looked in excellent health, appeared repeatedly at hisivinciow, and was greeted with the utmost enthusiasm by the vast crowds assembled in front of the palace. During the day the Emperor re- ceived messages of coni,Pratulation from all foreigu Sover- eigns, including the Pope besides several thousands of telegrams from all parts of Germany and all foreign coun- tries. His Majesty attended a banquet given by the Crown Prince this afternoon, and this evening was present at a grand soiree in the White Hall of the Imperial Palace. The city has been gaily decorated all day, and to-night is brilliantly illuminated in honour of the occasion. THE SOCIALISTS IN GERMANY AND BELGIUM. BERLIN, SATURDAY.—After the police had dispersed a numeronsly-attanded meeting of Social Democrats last night in the Andreas Plate, at which Herr Bebe', the Social- ist deputy, spoke, a large crowd of people assembled in the aquare, and were only dispersed with difficulty. The police, however, did not use their swords. Seven arrests were made. BRUSSEVs SIINDAY.—N serious disturbance broke out last night at Jemappe, in the province of Namur. An en- counter occurred between some workmen and the gendarme- rie, in which several a the latter were injured. Ten arrests were made. LIEGE, WEDNESDAY, 1 P.M.—A general strike has broken out at Gerard, Cloes, and Lebaneux. At this moment there are between 1,000 and 2,000 strikers at the entrance to the town, all work being stopped at the Sainte Marguerite, Lahaye, and Esperanc pits. AMERICA. . PIIILADELPHIA, SUNDAY.—The Canadian Government has begun to enforce its policy of Protection for the fisher- ies of the Dominion. The steamer Lansdoeme has left St. John. Her captain has issued a nroclamation warning. Americans to observe the treaty of 1818, and forbidding in- shore fishing. NEw YORK, MONDAY.—AII the pointsmen on the railway at Kansas city have struck work, and freight traffic is con- sequently stopped. Tne Wabash Railway has applied to the United States Marshal for protection. A strike has com- menced among the coalminers in Western Pennsylvania. The men who have joined the movement number four thousand.

soura AFRICA. DURBAN, SIINDAY.--AII outrage which has been commit- ted by Basutos on the sons of some border fr.le state farmers, who were flogged by Basuto thieves for protecting their father's stock, may lead to complications. The Bloemfon- tein press demands that the English Government should control its Basuto subjects. DuRBAs, Morway.—Sir A. Havelock has stated publicly that the Government are coming to some arrangement which
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MoNnAv. The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after 4-0. TRINITY COLLEGE, Dtteme.—Lord LEITRIM moved for a Select Committee to inquire into and report upon the tea- ure of lands under Trinity College and the Provost in its corporate capacity.—Lerd ASHEURNE contended that no case had been made out for such an inquiry.—Lord Fitz- gerald, Lord Bramwell, and the Lord Chancellor made some observations and the motion was withdrawn. JUSTICES' aJuatspiariort.—The Justices' Jurisdiction Bill passed through Committee. Twe LAW OF EVIDENCE. -- Their Lordships went intol Committee on the Law of Evidence Amendment Bill, the object of which is to enable a person charged with a crime to give evidence. The Bill then passed through com- mittee. • Their Lordships adjourned at 7-40. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. THE ARMY IN EGYPT.—Mr. CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN in- formed Mr. W. H. Smith that it was the intention of ker Majesty's Goverment gradually and with due regard to local circumstances to withdraw her Majesty's troops to Assouan, and the frontier at Wady Haifa would be held by Egyptian troops. The number of our forces in Egypt according to the latest report was 17,108 officers and men. THE LoNDOII AND NORTH-WESTERN COMPANY'S Ear- \ PLOYEES.—Mr. Sgrore KARR asked Mr. Mundella whether he was aware that a few days ago 36,000 employes of the London and North-Western Railway Company met in Lon- don to consider their position in tegard to the proposed amendment of the Employers' Liability Act, and that they unanimously resolved to petition Parliament to have their case specially considered, being as they thought better protected by the present insurance society than they would be under the Act; and that their agreement to contract themeelves out of the Act was an entirely voluntary arrangement between themselves and the company, and had • resulted far more beneficially for the employs than if they 1 had not done so, the compensation paid in respect of claims I for accidents being relatively far greater, and compensation ' having frequently been paid for accidents in respect to which they would be unable to claim under the Act.—Mr. MUNDELLA said he believed the statement was correct, and' that the allegation that the men had signed the agreement, under compulsion was not in accordance with the fact. As the bill in question bad been referred to a Select Com- mittee, before which the men could be heard, he did not propose to take any further notice of the matter. BencorreNG.—Mr. DE COBAIN asked the Prime Minister whether his ateention had been drawn to the communica- tions addressed to the Record by 460 of the beneficed clergy ! of the Irish Church in Munster, Leinster, and Connaught ; showing that there were 314 cases of boycotting.—Mr. 1 GLADSTONE said if there were any cases not known to the! police he should be happy to make them special subjects of inquiry. There was a serious amount of pressure on indi- viduals through the system known as boycotting in Ireland. ' In November there were 800 or 900 cases, and since that', time there had been no increase in the number of those ' cases. THE VOLUNTEER CAPITATION Geerer.—On going into Supply OR the Army Estimates, Mr. H. VINCENT drew at- tention to the growing requirements of the Volunteer force, and, in an interesting review of the history of the force, showed how its cost bad gone on gradually increasing, and how the officers, out of whose pockets this cost had in a great measure been borne, were getting wearied, and were no longer willing to come forward with the same liberality. Taking a hundred corps at random, he found that they spent £28,000 on headquarters, £14,500 on ranges, £53,000 on uniforms, £9,000 on salaries and incidental expenses. and £34,000 on camp and training expenses. Out of the total of these expenses' he found thet the absolutely neces- sary expense incurred by these 100 corps was no less than £32,000 in excess of the Government grant. An additional grant of lOs per head, amounting to about £lOO,OOO, was urgently needed, and he moved a resolution which was seconded by Mr. GURDON, who spoke on behalf of the coun- try corps, setting out that for the thorough efficiency, maintenance, and development of the Volunteer force an immediate increase of the capitation grant was absolutely and urgently necessary.—Mr. ISAACS maintained that the present capitation grant was totally inadequate to secure efficiency; and Colonel Seees-Scetweese, although strongly opposed to any unnecessary increase in the Army Estimates, protested against the expense of maintaining the Volunteers falling upon the officers of the force.—Mr. GLADSTONE energetically condemned the unconstitutional character of a proposal to increase the charges upon the people beyond the amount asked for by the Executive. It was the duty of Parliament to accept or reject or to alter those proposals, but the Constitution did not permit Parliament to increase the stems that were asked by the Executive Government for the Shafence of the country. At the same time the Secretary for War would fulfil his promise to consider the matter care- fully. If the resolution were carried it would make no dif- ference.—Sir M. Nem-BEACH expressed surprise at the uncalled-for speech of the Primo Minister, and, while ad- mitting the general accuracy of tlee constitutional doctrine he had propounded, insisted that any member of the Honee was entitled to call attention to a grievance, which was all that the motion aimed at.—The CHANCELLOR of the Ex- cemertesn, referring to the wording of the resolution, con- tended that it was in reality a vote for an increased sum on that proposed.—Sir H. HAVELOCK-ALLAN suggested an alter- ation in the wording of the resolution, which, however, Mr. VINCENT refused to accept, and, on a division, it was nega- tived by 187 to 166.—The announcement of the num- bers was received witk much cheering from the Opposition benches. EGYPT: COAST DEFENCE, &C.—Sir GEORGE CAMPBELL next called attention to the cost of the army in Egypt, which he thought ought not to be borne by the British taxpayer, but should be a first charge on the Egyptian Revenues.--Mr. Deteoer, on the other hand, opposed this proposal, and in- sisted that the entire cost of the occupation of Egypt, in- cluding the cost of all English officials engaged in the Civil Administration of the country, should be defrayed out of the English Exchequer.—Sir R. N. FOWLER objected to withdrawing the British troops from Egypt; and Mr. BRYCE pointed out that it would be impossible to throw upon Egypt the whole cost of the defence of that country. It was, ha said, intended to reduce the expenditure, and there was every reason to believe that the resources of Egypt were improv- ing --Among other subjects mentioned were the position , of Militia staff sergeants, introduced by Colonel WARING ; I the insufficiency of the soldier's rations, by Dr. FARQUHAR- I SON ; the arming of the Voluntary Artillery, by Mr. MARK STEWART ; and compulsory retirement by Colonel Duieceer. —Mr. CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN made a comprehensive and general reply; and Sir M. Hicees-Beecir, in regard to the coaling stations, while he admitted that things were better than he expected, regretted that the Government bad not gene further with the plans of their predecessors—Lord HARTINGTON admitted that any Government which dallied with a subject of this kind incurred great responi- bility, though there was some excuse in the present uncer- tain state of our guns. THE ARMY ESTIMATES. The House went into Committee of' Supply at 12-10, and upon the vote for 151.867 land forces of all ranks, Mr. CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN made the usual statement explana- tory of the Army Estimates. The total sum asked is £18,933,000, of which £15,156,000 is for effective service, being an increase of £440,000 for effective and £385,000 for non-effective, and the increase was due chiefly to India and Egypt. These Estimates, he said, reckoned that the British forces in Egypt would be reduced in the course of the year to 8,000, but it was impossible to say at present how this could be effected. On the other hand, the Increase ef the Indian establishment would be 10,000, for each battalion of infantry was to be increased by 100 men, three battalions were to be added to the army of India, and two troops were to be added to each cavalry regiment. With regard to or- ganisation, he regretted that the necessitles of our Egyptian operations were answerable for great derabge- tnents. Passing to the details of the votes, he explained and justified at length the considerable increases which had occurred in several of the chief items, drawing attention, among others, to the increase of £lO,OOO for horses, of £50,000 for the auxiliary forces, £38,500 for the army reserve, and £361,200 for the stores vote. Egypt, he said, was responsible for £474,000. The net increase was £lB2,soo—there being £500,000 on account of the Bechuana- laud expedition to deduct £120,000 in consequence of reduc- tion in contract prices for supplies, and £200,000 in conse- quence of Indian contribution. The number of recruits during last year was 39,971, far exceeding the number in any recent year. These were the men actually passed into the service, and even more surprising was the number of 1 men who offered themselves—namely, 09,401, or more than 23 per cent. in excess of the number which offered them- selves five years ago. No doubt the depression in trade went for to account for these large figures The results of localisation were most satisfactory, inasmuch as the army had been brouaht into closer connection with the auxiliary forces. The report showed that the quality of the recruits was on the whole satisfactory. The deserters were only 2,975. There was an increase in the yeomanry vote, due entirely to increased efficiency. The Martini-Henry carbine would be issued this week to the yeomanry. (Hear, hear.) With regard to the volunteers, the reports showed a steady improvement in almost every respect. The vote was in- creased by £18,500 this year, due to the capitation earned, as there were 10,000 more efficients. The army reserve was estimated to number 51,000 men, showing a steady but not

a rapid increase. The amount asked for storee was £2,569,000, a net increase of £341,200 over the amount taken In last year's estimate, although last year exceeded that of the previous year by £965,300. We had been slower than rother countries to adopt new types of guns, aad we might flatter ourselves that we had benefited by the improvements lof others, but the result was that the expenditure fell upon las ranter heavily at the present time. The vote was agreed to, and also a vote of £4,457,300 for pay and allowances. Progress was then reported. MISCELLANEOUS.—In Committee of Ways and Means, a lsum of £4,457,000 was granted out of the Consolidated. 'Fund towards the service of the year.—The Consolidated Fund (No. 2 Bill) and the Drill Grounds Bill were read a: seoond time.—Mr. DUCSEIAM brought in a bill to amend the law relating to Highways. 4i;• ' The House adjourned at 1-10. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TVESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4-15. IntoTs.—The Lord Chancellor laid on the table a bill for facilitating the care, education, and traiaing of imbeciles and idiots.—The bill was read a first t me. DISUSED CHURCH BURIAL GrROUNDS.—The Earl of MIL- Eowat moved the second reading of the Union Benefices Bill.—The Bishop of LONDON moved that the bill should be read a second time that day six months. If the air sure were passed. it would amount practically to a repeat of the Union of Benefices Act ef 1860, and would arrest the beneficial work carried out under that Act.—The Earl of Powts and the Archbishop of CANTERBURY opposed the bill.—The amendment was agreed to, and the bill was re- jected. INDIAN TIorkTION.—LOWFITSGERALD moved for a re- turn of the taxes and duties raised of levied en the adminis- tration of justice in India by the stamp which it is neces- sary to affix to the documents used in legal procedur..—The Earl of KIMBERLEY said the return asked for would involve great expense, and the information desired was in substance contained in papers already on the table. He therefore trusted that the motion would net be pressed.—lhe motion was withdrawn. MODE AND MILITARY.—Lord DE Ros called attention to the uncertainty which exists as to what is expected of the military during mob riots in the metropolis.—Lard GRAN- VILLE said that no precise rules of law could be laid down as to when soldiers might or might not act against a mob, or interfere to suppress riot.—The Lord CHANCELLOR said that the military would not be justified in using deadly weapon?in attacking and dispersing an ordinary tumultuous assembly which was not engaged in committing a felony or felonies before the Rie,t Act was read. When the Riot Act was read, it became a felony on the part of those composing the mob not to disperse, and then the military were jua`ified in acting.—Tbe subject then drepped. The House adjourned at 7-35. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TrESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QUESTIONS.—ht reply to Mr. Mackintosh, Mr. TR ETELYIN said an officer of the Board of Supervision was at the mo- ment in Skye making inquiries into the distress there, and upon receipt of his report the right hon, gentleman would consider what should be done.—ln reply to Mr. T. M. Healy, Mr. MORLEY said as to the admission of solicitors of candidates at the scrutiny of votes at the pending poor law elections, so many difficulties had to be considered that he mast reserve the question for personal considera- tion. LOCAL TAXATION.—Mr. THOROLD R9GERS brought for- ward a motion on the incidence of local taxation, which he proposed to apportion between owners and occupiers. The motion also affirmed that the system of rating country mansions is unfair, and raised anew the question of the tax- ation of ground rents.—Sir R. PAGET moved an amend- ment, which admitted that the apportionment of rates be- tween landlerd and tenant might be desirable, but expressed the opinion that grievances could only be removed by a comprehensive measure. The amendment further affirmed that an equitable readjustment of taxation as between real and personal property is urgently rcquired.—Several speakers in the debate, including Mr. Atherley Jones, son of the late Ernest Jones, of Chartist fame, made a promis- ing first appearance. The discussion revealed a curious bal- ancing of opinion between motion and amendment in the minds of hon. members. After the dinner hour. the House rapidly filled to hear Mr. Chamberlain's reply on behalf of ; the Government. The right hon. gentleman said he spoke , in some difficulty, as being under the necessity of avoid- ing any anticipation of plans which would have to be ex- plained " when a bill is introduced hereafter by the Govern- ! ment." Meanwhile he was in the exceptional position of •being in complete agreement with everybody. He agreed with the resolution ; he agreed generally with the amend- ment, and the House seemed to be for once on this subject of local taxation a happy family. While objecting to the assessment of palaces like Blenheim on their orginal cost, he suggested that the rating value should be four per I cent. on the selling value. Fresh official experience had linduced him to abandon his former opinion that a portion of the income-tax might be reserved to local authorities, but , he did not see why some other tax which distinctly brought personal property under contribution might not be available ;in aid of local taxation. He suggested the withdrawal of ; both motion and amendment. Division being taken, how- ever, the amendment was negatived by 205 to 186.—There- upon Sir M. RICKS-BEACH complained that Mr. Chamber- lain, after speaking in favour of the amendment had voted ; for the motion, but the President of the Local Government ; Zoard maintained that his position had been that of Captain ; Macheath. He could have been happy with either, and ; should have voted for both had it been possible.—ln the heat engendered by this misunderstanding a second division ; was taken on the motion, and it was adopted by the in- creased majority of 216 to 176. THE ORDNANCE DEPARTMENT.—Mr. CARITUTT, rising shortly before midnight. called attention to the administra- tion of the Ordnance Department, and moved that a Cern- mittee be appointed to inquire into the whole question of ; guns and the working of the factories at Woolwich, Enfield, and Birmingham.—Mr. RUSTON seconded the motion.—Mr. • CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN deprecated an inquiry into the question of the guns, and the motion was withdrawn. The House adjourned at 10 minutes past 1 o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Weeexasmat.
