kea- 1

The Speaker took the chair at half-past twelve o'clock. Amendments to the Liverpool United Gas Bill, proposed by the promoters, were considered and agreed to. Tema^ RENT Cum:tem.—Mr. Nos Toes moved the second reading of a bill to abolish extraordinary tithe rent charge in the hop and fruit growing districts of Kent and Sussex, and to substitute a fixed rent charge payable by the owner instead of the occapier.—The motion having been seconded by Mr. Knatchbull-Hugessen, it was proposed by Mr. T. He BOLTON that the bill should be sent to a Select Committee, and Mr. CHILDERS thought the plan so suggested a good' one.—Tbe bill was then read a second time, and was refer- red to a committee.—Two other bills dealing with tithe rent charges were also referred. SUNDAY CLOSING.—The second reading of the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sunday (Durham) Bill was moved by Mr. THEODORE FRY, who stated that of the 16 members representing the county of Durham 15 were in favour of the measure.—Mr. Muslim moved the rejection of the bill, believing that it would not attain the object its promo- ters had in view.—Mr. JOHN WILSON reminded the House that the 150 miners' delegates who every half-year held a political gathering had several times expressed themselves unanimously in support of closing public-houses on Sun- days, and the majority of the men were in favour of Sunday closing.—Mr. CHILDERS stated that he should vote for the second reading. -- Bic RICHARD CROSS re- marked that it bad been the intent ion of the late Government to produce a measure dealing with local government, send Lord Salisbury had stated that he should have been perfectly willing to leave the question of Sunday closieg to the lecal autho- rities. If the Government meant to bring in a comprehen- sive measure of local option it would be well to wait for it. He preferred the measure proposed by Sir J. Pease to the present bill. He suggested that if the bill became law next year the Durham publicans sheuld be required to take out six-day licenses, and that this Tear the differeece between seven and six dart in the licenses should be repaid to the holders.—The second reading of the bill was carried by 169 to 82. DROWNED PERSONS BILL.—Mr. HUGHES moved the second reading of this bill, which provided that where drowned persons were buried by the parish the cost should be recover- able from the county. He reminded the House that the parish of Woolwich incurred an expenditure of £1,20) in the recovery and interment of the bodies of nersons who lost their lives when the Princess Alice steamer was run down on the Thames.—Mr. CHILDERS thought the principle of the bill was a sound one so far as regarded bodies found in navigable rivers.—The motion for the second reading was agreed to. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Lunacy (Vacating of Seats) Bill was read a third time.—The Consolidated Fund (No. 2) Bill was considered and ordered for third reading. The House adjourned at ten minutes past five. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TRUILSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly , after four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Consolidated Fund (No. 11 Bill and the Vacating of Seats (Lunacy) Bill were brought in. and read a first time.—Lord DENMAN called attention to the two majorities of the House for opening museums in the evenings of weekdays and for opening them in the after- noons of Sundays. He moved a resolution in favour of opening by daylight only and closing before dark, and dar- ing tie time of afternoon divine service on Sundays —The resolution was negatived without diecussion. Their Lordships adjourned at twenty minntes to .five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TEMRSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. BARROW ELECTION.—In the House of Commons the SPEASEER reported that he had received an intimation that Mr. Duncan had not been duly elected for Barrow be- cause of corrupt practices, but that no corrupt prac- tices had been committed by or with the consent of the candidate. THE OREGON.—Mr. MIINDELLA., in the course of a state- ment on the capacity and equipment of the Oregon, in- formed the House that the steamer had on board 878 persons, and had only boat accommodation for 365. The vessel had boat accommodation largely in excess of the statutory requirements. LORD R. CHURCHILL'S " ACCURACY."—Lord W. COMP- TON put a further question respecting the Treasury minute stated by Lord R. Churchill, in a speech at Manchester, to have been issued by Mr. Cl:tilde's to the detriment of British trade, and also respecting the special instructions which, Lord Randolph added, had been sent to her Majesty's agents aborad with a view to the encouragement of British corn- merce.—Mr. BRYCE replied that he could now positively

state that no such Treasury minute or special instructions as those referred to existed. Ma. GrADSTOKE'S ,STATEMENT.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER stated that on Thursday, the Sth ef April, Mr. Gladstone proposed to bring forward the subject of Irish policy, and that the Budget statement would be made in the first fortnight in April. THE AIME Esvraravns.—ln Committee-of Supply on the ..ay Estimates Colonel TOTTENHAM maintained that more men were neceisary in order to relax the strain put upon the army by the extra requirements of Egypt and Burmah. —Mr. MiGNIAC cemplained that the workpeople in the army clothing department were paid starvation wages.—Mr._ W. H. SMITH urged that it was the duty of the Govern- ment to take advantage ef the state of the labour markets and to put labourers upon the work of bringing up the stores to the proper amount. He also drew attention to the slot, progress which was being made with the new rifle.—Colonel SCHWABE called attention to some points °which economy might he obtained, and, referring to cavalry swords, he mentioned that when he was command- ing the 16th Lancers he objected to the swords.— Lord R. CEttratenthr, asked for an assurance that tha pro-; pescd addition of 10,000 men -to the British troops in India should not be an illusory increase.—Mr. CAMPBELL-BAN- KERMAN at ence gave an assurance that the Government had no desire to do otherwise than maintain the full estab- lishment of the forces in India.—Sir H. HAVELOCK-ALLAN thought the estimates afforded a prospect of the realisation of those improvements Which military reforms had so often', pressed on seccessive Governments, and he congratulated the country on the excellent results which had attended the I introduction of the short-service system.—Sir G. CAMP- BELL urged that the Government should either withdrow the British troops from Egypt or should put the coat of their maintenance upon the Egyptian Treasury. He moved the reduction of the vote by £17,900, half the amount for the clothing of the troops in Egypt.—The motion was re- jected by 290 to 66, and progress was reported.

COUMERCE.

A special meeting of this chamber was held in Bewsey Chambers, on Wednesday afternoon. There were present—Messrs. J. Fairclough (in the chair), R. Garnett, T. Jolley, W. Tinsley, and Taylor; Alder- man Davies and J. L. Tunstall (hon. secs).

EMPLOYEES' LIABILITY. It was stated that a copy of the Employers' Lia- bility Act, 1880, Amendment Bill, had been forwarded to the Chamber.—Alderman DAVIES said it was in- tended to set aside the opportunity that existed at present for anyone to contract themselves out of the Act of Parliainent.—Mr. JOLLEY thought it would be unwise to take action in that direction. He was of opinion people ought to have the right of freedom of contract.—Alderman DAVIES considered it was a very serious thing indeed for employers of labour.—Mr. TINiLEY was of the same opinion as Mr. JOLLEY. It was then resolved on the motion of Mr. JOLLEY, seconded by Mr. TINSLEY, that a memorial from that chamber be presented against the proposed legislation, and that it be sent through the borough member, Sir G. Greenall. RAILWAY AND CANAL TRAFFIC BILL. With regard to this bill the following communica- tion was read from the Railway and Canal Traders' Association, viz :—Sir,—l am directed to draw your attention to the annexed resolutions and invite the attendance of your chamber at a conference to be held at the Cannon-street Hotel, London, on Mon- day, 29th March, at 2 p.m., for the purpose of con- sidering and determining the action. which should be taken with reference to the above-mentioned bill. In view of the great importance of this bill to trade and agriculture, it is necessary that the confer- ence should be numerously and influentially atten- ded, and I shall be glad to know as soon as possible how many representatives of your chatn- ber will attend.—' am, yours obediently, EDWIN CLEMENTE, sec.—The resolutions adopted by the Council of the Railway and Canal Traders' Assoeia- , tion at a special meeting held on the 15t March, to I consider the bill, were as follows :—(1) That in the opinion of this Council the mode of constitution of the existing Railway Commission should not be al- tered. (2) That no second appeal from the decision of the Railway Commissioners should be allowed. (3) That as sub-section 2, section 25, practically repeals Lord Cardwell's Act of 1854, and legalises preferen- tial rates in favour of foreign manufacturers and farmers, it ought to be strenuously opposed. (4) That the Railway Commissioners should have power to • classify any articles that are not enumerated in any Act of the railway company, and that this proposal I offers a more satisfactory solution than the proposals ' in the bill for an entirely new classification Of goods and maximum rates to be sanctioned by the Board of Trade. (5) That the provisions of the bill in regard to canals are altogether indequate and unsatisfactory. (6) That a Conference of Traders and Representatives t of Chambers of Trade, Commeroe and Agriculture, and Municipal Corporations be called to meet at the Can- non-street Hotel at two p.m. on Monday, the 29th inst., for the purpose of considering and determining the action which should be taken with reference to , Mr. Mundella's Bill.—lt was agreed on the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Alderman Davis, that the chairman and vice-chairman and such members of the Chamber as could make it convenient should at- tend the Conference and support the resolutions ad- opted by the Railway and Canals Association.

_ 81-ILETALLIM. A circular was read from the Bi-Metallic League asking the Chamber to petition for a Royal Commis- sion to inquire into the question of bi-metallism.—Mr. JOLLEY did not think much good would be done by a Royal Commission. They all knew that there was a depreciation of silver, but he did not see how they could increase its value unless they made it legal tender. They could not increase the value of a metal as a metal. It was, in fact, one of those things that demand and supply must be left to regulate.—Mr. GARNE.Tr pointed out that it was only desired that an inquiry should be held to see if there was anything to justify further action.—Mr. TAYLOR referred to the injury that was being done to commerce with India by the depreciation of silver, and spoke in favour of a petition being sent as requested.—lt was agreed that a petition in favour of inquiry should be sent from that Chamber. A communication having reference to Fair Trade was laid on the lable, after which the meeting ter- minated.

Chemisfs.—A.dvt. RIEL'S REBELLION —A vote of censure, brought forward against the Government in the Dominion House of Com- mons on account of Riel's execution, has been rejected by a majority of 94. The French Ambassador paid a neat compliment, a little while back, to a Washington lady who had been talking to him for an hour. The lady said, "You must think lam fond of the sound of my own voice." The Frenchmm replied, "I knew you liked music." ATTEMPTED tirICIDE.—On Thursday morning John Wil- liam Stanley, aged 25, was removed to the Oldham Infir- mary suffering from a wound three inches long in his throat. It appears he has been out of work since Christ- mas, and was consequently in a state of desperation. He cut his throat on Thursday morning, and then informed a constable, who took him to the infirmary. FATAL BOAT ACCIDENT.—The screw steamer )Ung Moor, of Newcastle, has arrived at Shields from Ostend, and while engaged mooring, a boat containing two men was capsized. One was saved with difficulty, but the other, namsd Arthur Bettinson, was drowned. He was aged 22, and was a sea- man belonging to Boston. div.head: -VACANCY IN THE ALTRINCHA.III
div.p: THE -VACANCY IN THE ALTRINCHA.III

DIVISION. __AL AND CONSERVATIVE MEETINGS. The two candidates for the seat in Parliament ren- dered vacant by tke death of Mr. John Brooks, the first member for the AlLl.trincham Division of Cheshire —Mr. I. S. Leadam in the Liberal, and Sir W. Can- life Brooks in the Conservative, interest—have thik week actively prosecuted the campaign, and have ade, dressed meetings in different parts of the division. Summarised accounts of the meetings are appended. , OONSERVATIrE MEETING AT TIM:WALL. A meeting in support of Sir W. C. Brooks was held in the Temperance Hall, at Thelwall, on Saturday evening. Mr. R. A. Naylor (Thelwall) presided, and in his opening re-- marks drew a gloomy picture of the condition of the coun- try—a dark cloud, he said, was gathering over the nation, and it was one to which there was not much sign of a silver lining. The commercial interests of the nation were much depressed, and, under the present coadition of things, there was not the slightest prospect of a revival. Commercial men of to-day had a gloomy future to face, and unless some unforeseen piece of good fortune took place, they as a com- mercial community would go down the "Hill of Destruc- tion." The present proposals before the country were of a most revolutionary character; the integrity of the Empire was threttened, and they were told that there would be piecemeal sep,aratien. Disunity would bring no satisfaction, but, on the contrary, the way to make an empire truly great and prosperous was by maintaining its integrity. What the electors must do was to send men to Parliament whe had a stake In the country's interests, and for that reason he asked their support for Sir W. C. Brooks.—A resolution support- ing that gentleman's candidature was proposed by Mr. John Marsh, and supported by Mr. James Croston (Manchester), who described Mr. Leadam as a "carpet-bagger" fighting the contest in the intensts of the Reform Club and the Bir- mingham Cancue, and not those of the country, and extolled Mr. Brooks ac a man of experience, who had been many years in the House of Commons and before the public, and whose intereets were identical with their own.—Mr. W. J. Burgess (Warrington) also supported the resolution, which was carried. MR. LEADLM AT HAZEL GROVE. Mr. I. S. Leadam addressed a meeting on Saturday even- ing at Hazel Grove, when Mr. Joseph Leigh presided, and Mr.tLeadam again spoke on the Irish question. It was quite clear to him, though they might not all agree with him, that if we were to make concessions to Ireland in the direc- tion of Hoine Rule it was our duty, considering the history of the relations of the two countries, to make some provi- sion, should it be necessary, for the security of our Irish landlords. (Applause-) In conclusion, Mr. Leadam said one thing they desired was a thorough improvement, so far as law could secure it, in the condition of the working classes. The present Parliament was a people's Parliament, and one in which such questions as affected the daily life of the people would be brought up for consideration. In the view of the Liberal party no society was really safe, and no conditions of social life likely to be permanent, un- less earnest efforts were made to raise the condition of the labouring classes. (Applause.) The true happiness of the nation was to be sought in the improvement of the cottage home and in furthering as beet they could the prosperity of the great mass of the people. (Applause.)—On the motion of Mr. S. Penny, seconded by Mr. W. Blakeley. a resolu- tion of confidence in Mr. Leadam was passed with much enthusiasm.
J LIBER

SIR W. C. BROOKS AT BOWDON. On Saturday evening, the Conservative candidate, who Ives supported by Mr. W. IL Houldsworth, MP., addressed a meeting at Bowdon, when a resolution approving his candidature was passed. In his address the candidate ex- pressed himself vehemently opposed to any proposition that the landlords of Ireland should be bought out. Referring to the existing distress, he urged that it 'was all owing to the fact that Free Trade was adopted by this country before guarantees had been obtained from other nations that they would follow the same course. Now that the folly of keep- ing on in this course was seen we ought to have no more Fret Trade, but ought at once to protect certain industries. He would get a tax on articles of luxury, but he would not tax raw material. He would protect all those articles in the cost of which labour was the chief component part. (Applause.) It would be a crime to put a tax upon the food of the people, and he would never support any such pre- posal.—Mr. Houldsvorth, M.P., did not know what claim Mr. Gladstone had upon either the Liberal party or the country. It appeared to him that during the last 20 years Mr. Gladstone bad been an instrument in the hands of Pro- vidence to break up the Liberal party.

MR. LEADAII AT CHEADLE. On Monday evening Mr. Leaden), addressing a crowded meeting at Cheadle, said it must not Be forgotten that the Irish proposals of Mr. Gladstone had not been made known. Mr. Gladstone had been a servant of the Queen for helf a century, and it was not to be supposed that, with a record of that kind, he was going suddenly to become a traitor to his country. It was also to be recollected that there never Was a time when Mr. Gladstone had propounded a financial scheme which was to the injury of the British taxpayer. (Cheers.) With regard to the question of fair trade or pro- tection, he Noticed that his opponent, Sir W. C. Brooks, would protect everybody except two classes. He would not protect the farmer, for he would net put a duty on corn, nor would he de anything for the agricultural labourer, so that the farmers and labourers would get very cold comfort in- deed from the proposals of kis opponent. Sir W. C. Brooks said that protection would make things dearer, and that he did not think cheapness was the idol which they were to bow down and worship. That was a very comfortable doc- trine indeed for a wealthy man. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) So far as the farmers and labourers were concerned, his opponent proposed that they should pay more for their clothing and implements and get nothing in return. Pro- tection would utterly destroy several of our industries. Protection, in fact, was a species of communism, and a tax- ing of the poor for the benefit of the rich. Having referred to the questions of local government and technical educa- tion, Mr. Leadam said the Tory programme at present ap- peared to be contained in the words "No surrender." It was a hopeful circumstance, however, that, with the Tory party, that cry always preceded capitulation.—A resolution pledging the meeting to support Mr. Leadam having been carried, Sir H. E. Roscoe. M.P., also addressed th<, meet- ing, contrasting Tory with Liberal legislation. There was no country in the world, he said, where the condition of the working-man was so favourable as in Great Britain. ?or that he had to thank the Liberal party. (Cheers.) In going abroad and seeing the condition of things in protected countries he had come to the conclusion that protection did not only make the poor man poorer, but it did net even suc- ceed in making the rich man richer. The country must stick to the principles of free trade, which would in the long run bring about the greatest happiness of the greatest number. Sir H. Roscoe pointed to the advantages which our foreign competitors enjoyed in the matter of education, especially technical, and urged that in that particular, which was so essential to our future progress, we might very well take a leaf out of the foreigner's book.—Sir J. C. Lee also addressed the meeting, which concluded with a vote of thanks to the chairman. Sin W. C. BROOKS AT SALE. The Conservative candidate, who was supported by Sir R. Cross, M.P., and the Hon. Alan de Teton Egerton, M.P., ad- dressed a meeting of his supporters at Sale Public Hall on Monday evening, and, asked whether it was true that he had voted six times against Mr. Trevelyan's annual motion for the extension of the county franchise, and that he bad voted twice against Mr. Gladstone's Franchise Bill, he ad- mitted that it was so, and said he did so in accordance with Mr. Bright's advice to repudiate all proposals to extend the franchise until redistribution was obtained.—Sir R. A. Cross, who afterwards spoke, said that Mr. Gladstone, who so assiduously advocated the unity of the Liberal patty while the election Was in progress, had utterly, entirely, and for ever shattered that Liberal party to pieces. There never was an act of such mad folly as the making of the proposals which it was believed Mr. Gladstone was about to Mile. The eyes of the country and of the woad were no doubt very largely set on Mr. Gladstone, but there was one man on whom, he thought, their eyes ought tee be fixed with more keenness and determination than on Mr. Gladstone, and that was Lord Hartington. (Cheers.) If Lord liar- tington would put his foot down and say he would not al- low the old Liberal 'Arty to be a party to a scheme such as that Mr. Gladstone proposed, and say that he would oppose it, and if necessary drive Mr. Gladstone out of office to save the Empire, he would play the part of an Englishman and deserve the thanks of the country. LIBERAL MEETING AT LYMIL.

A meeting In support of Mr. Leadam's candidature was held at Lynam on Monday evening, when Mr. Miluer occu- pied the chair. A resolution pledging the meeting to sup- port Mr. Leadarn was carried. A speech was delive-ed by Mr. C. M. Percy, who upheld the policy of Mr. Glad- stone in regard to Ireland. He could not believe that a statesman who had done so much for the United Kingdom, and for Ireland in particular, would, at tha close of his career perhaps, do anything that loyal Liberals could not support. (Applause.) CONSERVITIVIC MEETING AT OUGHTEINGTON.

On Monday evening, a meeting in support of the Con- servative candidate was held at Oughtringten, when Mr. Leigh presided, and a resolution approving the candidature was carried, on the motion of Mr. J. D. Andrews, seconded by Mr. Joseph Smith. Mr. N. C. Schou (Manchester), in a lengthy address, supported the resolution. He said that by a policy of alternate concessions and violence Mr. Glad- stone hal himself done much to bring about the Irish troubles. Votes of thanks concluded the proceedings. MEETING AT GITLEY.-SPEECII BY MR. ARCH, MP. A crowded meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. Leadam was held on Tuesday evening in the Congregational schools, Gatley, near Cheadle.—Mr. Jos. ARC'!, M.P., was the principal speaker, and in commencing his remarks invited the audience to institute a contrast between the Irish policy of the late Government and that of Mr. Gladstone. Efforts had been made for a long time to govern Ireland by force. We ought now to try to govern that country on the prin- ciples of justice and humanity. How would Englishmen like to be governed on the lines of a repressive policy like that which had obtained in Ireland? The trade unionists of England had formerly to suffer severely because they were determined to combine. At that time there were out- rages, bet when Parliament legalised the unions of work- men then outrages ceased. In the same way. when Ireland felt that she was being ruled by the hand of justice instead of by the hand of terror outrages in that country would cease and we should have the people boned to us by the strongest of ties—not those of fear, hut of affection. Just now the Conservatives were trying to scare the English people by wild rumours. Many of the English landlords were good Conservatives, and were, perhaps, none the worse landlords for that. They were to be admired in many res-

div.head: pects, but their politics were hopelessly wrong. At the recent general election Conservative principles were discredited . _ _ . _
div.p: pects, but their politics were hopelessly wrong. At the re- cent general election Conservative principles were discredited . _ _ . _
—end they would be still more discredited in the future. Trade was depressed at the present time, labourers were lack.

ing employment, farmers were unable to make a profit, and landlord!) said they could not get their rents. That was r ' very sad picture. To change it he would urge, in the name ef everything that was honest, and for the sake of the wel- fare of the country, that the vested and feudal interests which interfered with the proper cultivation of the soil should be swept away. (Cheers.) At the present moment there were fifteen million acres in this eountry waiting cul- tivation. For the sake of ourselves and posterity it was desirable that land should be made of some use to the nation. , If justice were done, if every cultivator could feel perfectly ' secure 00 the soil he tilled, then ,he believed there would not be the distress in the towns that exists to-dan, and as for pauperism in the rural districts, that would be a thing unknown. (Loud applause.)

LIBERAL MEETING AT LYMM. On Tuesday evening, a meeting in support of Mr. Lea. dam's candidature was held at the Plough Hotel, Lymm, .when the room was crowded. The chair was occupied by Mr. Swanwick, and amongst those present were Sir J. lee (Manchester), Captain Balks (Liverpool). Mr. W. Long (Thelwall), Mr. D. Boyd (Lytntn), and Mr. H. Whitham (Warrington).—The Chairman referred to speeches made by the Conservative candidate in reference to the silk industry, and on that subject reai a letter that had been received from Mr. Howell, M.P. for the Spitalfields Division, who said that by the Board of Trade returns it was shown that dur- ing the years 1850 84, inclusive, we imported less and ex- ported more of silk manufactured goods than during the preceding five years of Tory rule, so that under Mr. Glad- stone's Government the silk trade gained in both ways. The speaker upheld the policy of Mr. Gladstone with re- gard to the Irish question, and asked the electors to show their confidence in Mr. Gladstone by returning Mr. Leadam to Parliament.—Sir Joseph Lee proposed "That this meet- ing desires to express its hearty confidence in Mr. Glad. atone at this juncture, and its determination to do its utmost to support him by sending Mr. Leadam to the House of Commons on Friday next." The government of Ireland, he remarked, had been in the power of the lory and Liberal parties alternately now for 70 or 80 years. All kinds of measures had been tried, coercion in every possible shape, and the Liberal party had now come to the conclu- sion, in the words of Mr. Bright, that force was no remedy. The Tory party seemed to think that it was a remedy, and were prepared to bring in a bill for coercion, but so far as Ireland was concerned, coercion was dead. Having criti- cised the speeches of Sir W. C. Brooks, Sir Joseph referred to the question of local Government.—Captain BAILS (Liver- pool), seconded the resolution, which was supported by Air. , BRIARS (Sale), and by Mr. JOSEPH HOWES (Leeds).—The I resolution was carried with applause, and a vote of thanks to the chairman brought the proceedings to a close.
LIBERAL MEETINGS AT ALTRINCHAM AND NORTHENDEN.

Meetings in support of the candidature of Mr. I. S. Leadam, the Liberal candidate, were held at Nortbenden, and in the British schools, Altrinchain, on Wednesday I night. At the latter place, Mr WILLIAM MILE presided, and moved a resolution declaring Mr. Leadam to be a fit , and proper person to represent the division in Parliament. —Mr. CLAUD MORRIS seconded the resolution, and Mr. THOMAS STELFOX (Lymw) spoke in support of it. Ho said the thing to put England right was free trade, and more of it. Sir William Cunliffe Brooks, at Lymm, had spoken in favour of fair trade, and wished to benefit the working classes by putting a tax on silk, but that tax would not only fall upon the upper ten thousand—it would fall upon all. He (Mr. Stelfox) was a Churchman. He did not say that he paid one pepny too much to the church. He be- lieved the church ought to be supported, but he, as a tenant farmer, would not pay tithes if it were not for fear of the "bums." (Laughter.) He paid tithes " grudging,ly and of necessity," therefore the Lord did not value them. (More laughher.)—The resolution was carried with a few dissen- tients.—Mr. JOSEPH ARCH, M.P., urged those present to educate themselves in political matters—to read both sides of a question, and then come to an honest decision about it. Land reform, was one of the most important subje:ts of the day. The introduction ard increase of machinery into agricultural pursuits had reduced the number of labourers required on the land, and they had of necessity migrated into the towns where they had become the competitors of the townspeople instead of their customers: How could that be altered? By. bringing those men back to the land which they ought never to have been compelled to leave. Most of the great legislative reforms bad been passed by the Liberal party. Lord t.alisbury, however, was a man of profound intelligence.—Mr. LEADAM said if returnesl to Par- liamen he would not vote for granting Ireland a Parliament having imperial powers, bat was in favour of the sister island having a Parliament that could control local affairs.

div.head: MR. LEADAM AT TIMPERLEY.
div.p: MR. LEADAM AT TIMPERLEY.

On Thursday evening Mr. I. S. Lea.darn addressed a meeting at Timperlev. Mr. W. Milne presided, and there was a crowded attendance.—Mr. Leadam remarked that it was said that Mr. Gladstone was going to take a sum of £100,000,000 or £150,000,000 in order to carry out his Irish scheme. Mr. Gladstone, he thought, was the last man in the world to embark in any scheme such as that attribu- ted to him. Mr. Leadarn proceeded to discuss agricultural questions, and pointed out that the Conservative party had considered the proposals of the Liberals for impreving the condition of the tenant farmers and agricultural labeurers ,as fit subject for jest and merriment. When the Liberal party had tried to do anything for the agricultural commu- nity the Conservatives had had no answer to give to their demands but an unqualified "No."—Mr. H. L. W. Law- son, M.P., who also addressed the meeting, said Mr. Leadam came before the electors as the supporter of a great political party and ef a leader whose life work had been devoted mainly to raising the condition of the working classes of this country. Ou the other hand they had Lord Salisbury and national stagnation, or Lord Randolph and Churchill and the confidence trick. (Laughter and cheers.) —A resolution pledging the meeting to support Mr. Leadam at the poll was passed.

div.head: OTHER CONSERVATIVE MEETINGS.
div.p: OTHER CONSERVATIVE MEETINGS.

The Conservative candidate addressed a meeting on : Tuesday night at Northenden, in the hall of the Litton Arms.—Mr. L. J. Jennings, M.P., said he heard nothing in the House of Commons hut Irish grievances, Scotch griev- ances, and all sorts of grievances. An English question had not the slightest chance of being discussed. Any num- ber of nights would be given to Ireland, or to Scotland, or to Wales, but England was left completely out in the cold. It was time that attention was turned to our own affairs, to the state of our great industries, the state of our commerce, and the state of our working people, with the view of see- ing whether something could not be done for their improve- ment. (Applause.)—Sir W. Cunliffe Brooks dealt chiefly with the Irish question. He was Prepared, he said, to be just, and even generous to Ireland, and in his opinion Mr. Glahtone was incapable of dealing with the question, for he had shown himself ignorant of the true principles of government.—A. vote of confidence in Sir W. Cunliffe Brooks was passed.—Meetings in support of the Conserva- tive candidate were also held the same evening at Timperley and at Northern Etchelis. On Wednesday afternoon Sir W. C. Brooks addres;sed a meeting of electors at Handforth, and in the evening one at Cheadle. Resolutions approving his candidature were ; passed. On Tuesday the candidate addressed a meeting ! at Dunham.

A meeting of the Conservative electors of Cheadle mime was held on Thursday .nightin the AllSaints' Schools, Cheadle Hulme. in support of the candidature of Sir W. C. Brooks. —Sir W. C. BROOKS, in the course of his address, said he thought true Free Trade would be the greatest boon that could be conferred upon the land, but if they were sure, as reasonable men, that they could nat get it, why should they go on hunting for it? A meeting in furtherance of Sir W. C. Brook's cindida- ture was held on Thursday evening at the Plough Inn, Lymm. The chair was occupied by Mr. P. Stubs, who was supported by Mr. W. H. Houldswor:h, M.P., and others.— Mr. HOULDSWORTII, M.P., expressed his opinion that the Liberal party since 1868, when Mr. Gladstone became its leader, had been a dwindling party, and that at the present 1 time it was in a condition of disintegration and decomposi- tion. He blamed Mr. Gladstone also for the present condi- tion of affairs in Ireland.
THE NOMINATIONS.

The nominations of the two candidates for the vacancy in the representation of Altrincham were handed in on Wednesday to the Returning Officer and Sheriff, F. D. Breckle- burst, Esq., at the Altrincham Police Court. Sir William Cunliffe Brooks, Bart, was nominated on three separate sheets. On the first he was proposed by the Hon. Alan de Tattoo Egerton, M.P., seconded by Thomas Hardcastle Sykes, and supported by R. H. Joynson, John Allen, Robert Cocks, James Kay, Peter Stubs, John Daine, David James, and Richard Curtis. On the second paper the proposer was William Griffin (chairman of the Altrinc- ham Conservative Club). seconded by William Plant (chair- man of the Altrincham Conservative Workirg•men's Club), and supported by William Hulme, George fyd, Robert Benson, John Hulme, Henry Wilton. Thomas 1 eylor, John Airey, and Henry Smith. The third paper contained the names of G. W Fereley, proposer; Henry Bell, seconder ; and supported ley Richard Brown, Alfred E. Ferns, Joseph Rains, Jas. Thorneley, Thos. Moore, Alfred Memory, John Peter Bardslev, and Isaac Higginbottom. Isaac Saunders Leadam was proposed by Sir Joseph C. Lee, seconded by James Worthington, and supported by Thomas Stelfox, William Long, H. T. Gaddum, Jesse Haworth, Adam Hogg, Thomas Maston, Abel Heywood, and J. A. Swanwick. A second paper contains the names of James Edward Platt, as proposer ; Thomas William Killick, seconder •, and is signed by Albert Clegg, George Bowen, James H. Milne, Thomas Stephens, John Pem- berton, Thomas Forster, Thomas Henry Vernon, and Wil- lam Roughton.

SUSPECTED INIPRDER NEAR CHESTEEFIELD.—EarIy on Thursday morning a dead body was found floating in the canal at Brimingtou, near Chesterfield, near to a planta- tion known as the Blue Dell. The police were communica• ted with, and the body was recognised at that of Herbert Brookes, butcher, residing at Culthorpe, but having a shop at Clowne. The deceased's pockets were found to be turned inside out, and nothing was found upon him except a key. The plantation close to the canal bare traces as of a body having been dragged through, and this, with the fact of nothing having been found upon the deceased, leads to the belief that a most atrocious robbery and murder have been perpetrated by persons unknown. In 1833 the number of emigrants who left 'civil ports wai, G 2,420, of which 62,034 were natives of Ireland. A married woman named Belot died at Jersey on Sat- urday night in her 102nd year, retaining all het faculties till death. It is snzgested by "An Irishman" that the infant daughter of the Duke of Connaught, .born on St. Patrick's Day, should be named Kathleen. Mrs. Mortimer Collins, wife of the late Mr. Mortimer Collins, the novelist, was cremated at Woking en Saturday. The deceased died on Tuesday. The Queen has signified her intention of c,eaferring the honour of knighthood upon Mr. James Brunlees, C.E., chief engineer of the Mersey Tunnel. The "Standard" printing works, Wellington, Salop, were destroyed by fire on Monday night. The type, plant, and machinery were rendered worthless. The Exchequer returns from April Ist to Mareh 20th show receipts £85,964,238, last year £85,235,033 ; expendi- ture, £84,769,560; balances, £9,480,532. As a mark of her great respect for the late Principal Tulloch, the Queen has been pleased to grant to Mrs. Tulloch a pension of £2OO a year from her privy purse. A remarkable case of longevity is reported from the Caucasus, that of a shepherd who has just died at the great age of 124, and was in full possession of h:ts faculties to the last.
The Westborough New Connexien Chapel at Dewsbary, which was erected nine years ago at a cost of over £5,300, was destroyed by fir:: on Monday morning. The building was insured.

A serious accident has occurrrd on board her Majeety's sloop Albatross on the China station, by the bursting of a Nordenfelt gun during practice. Two of the crew were killed and two seriously injured. The Queen, after holding a drawing-room on Tuesday, visited the Duchess of Connaught, and subsequenCy drove with Princess Beatrice in an open carriage through Nycie Park to Kensington Palace, returning about seven p..n. to Buckingham Palace. SHOC.)TING HIS WIFE. —Eli Wilsr, potter, Bradford, Manchester, is in the custody of the city police, charged with shooting his wife with intent to kill her. It appears that the couple have for some time lived unhapplly together. Recently Mrs:Wilson took out a summens against her husband for assault. By threats he tried to induce iser to withdraw the summons. She refused to do what he wished, and on Tuesday night he fired a pietel in her face, inflicting severe injuries. THE DIIRBY RAGIRDY.—The death is reported of the man Wagstaff, who recently in a paroxysm of madness mur- dered a female relative in the presence of his sick son, at Quarndon, near Derby. Last week the son died, and the father has died in gaol before he could he removed to Broadmeor. His madness was of a very violent character, and tlae coroner's jury on Monday found that he had died from es. haustien consequent on acute mania. CURE or HYDROEHOBIA.—Henry Bradley: a man who courageously attacked and killed a mad dog at Peckham on the 4th inst., and who has been under the care cf M. Pasteur at Paris for the last ten days, returned on Sunday to his family. Dr. De Lacy Evans saw the man on his arrival, and found him better in health and spirits than ;etc ; his leaving England. Ali his wound, excepting one, have healed, and the physician has no fear of the deve-lopment.of hydrophobia. THE DAISGRRS or QUACK MEDICINRS.—At Nottingham, on Tuesday, an ircinest was held on the body of Ethel- Bias- dale, a child, who died under somewhat mystericius circam • ' stances. The evidence showed that deceased, with four other children, took same cough mixture composed. of ; squills, supplied by 3 local chemist. Two of the children ; died, but the other recovered with cireful treatment. The jury returned a verdict of "Death by misadventure," and exonerated the chemist from blame. _ -

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY MARCH 27, 1886.

SIR WILLIAM CUNLIFFE BROOKS, at a Meeting at Bowdon on Saturday, held for the promotion of his candidature for the Altrincham Division, announced himself as a convert to the doctrines of the Fair Traders. "Think no more," he said, "of Free Trade; it is a humbug." It would seem that he has had it on his mind to say this for some time, but he could not screw his courage to the Sticking place. He now thanks God that he iS in that happy and independent position that he fears no man; hence his deliverance on the question of Free Trade. He speaks professedly from a business experience of nearly half a century; and. as he challenges anyone to find fault with accuracy of his Position, or the facts laid before his audience, it is to be hoped we shall be pardoned if we accept the challenge. Let us confess, how- ever, that we never approach this question of Free Trade versus Fair Trade without think- ing of the superfluous labour involved in flogging a dead horse; but when a candidate for parliamentary honours comes on the scene with what may be regarded as a re- cantation and a brand new view of the sub- ject, it is due to him that what he has to say Should receive attention. The cardinal point Of Sir W. C. BROOKS' indictment of Free Trade is contained in the statement that The ruin which is gradually spreading it- self over this England of ours dates from the time that Mr. COBDEN proposed and per- suaded the PRIME MINISTER of • that day to take off all the import duties possible without obtaining the consent of other nations that they also would take off theirs." This is a direct charge; let us examine it. Sir , WILLIAM does not give statistics by way of I Proving his assertion he seems to take it ; for granted that it is not to be denied. But 1 this is not a satisfactory mode of reasoning; it may do for a convert in the heat of an election campaign, but it will not suffice for the dispassionate public. We turn then to our trade records; and we find that his ex- traordinary and unsupported statement is a I figment of the imagination which is about as far from the truth as any statement can be. In 1860, immediately after Mr. COBDEN had negotiated his great treaty, the total value of our imports and exports was £375,052,000. In i 884., after 24 years' experience of gradually Spreading "ruin," they had increased to £688,000,000 ; that is to say, the trade of the country has well nigh doubled under the xgis of Free Trade. Talk about humbu?,l If I there is any humbug, it is in men like Sir WILLIAM CUNLIFFE BROOKS, who have made enormous fortunes out of Free Trade, belie- ing their half century's experience, and ; kicking down the ladder by which they have climbed to affluence and power. But it may be urged that we should confine ourselves to I our export trade; Sir WILLIAM says the 1 manufacturer "cannot employ the labour for 1 making goods when he finds that they will . not be received by foreign nations." The implication—it is not a statement this time— is that we are being ruined because, under Free Trade, foreigners will not receive our goods. But what is the fact ? In 1860 the total value of ' our export's was £164.,52i,000 ; in 1880, twenty years later, it had risen to £286,415,000. Not to leave the Tory baronet a loophole of escape, we may add that the same tale is told if we confine the inquiry to exports to foreign countries pure and simple, that is excluding goods sent to British posses- sions. In 1860 the total value of our exports to "foreign countries only" was Li 17,988,000; in 1886 the total was £204,887,000. Turn which vay we will, there is evidence beyond the possibility of dispute of an increase of trade. since the adoption of the Cobden Treaty, of from 8o to 90 per cent. ; and yet the Fair Trade neophyte would have us believe that we are being ruined by Free Trade! Sir WILLIAM oracularly tells us that " Free Trade means free selling as well as free buy- ing. Free buying we have got, but what is the use of free buying if you have not the money in your pocket to buy with ?" This brilliant sally was, we learn, received with laughter and cheers. It is a bit of clap-trap which is often used by the Fair Traders, and has, we suppose, been passed on to the new member of that muddle-headed body of poli- cal imposters. But what does it imply? It means, if it means anything, that if the work- ing classes of this country would improve their position, if they would have money in their pockets to buy with, they must do as other countries have done—fall back on pro I tective tariffs. Sir WILLIAM has just come I back from France, which is a Protectionistl country. Why did he not give his audiencel some account of the lot of the French capitalist and the French workman? We' should have thought his historical imagi- nation was equal to anything after tty-I ing to make it out that we in this country were being ruined by Free Trade. Let us supply the omission with- a little sober fact. The Economic Investigation Committee has reperted with regard to Lille and the cotton distrc's of France generally,' that there is the g re itest distress. There Were 28,000 names on the Relief Fund

Register of Lille. The principal cause of this distress, it was stated, was the agricul- tural crisis—a crisis which has decreased the value of landed property by two-thirds, notwithstanding that the corn growers are " protected." In Paris there have been as many as so,ooo masons out of I mow) out of work. "The Shipbuilding trade," says Mr. G. W. MEDLEY, " nurtured by the State, was as depressed as here, and was permanently in disfavour, except when English shipbuilders were too busy to take ' orders." This does not look as if Protection is calculated to " create " that trade about , which Sir WILLIAM talks so much but ap- ' parently knows so little. Then as to hours and wages, French artisans, etc., are much worse of than are the same class in this country. Roundly speaking, the hours of , labour in England are from 9 to i o per day; "throughout France, they are rarely, if ever, under rz hours per day ;" while the rule in , French factories is to work 72 hours per week, as against 564 in England. Notwith- standing these long hours, French worker's are stated to receive less wages by 50 per cent than English operatives. It is the same with Germany and Austria; 'Protection" has brought worse trade than we have here, with longer hours and lower wages. In some of the factories of Austria the workmen sleep on the premises on wool sacks; they work 96 hours per week; and they get a wage which barely keeps body and soul together. In Germany the imposts on foreign goods have been met by the manufacturers by reduc- tions of wages; and it is obvious that if we resort in this country to 'Fair Trade, which is another name for Protection, we shall have a like result. It is appalling to learn that in 1882, after three years of extreme Protective tariffs, there were seven million heads of families exempted from taxation because their earn- ings were less than ten shillings per week We have not yet come to that in England; but we may get somewhere near it in a few years, if we turn Fair Traders, reduce wages, and lengthen the hours of labour. ir WIL- LIAM CUNLIFFE BRCOKS says we are "like great fools ;" let him speak for himself. We shall be greater fools if we take his advice, and adopt a remedy which is worse than the disease.

THE House of Lords, as we recorded in our last issue, has decided, for the first time, in favour of opening Metropolitan Museums and Art Galleries on Sunday. Their lardships are usually a stumbling block in the path of pro- gress, but in this matter they are certainly paving the way. As a cultured body of men, they may be said to have a special interest in matters of art, and know that it has refining and elevating influences. A considerable portion of the clergy of all denominations gladly recognise the same fact, and are there- fore in favour of the movement. On the other hand there are many who fear that the opening of London Art Galleries would have a bad effect in secularising the Sabbath; they would rather see the people in churches and chapels. Granted, but supposing the masses decline to go to church and it is the cry all round that they do not—is it not better that they should spend their spare hours on a Sunday in Museum or Art Gal- lery rather than in a public-house or beer shop ? It savours of cant to profess to be horrified at the idea of secularising the Sabbath, when the same people act as if they were utterly oblivious of the fact that the open drink-shop is doing more harm in a single Sunday than the open Museums could do in a year of Sundays. The case of the London workman is particularly hard. He is taxed for the maintenance of the National Gallery and British Museum ; and he may live within an hour's walk of them; but they might as well be in Timbuctoo for any good they are to him. Whilst he is at work, they ate open to all corners; but when he is at liberty—when he has finished his day's labour—the doors are closed upon him. Sunday is the only day he can call his own ; and, as he is suriounded on Sunday with temptations of all kinds to go astray, it is fitting—it is needful—that there should be a counteracting influence at work which shall be alike attractive and elevating. It is sug- gested, as an alternative, that the Museums and Art Galleries of London should be open two or three evenings in the week; but it would seem from a report just issued by Sir F. W. BURTON, the Director of the National Gallery, that there are many gm ve.objections to such a course—not the least of which is the damage which would be done to priceless oil paintings by the use in crowded rooms of artificial light. For our part we are inclined to think that if the rooms were crowded the good that would be done would more than counterbalance the "hazard- ous evil of artificial lighting." National institutions of the kind under con- sideration should be made More accessible to the nation. The Museums were made for man, not man for the Museums. Nothing is said about opening Parks on Sunday, where flowers and trees and statuesaread- mired. Why should it become objection- able to walk out of a Park into a Picture Gallery and admire representations of all that is beautiful in nature? There is n 3 satisfactory answer to such a question. We are martyrs to custom ; and the custom has been to open God's church and the Devil's chapel—the drink shop—and to close the door upon everything else. We must try to get the better of our bad habits as a nation, for it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath Day, not in one way merely, but in every way. ••••••••••..........•••••11.18

THE Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON does not appear to have been very considerately treated by the Distress Fund Committee at the weekly meeting held at Warrington on Tuesday last. He had a serious charge to bring against the editor of this journal—that of having allcwed a correspondent to make a statement which the reverend gentleman could not possibly approve. Could anything be more shocking to a well-regulated mind? Fired with the most virtuous indignation, he suggested, after unfolding his indictment, that they should "ask the Editor for the name of the writer' or ask him to apologise." But, will it be believed? the Committee positively turned a deaf ear to this appeal; they wouldn't ask for anything. The Rev. JOHN YONGE—who might have been expected to sympathise with a brother cleric—sought to quash the indictment by remarking. in a cold-blooded matter of fact sort of way, that "he had always been under the impression that editors did not hold themselves resnonsi- t ble for the opinions of their correspondents." Mr. Mothcs asked where they would end if they began to take notice of anonymous correspondents? Oh, why was Mr. Monks so inconsiderate of Mr. Carleton's feelings as to put a question of that kind, at that time, and in that way ? Mr. GA RNETT said he did not think it was a _-matter they should discuss there, as if, for-

sooth, Mr. CARLETON'S remarks were posi- tively out of place. Really, all this is too had. It is like treading on a budding corn when the unhappy victim is appealing for sympathy. We are not so heartless ; we would rather encourage the Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON in the noble task he has taken upon himself of teaching editors how to conduct their journals. He, of course, would know what to do when by one post he received a Tory communication from a Church Parson, like (say) Mr. CARLETON himself; and, by the next post. a Radical epistle from an unmen- tionable Dissenter of the "Clifford Dix" type. But what would he do? Would he trample them both under foot to show that he was "mighty impartial?" Or would he cleave ;to the one and despise the other? We can only say, when thus perplexed : How happy could I be with either Were t'other dear charmer away t And end by yielding to the charms of both— that is, introducing them to our readers with- out expressing any opinion as to. their graces and virtues. Evidently this is very wrong, for the Vicar of Holy Trinity holds that an editor is responsible not only for him- self, but everybody else. But he must show us how it is to be done. Suppose, seeing we are willing to learn, that we exchange rostrums for a week? The Fress, cf course, is not to be compared with the Pulpit ; but then it would be some com- pensation to the reverend gentleman to have a larger audience than usual. And then think of the example he would set as the Model Editor—and how delighted his congregation would be to have him back after missing him for a whole week ! Mr. CARLETON will see that we are in a generous mood—that we are not like the unregenerate Distress Committee which " turned to other business and let the matter"drop." We ex- pect to hear from him.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCTI 27. 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCTI 27. 1886.
"TOUCH AND GO."

There is a prospect of thr; poor rate in Warrington being reduced by fourpence in the pound. This will be a relief to many who, though distressed, cannot put them- selves on the Distress Fund. At the " Distress Fund" Concert at War- rington, on Wednesday, the windows were open as the latest mode of ventilation. It was a sort of open-air entertainment. When the weather gets warmer, they will probably take down an end or side of the building. People must have fresh air, even if they sneeze, and cough, and die through it.

A Tory contemporary would have its readers believe that the members of the pre- sent Government must be either knaves or fools for not falling down at the shrine of Fair Trade. But what of the late (Tory) Government? They, too, turned their backs upon the Fair Traders. In which category are they to be placed ?

What is the name of the Queen of Eng- land? This may seem a simple sort of ques- tion, but it is one which two convalescent patients at the hospital are unable to answer. They are scholars from two of the schools in Warrington. Possibly at the schools they attend they hear more about the Church Catechism than English history.

The proposal to apply the balance result- ing from the Earlestown Liberal ball to a dinner to the unemployed was a happy thought. It has caused additions to the fund to pour in from Conservatives as well as Liberals. This is as it should. be. As "Christopher North" once said "The animosities are mortal, but the humanities are eternal."

At St. Helens on Monday Mary Thompson, 19 years of age, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Church-street at quarter past one that morning. Superinten- dent Johnston stated that that was her 4oth appearance in four years. Nineteen years of age and a drunkard four years ago ! Could anything be more pitiful ? Wonder if brewers ever think of these cases, and, if they do, are they the happier for it? .

Temperance Societies will please note that the Sunday Closing (Durham) Bill was sup- ported by Messrs. Ashton, Brunner, Hoyle, Leake, Mather, Peacock, and Potter, Sir H. Roscoe, Messrs. Rylands and Wright. Amongst the opponents were Messrs. A J. Balfour and Coddington, Sir J. Ferguson, Mr. F. S. Powell, Sir F. Stanley, Messrs. Tipping, H. J. Tollemache, and Tomlinson. Where was Sir Gilbert Greenall ? Absent again?

Mr. Joseph Arch, M.P., hit the right nail on the head in his speech near Cheadle, on Tuesday, when he urged that 'if the fifteen millions of acres in this country that were waiting for cultivation, were set free from feudal restrictions, there would soon be less distress in the country. The land is fettered bybad laws, and firmers are being ruined, while labourers are driven from the country into the town to compete with their fellows in an overcrowded market.

- People cannot be too careful as to their record in filling up forms with a view to in- surance. The representatives of a deceased miner of Haydock have found that the policy they held on the London, Edinburgh, and Glasgow Assurance Company was void be- cause of false statements made in the form of application. Honesty is the best " policy" in insurance as in other matters ; and this applies to agents, too, who are sometimes more anxious about securing commission than "a good life."

Can anybody explain how it is that men who would never think of stealing do not hesi- tate to defraud a Railway Company? A commercial traveller, hailing from Horwich, was brought before the magistrates, on Mon - day, for travelling from Prescot to St. Helens without a ticket. After taking French leave, he waited half an hour at St. Helens Station, and then booked to St. IL lens Junction. 'His four-penny fraud cost him over twenty shil- lings. This " commercial " has something to learn yet in the way of commerce-4:o say nothing of honesty.

History repeats itself. Here is a paragraph which is suggestive of early English history. "As a lad about fifteen years of age was gathering samphire on the cliffs of Dover he slipped and fell a distance of over 300 feet. His dead body, terribly mangled, was picked up on the rocks by the Coastguard." Shake- speare, in "King Lear," mades "Edgar" say, whilst standing:on one of the cliffs at Dover : Half-way down Hangs one that gathers .samphire ; dreadful trade! ' Methinks he seems no bigger than his head. The fishermen that walk upon the beach , Appear like mice. "Dreadful trade," indeed, as the lifeless , body of the poor youth sadly testifies.
