THE. DIATII RATE OF ROI:COWL—During the week, the 18th to the 25th inst., not a death has betn registered in Runcorn. Potreo Crutrons AT RUNCOEN.—P.C. Egerton has been removed to Lostock GrAlam, and P.S. Cooper, of Crewe, has

een transferred to Runcorn. LacronE RV TITS RIM W. VAUSE.—The Rev. W. Vause, of Runcorn, on Friday evening last week delivered his lecture on "Oar national expenditure; or how we are robbed," before a good number of the members of Win3ford Lib ral Club. NELSON-STRERT BA_WIST CHAPEL, WIDNES.—The Rev. Yeatmau continues his special discourses to fair congre- gations. On Suaday morning the subject WAS "The secret place of the Most High," and in the evening "The cessa- tion of Divine anger." TEMPERANCS ORGANISATIONS AT WIDNES.—An enter- tainment of songs, recitations, &c., was given in Nelson- street Baptist Chapel, on Monday evening, by the members of the Band of Hope. Mr. J. R. Hudson presided, and a pleasant time was spent. ZION FREE CHURCR, WIDNES.—In the Methodist Free Church, Oakland-street, on 'Monday evening, the choir and members of the Band of Hope, assisted by a few friends be- longing to other denominations, performed a service of song entitled "The River Singers." Mr. John Betney ably con- ducted. Mr. F. J. Norman, of Runcorn, read the narra- tive. The proceeds are to be devoted to the erection of a new scliool. CONCERT AT 81:m-on:v.—The annual concert arranged by Mr. S. Ravenscroft. organist at Bethesda Chapel, took place on Tuesday evening in Bethesda Lecture Hall. There was a moderate attendance. Tbe Vocalists were Miss Clark and Miss Howard, and Messrs. 4. Fox, J. Lea, P. Smith, F Scott, and Mr. Moore. Mr. J. Wood gave a cornet solo, and the Volunteer Band played selections. Miss Jukes and Mr. Ravenscroft were the accompanists. A GOOD INTENTION FRUSTRATED.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Annie Ryan was charged with stealing a pair of boots, value 55, from the second-hand clothes shop of Michael Boyle, 8, Grenfell-street, on the 16th March. Mrs. Boyle was absent from the house a few minutes, and on her return saw the prisoner leaving the shop. She after- wards missed the boots, and the prisoner, when apprehended on Thursday, said "I never did the like before. I in- tended to take them back to-night." A fine of 303 was imposed. WARNING TO RuNCORN TRADESMEN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday. William Rudd. manager of the shop in Bridge-street, occupied by Mr. E. Johnson, was charged with obstructing the footpath.—P.C. Smith stated that on Saturday, the 13th inst., defendant had 15 tubs placed in a line outside the shop window, and used for dis- playing bacon and cheese for sale.—P.S. Neild said he had previously warned the defendant about the obstruction.-- The defendant contended that the tubs were so narrow that they did not cause any obstruction.—A fine of 53 and costs was imposed. ACCIDENT AT WIDNES —CbriSlOPher Middleburst, 45 years of age, who resides at 16, South-street, Widnes, met with a serious accident at midnight on Saturday, at the works of the Widnes Alkali Company, Moss Bank, where he is employed. He slipped from the "high level" in some unexplained way, and alighted on his head, which was ter- ribly wounded. The distance of his fall was 20 feet. He was found in an unconscious state by several fellow-work- men shortly after the occurrence, and was conveyed home, where be received every attention at the hands of Dr. MeCambridee. RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.—A special meeting was held on Monday night under the presidency of Mr. P. Speakman. Present—Messrs. Pritchard, Lightbura, Taylor, Meadowcreft, Once, Imison, Marshall (secretary), and Barker (surveyor). With the object of closing the financial year, accounts amounting to £539 193 2d were pessed fer payment, on the recommendation of the Finance Committee. These accounts included an item of £3OO 163 9d, balance of Mr. W. H. Linaker's law charges and expenses respecting the opposition of the Board to the Man- chester Ship Canal Bill, 1885. WIDNES MANSTAINHTER PETITION—Upwards Of 1,000 signatures have been obtained in Widnes to the petitim for the release of Wm. Percy, late farmer and contractor, Sut- ton's-lane, Widnes, who is now in his 84th year, and who three years ago was found guilty of the manslaughtrr of his wife, and sentenced to penal servitude for 20 years. The petition will be forwarded to the Home Secretary in a few days, and it is expected that the Queen will exercise her royal prerogative in the prisoner's favour. Besides the Howard Society which took the initiative in the matter, several members of the House of Commons are interesting themselves in Percy's case. SENT TO A. REFORMATORY FROM RUNCORN.— At RUA. corn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Walter Kinsey. aged 14, was charged with stealing a coat, value 12s 6d, the property of Marsh and Smith, pawnbrokers, Church-street. The coat was hanging outside the prosecutors' shop on Saturday afternoon. At night it was missed. The prisoner attempted to pawn the coat at Mr. Dodd's shop for half-a-crown, and he was given into the custody of P.C. Millington. The prisoner pleaded guilty, and Superintendent Leah stated he had been twice before the magistrates for sleeping out. He was sentenced to twenty-one days' imprisonment, and after- wards to be detained in a reformatory until be was 16 years

of age. A LUNATIC AT LARGE AT RUNCORN.—Between twelve and one o'clock on Sun4ay morning P.S. Neild saw a young man acting in a strange fashion in Bridge-street, and the officer deemed it advisable to lock the wanderer in the police station. On Sunday he gave many signs of mental derange- ment, and he was provided with suitable quarters by &per- intendent Leah until he was brought before the magistrates. On Monday morning, when being escorted from the police station to the courthouse, he bolted up Bridge-street fol- lowed by an excited crowd. He was, however, stopped by Mr. Percival, the inspector of nuisances, and his friends at Kilcaldy, Scotland, being communicated with, they took charge of him on Tuesday. WIDNES SECOND STARR-BOWE= BUILDING SOCIETY.— Under the auspices of this society a successful concert was given in Mali's Temperance Hall, on Wednesday evening, under the presidency of Mr. D. Wright. There was a capi- tal attendance, and an excellent programme was gone through by Miss Gertrude Owen, Miss Thomas; Messrs. Hesketh, Heslip, Bate, Eaton, Tuson, Griffiths and C. A. Bate. Mr. Gandy performed a skilful violin solo. Master J. R. Bate was the accompanist. Mr. S. Owens, secretary to the society, gave an address on the principles and advan- tages of Starr-Bowkett building societies. At the close an appropriation took place in connection with the first society, the result being that Mr. S. Owens was entitled to £4OO free of interest for 12i years. Sour DINNERS AT RUNCORN. With the advent of warmer atmospheric conditions, Mr. W. Shaw' of the Mer- sey Missions, has closed his soup kitchen which has proved a boon to hundreds of poor children in the town. Alto- gether the kitchen has been open 16 days, and a total of 2,822 dinners have been provided at a cost of £23 103 4d, to which the Y.M.C.A. have liberally contributed. Mr. P. Speakman gave a generous donation, and Captain H +zle- burst, Mr. F. A. Lake (president of the Y.M.C.A.), C. Wigv, and many others have contributed. The lab3ur of preparing the food has devolved to a great extent upon Mrs. Shaw, and the work connected with the distribution, &c, of the soup, has been performed by Miss Garrett, Miss Tuft, Mr. Greaves, and others connected with the mission. Mr. W. Shaw, as the organiser, deserves great praise, as the children have been enabled to withstand the rigours of a severe period with greater comfort. _ _

CLIIM AGAINST TIIE WESTON POINT TUG COMPANY.— At the Liverpool County Court, on Tuesday, his Honour Judge Thompson resumed the hearing of actions com- menced on the previous day, in which the Weston Point Steam Tiwing Company was sued by Thomas Wilkinson, owner of the flat Elizabeth, and Thomas Whitehemi, owner of the fiat Intrepid, for damages caused to those flats through alleged negligence in towing. The first-named plaintiff claimed £lOO, and the second £5O, as the amount of dam- age. His Honour having heard the evidence, which was somewhat conflicting, held that the printed conditions were binding upon the plaintiffs, and, further, that the damage 'arose from the flats interfering with the navigation. He therefore gave judgement for the defendants, with costs.— Mr. Carver and Mr. Hardy, instructed by Mr. J. W. Thomp- son, appeared for the plaintiffs; Mr. Pickford and Mr. Stewart, instructed by Messrs. Masters and Rogers, appeared for the defendants.

THE WIDNES WOUNDING CASE.—THE PRISONER COM- mirrED.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursda:,, Michael Carr, 17 years of age, a iabolrer, who lived in Oxford-street, was charged on remand with unlawfully rounding John Riley, labourer, of 57, Victoria-street. Evidence was given by the prosecutor, Dr. McCambridge, Joseph Collier, John Keensghan, Oxford-street; Frank Bennett. 30, J Imes- street, West Bank: and Frank Hanley, 97, Midwood- street. On the 14th January the prisoner and two young men were in the yard of the Widnes Alkali Company's works, and the watchman, Joseph Collier, ordered them away. The prisoner and a man named Murray went upon the London and North-Western Itiilvray, and the prisoner sent stones at Collier. One missile, a large clinker, struck Riley, who was engaged in unloading a wagon, on the heal, inflicting a wound which made him unconscious. For seven weeks Riley had been confined to bed, and at one time his condition was so critical that on D. McCambridge's advice his depositions were taken. He had a severe fracture of the skull, and part of the bone had sloughed away. He would not be able to follow his employment for some time to come. The prisoner was committed to the sessions for trial. CHLORO-LINSEED COUGH LOZENGES. a medicated linseed ex- tract. 6d ; postage, 2d. Kay Bros., Stockport, and all Chemists. A —Advt.
M. and Mits. WIGGAN, the evangelists, have this week again conducted services in the Primitive Mttbodist Chapel,

Widnes, with a considerable amount of success. BAND or HOPE, RuNcome.—An admirable entertainment was given at the fortnightly meeting held ow Thursday night. Mr. A. Sayle presided. There was a numerous at- tendance. WIDNES C.F.T.S.—The members of this society hold a "devotional meeting" on Thursday night. Prayers were offered up, and addresses delivered by the Vicar and his curate, the Rev. A. P. R. Wilson. FARNWORTH WESLEYAN BAND OF Hops.—The members
of the above society gave a pleasing entertainment in the Derby-road Wesleyan Chapel, Faraworth, on Monday evening. Mr. T. S. wale presided, and there was a good attendance.
THE PRIMROSE LEAGUE AT RUNCORN At a meeting

In Holy Yriiii.lichool, on Wednesday night, steps weir; taken for forming a Habitatinn of the Primrose League at Runcorn. An executive committee was appointed pro tern. with Mr. T. H. Annett as secretary. The Rev. W. Preston consented to become president pro tem. WIDNES TEMPERANCR AND BAND.OF HOPR UNION.— In connection with this Union, a public meeting was held on Thursday evening in Oakland-street Wesleyan School- room. Tbe Rev. R. Yeatman, Baptist minister, presided, and Mr. W. Clarke, of the Hollies, Ditton, delivered an ad- dress. A musical entertainment was given, and tbere was a good audienco. Wiawns LOCAL BOAIRD ELECTION.—The following is a complete list of the nominations :—Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Robert .Cook, Barnett Dutton, W. W. Gossage, John Houghton, John Horabin (tool manufacturer, Halton View), Ed 'ard Martley, Joshua Midvrood, and R. Webster. The first five named are the nominees of the Owners and Occupiers Association, and the remainder are indepen- dents.

NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING AT RUNCORN.—An old woman named Mary MacDonald, who lives in Mersey- street, Runcorn, and makes a living by fiddling. was walk- ing the Old Quay Canal, near the wotics of Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele, on Wednesday, when she fell into tbs. water. A man named Charles Wood, who was near, suc- ceeded in rescuing ber. The woman had walked from Warrington. _

RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB AND THE WEST LANCASHIBB CM—Leigh should have played off the drawn game at Runcorn on Thursday evening, but early on that day a telegram was received by the secretary, in which it was stated that Leigh refused to play the mat di. Numerous persons from Widnes and NVarrington arrived Is town to witness the game, but had to return home disappointed. The Runcorn dub will of course be awarded the game, and will meet Wigan to-day in the third round of the competi- tion. MR FOLEY, OF WIDNES.—With the purpose of augment- ing the fund which is being raised to enable Mr. Foley. lay reader at Widnes Parish Church, to enter the ministry, a concert took place on Tuesday evening, in the Volunteer Hall. There was a very scanty attendance The vocalists had all given their s.rvices, and a capital programme was gone through. The Rev. George Bohd, M.A., vicar of Farnworth, presided, and explained that as the Vicar of Widnes, whom he thought the most fit person to take the chair on thtt occasion, had declined, he, con- sidering Mr. Foley as a brother, took the position.

Mn THROUGH DR: NK AT WIDNES —At Widnes Police Court, Edward Rowland, a commercial traveller, was charged with wandering about in an unsound state of mind in Victoria-road, Widnes, on Tuesday uight. The prisoner, who was conducting himself in a very strange fashion in the street, was taken to the police station where he was seen by a doctor. The medical man would not say that he was a lur atic, but he dii not c ,nsid.-r him fit to be at large. Next morning he app,ared ti be quite rational, and Inspector Wood asked for his discharge —in answer to Mr. Lewin, the prisoner said it was through drinking that these fits of insanity were brought on. The prisoner was dis- charged.

ST. Nut's WESLEYAN CHAPEL, RIINCORN.—A ft er being closed for several weeks, St. Paul's Chapel will be re-opened for divine service on Thureday, the Bth April. At consider- able cost the edifice has been thoroughly cleaned and decorated, its appearance having been much altered and greatly improved. Mr. George Yarwood, the painter, deserves the highest praise for the exceedingly successful and artis- tic way in which he has carried out the work entrusted to him. The Rev. Richard Roberts, president of the Wes- leyan Conference, will preach at the re-opening, and it is worthy of mention that the rev, gentleman took part is the services held upon the construction and completion of the building some 20 years ago. Additional ieformation may be gleaned from our announcement column. SHOCKING FATALITY AT WIDNES.—Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the West Bank Hot-I, on Wednesday,toucbing the death of Walter Guest Stringer, aged 17, whose father is a master mariner and resides at 50, Bank-road, Garston. The deceased was employed as a joiner's labourer at Messrs. Golding, Davies, and Co'o. works, and about seven o'clock on Saturday morning the deceased attempted to get into the cage of a hoist as it was being lowered. He missed his footing and dropped to the bottom. The cage squck him on the hack crushing him very seriously. The youth, who acknowledged to his aunt that it was his own fault, died on Monday morning —Mr. Richmond, inspector of factories, considered the plant was erected satiefactorily. A verdict of accidental death was recorded. RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT WIDNES.—The annual meet- ing of the ratepayers for the township of Widnes was held at the overseers' office, Victoria-road, on Thursday after- noon. Mr. James White cresided. The attendance was mall. The Chairman stated that the total amount required for all purposes last year was £13,200, which was raised by a tate of 21 in the £. He regretted that during the ensuing year it would be necessary to ley a rate of 2s 4d in the £. This would only produce the same amount as last .year. a circumstance caused by the heavy reductions in the assess- ments of the railways and chemical works. It was decided to submit the following list of names to the magistrates for the selection of overseers :—Messrs. Rogers, Fogg. John Matthews, James White, J Midwood, S. Owens, Joseph Morrison, John Kelm!). T. S. Swale, S. B. Stringer, and S. Robinson. CONFIRMATION SERVICE AT RUNCORN.—The Right Rev. Dr. Stubbs. Bishop of Chester, on Tuesday held a confirma- tion at Runcorn Parish Church, and there was a capital congregation. The candidates presented were as follows: Parish of Runcorn: females, 56; males, 28; presentsd by the Revs. Colon Barclay, A. Edwards (curate in charge of Newtown Mission Church). and T. Manton Armson; Holy Trinity Church, 9 females,3 males; presented by the R-v. William Preston; Weston Mission, 10 females, 1 male; Halton Parish, 8 females, 1 male; presented by the Rev. J. Lockwood; Christ Church, Weston Point, 7 females, 6 males; presented by the Rev. J. H. Wilcockson Daresbury Parish, 1 male, presented by the Revs Thomas Whitley (vicar) and H. T. Clark. The Bishop addressed the con- firmees on the importance of the step they had undertaken, and the spirit in which they ought to considGr the rite.

RUNCORN GYMNASIUM.—Mr. Alexander, director of the Liverpool Gymnasium, attended the Runcorn Gymnasium on Thereday evening for the purpose of choosing the "champion tight." A framed certificate has been presented by Mr. Alexander to the Runcorn Gymnasium, and upon this will be inscribed the names ef the eight leaders. The competition had been looked forward to with mach interest by the members, and there was a large number present. The competitors were awarded marks according to merit in the following exercises :—Dumh-liells, bar bells, Indian clubs, parallel bars, flying horse, high jumping, and long jump- ing. At the close of the contest the following were declared the champions :—First champion, T. T. Burrows, 46 marks; F. Hancem 451 marks; E. Lunt, 45 marks ; W. Riley, J. Bate, and W. Collier, 431 marks each ; J. 'Rhodes, 41 ' marks; and W. Garrett, 37 marks. The declaration of the winning names was received with cheers. Mr. Alexander, with his customary kindness, has signified his intention of presenting to Mr. Burrows, first champion, a silver medal. The presentation will be made at the assault at arms, which will take place in the Public Hall on the 6th April. Full particulars will be found in our advertising columns. FALL Or A CRANE AT WIDNES.—TWO MEN INJURED.— A steam crane, which was being used in the erection of a grain and flour warehouse at West Bank for Messre. Fair- eloupk, fell on Wednesday evening with serious effect. The crane was fixed upon a platform about 10 or 12 feet above i the ground, and had been there for about two months. By it about 50 stones, weighing from 5 cwt. to two tons, had I been lifted during the day, and it was considered equal to any strain put upon it. About a quarter past five on Wed- nesday evening a stone weighing 11 cwt. was raised from the hold of a fl at, and the man in charge, Samuel Moores, of 40, \Vest-street, was just about to "jib " the crane round to the required position, when one of the iron supports gave way, and the crane fell to the ground. Moores felt it giving way, and, shouting to his fellow workmen to stand clear, he jumped to the ground. His leg, however, got jammed between the falling boiler and some stones, and twenty minutes elapsed before he could be released from his painful Position, as the steam from a broken gauge was playisg upon him. He was badly scalded on the right leg, right hand, head and face, awl his head was bruised. Another man, named James Hooley, of White-street, had his right arm broken by a falling chain, and the back of his head bruised. Both ,men are under the care of Dr. McDonnell. The damage to the crane is estimated at £5O. The contrac- tors for the work are Messrs. G. and R. Rithbone, of North' wich.

MEDICINES ELASTIC STOCKINGS. CHEMICALS, DRI:O9. •. by parcels post, under Lb., 3d. Kay, Brothers, Stockport.— Advt. CHEMICAL WORKS AND FARMERS' CROPS.—At Warrington ' County Court on Thursday a farmer named John Smith, jun., of Whitley and Wash-la, Latchford, came before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes for his public examination in bankruptcy. Mr. Worsley, deputy official receiver, questioned the debtor as to his affairs. In his deficiency account the bankrupt put down £247 as being loss through chemical smoke from some works near a farm in the neighbourhood of Halton. In examination he said that Mr. Percival, farmer, Daresbury, had esti- mated the damage to the crops at that amount. He took the bill to the works, and asked to be allowed something, but was ordered out of the office. The loss was incurred in 1879, and to that, loss of live stock; and agricultural depression, he attribu- ted his failure. Mr. Worsley said that the answers of the bankrupt had been very satisfactory, as also had been his conduct. Mr. P. Davies, on behalf of ft creditor, haying put a few questions, the exami- nation was declared closed.

I LOCAL PATEN-T.—Messrs. J. Porritt and J. S. Gar- land, of Warrington have taken out a patent for fastening india-rubber tyres on bicycles. Tim SPEAKER'S LEVEE.—The following gentle- men attended the Speaker's levde on Wednesday evening :—Mr. J. T. Brunner, Captain Cotton, and the lion. A. de TtAton Egerton. APPOINTMENT OP THE NEW COUNTY COURT JUDGE.—Mr. Coventry, barrister, has received a communication from the Treasury offering him the position of County Court Judge for the Preston dis- trict, which has become vacant through the resigna- tion of Mr. Hulton. He has accepted the offer. Mr. Coventry is a barrister of considerable experience and a well-known figure in the civil .and criminal courts of Manchester and the towns in the vicinity of that city. He has acted as revising barrister for Warrington The new post is stated to be worth £2,000 a year. DEATH OF A CENTENARIAN.—Mr. James Kean, af Warrington, died on Tuesday at the advanced age of 103 years, having attained that birthday in No- vember last, and being consequently at the time of his death in his 104th year. The deceased gentle- man, who was the father of Alderman Kean, had sixteen children, of whom four are living. He had 27 grandchildren and 28 great grandchildren. He was an exceptionally active man, and remarkable for his walking powers. For the long term of 63 years be was manager of a cotton mill. The late Mr. Kean was born at Tarporley, and then came to live at Warrington. He enjoyed excellent health, and was very vigorous, and did not take to his bed until about a fortnight ago. AN EARLESTOWN SWEEP IN A "DEPLORABLE STATE."—At Warrington County Court on Thursday John Carling, described as a master chimney-sweep, of Earlestown, applied to his honour Judge Ffoulkes for an administration order. Applicant said that his average earnings were about 15s a week, and he had six children and a sick wife to keep. He corn- ! plained of having been persecuted by one of his creditors and said that at present he was in a de- plorable state. Were his Honour to listen to his story from beginning to end it would make him cry. Mr. H. L. Riley (St. Helens), who appeared for the creditors, did not object to an order being made, and his Honour directed debtor to pay 3s a month. ATTEMPT TO UPSET AN EARLESTOWN TRAIN.— A dastardly attempt to upset a passenger train run- ning through EarleAown from Manchester to Liver- pool was made on Saturday night, when the 10-55 passenger train from Exchange Station, through Tyldesley and Leigh, and stopping at Earlestown at 1148, narrowly escaped being thrown off the rails about half-way between Tyldesley and Leigh and Bedford stations. Some time between 10-30 and 11-30, what is known as a "rant.," a piece of iron which weighs about 1:1-cwt., and is used at rail- way and colliery sidings when trucks have left the rails, was placed across one of the rails. The train, which was about a quarter of an hour late, struck the obstruction, and fortunately the engine kept the rails, the only damage done being a slight bend- ing of one of the rails, a sleeper was displaced, and a signal rod and wire broken. The " rant " was thrown off the rails, and carried a distance of 30 yards along the line. The train proceeded to Liver- pool a'ter a delay of twenty minutes. Many pas- sengers were in the train, but they all escaped in- jury. No clue has been found to the perpetrators of the outrage. THE PENMON QUARRIES, LIMITED.—We would direct the attention of investors to the prospectus in another column of this new company. It bears on the face of it evidence of its sound and genuine character. There is no promotion paid or to pay, luid the directors are engaged not only to take no less than £4,000 worth of shares, but to accept no remuneration for their services until a dividend of 10 per cent. has been paid to the preference share- holders. The total capital is --E50,000 of each. There will be £30,000 preference shares of .E 1 each, the holders of which will be entitled to a ten per cent. dividend. "The Quarries, which comprise an area of about 35 acres, are situated on the western side of the Menai Straits, in the Island of Anglesea, opposite Liverpool and within about two hours' sea voyage of that port. Penmon building stone is of the finest grain, and has been used in the construc- tion of some of the most important works in the Kingdom, amongst which may be mentioned the Britanniq, Tubular Bridge, the Holyhead Break- water, Birkenhead Docks, and Birmingham Town Hall. The marble, too, is greatly in demand for decorative purposes, as well as for chimney pieces and monuments. It can hardly be doubted that the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal will necessitate a large demand for the building stone, which is particularly suitable for such docks as are to be constructed at Manchester, Salford, _and War- rington, Altogether the prospects of this com- pany may be said to be exceedingly favourable. FATAL RESULT OF A RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—On Thursday afternoon Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the White Hart hotel, Sankey-street, Warrington respecting the death of a widow named Eliza Parke, sixty years of age, who died at the Infirmary on Tuesday.—Thomas liar- bourne, relieving officer, Wellfield-street, Warring- ton, said that he knew the deceased, who was a little eccentric in her manner, but not So much so as to be particularly noticeable.—James Woolley, a porter at Earlestown railway station, said that he saw deceased on the platform of the station on the 11th inst., and she asked for the train from Wigan. A train came in the station, and deceased stood on the platform. When the train had been set in motion it was found that deceased had been run over, her leg being almost taken off. She was lifted up, and at once taken to the waiting-room. She said, " I wish it had killed me," and afterwards ! asked for laudanum. She was conveyed to the In- firmary at Warrington.—Joseph Nelson, Ince, near Wigan, said that he saw deceased standing at the end of the opposite platform opposite the engine that he was driving. When the train had gone a few yards he felt something under the wheel. Wit- ness then corroborated the evidence as to her being taken to the waiting-room, and a nurse from the Infirmary said that deceased died from delirium and exhaustion -consequent upon her leg having to be amputated. Drs. Richmond, Smith, and Joseph attended deceased.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that deceased died as stated, but found that there was no evidence to show how she came on the line.

THE SHIP CANAL BlLL.—This bill came before the Committee on unopposed bills in the House of Corn- mon.s on Wednesday, Mr. L. Courtney presiding.— Mr. Chandos Leigh (Speaker's counsel) asked for the clauses in the Companies Clauses Act which were prohibitory of payment of interest out of capital,—Mr. Coates said they were Nos. 23 and 121, the former being prohibitory by inference•only:— Mr. Leigh: It is provided that .a dividend is not to - be paid so as-to reduce capital? That is so.—Mr.. Leigh: The aggregate amount is not 'to be deemed capital ?—Mr. Coates: Not the aggregate amount of ; £8,752,000. The meaning of this is that the £752,000' shall be looked upon as interest, and shall , not be reckoned in the borrowing. powers. _ We re- ' duce the borrowing, power pro tanto. If, for in- stance, 'we borrow £lOO,OOO, we would take off I .£25,000.—Mr. Leigh: What is the time given you by the Act of last year for the first instalment of .E 5,000,000 ?—Mr. Coates: Two years.—Mr. Leigh: So that you have to raise it by next year ?-11r. Coates: That is so; and that makes it all the more important that we should get our bill si*edily. The five million is in addition to what we raise for the Bridgewater undertaking.—Mr. Leigh: Is the Salford Corporation Bill opposed ?--11r. Coates: Yes; It proposes to contribute £250,000 towards the capital of the Canal Company.—ln the course of a conversation it was stated that according to Standing Order 215, a bill should pass third reading on the presentation of the report in the event of their being no amendments.—Mr. Leigh: This bill is not likely to be again discussed in the House.— Mr. Coates: I should think not.—The bill was then ordered for third reading.—salford Corporation and the Ship Canal The report of the Local Government Board upon th 6 bill empowering the Salford Cor- poration-to contribute .£250,003 to the Manchester Ship Canal has been issued. The Board submit for the consideration of the committee (which meets on Tuesday next) whether it is desirable that the Corporation should be allowed to borrow £250,000 for the purpose, and whether, unless it can be shown that the construction of the docks and works will be a direct advantage to the borough of Salford, it is desirable to confer on the Corporation any power of raising money for the purpose of taking shares in the company. Having regard to the fact that the purposes contemplaled do not come within the. ordinary duties of local authori- ties, that of late years a great increase has taken place in the indebtedness of local authorities, and that Parliament has in many cases refused to enter- tain propositions to subsidize trading concerns, the Board think the Committee should be very fully informed of the probability of the success of the undertaking. It seems desirable to the Board that the costs of promoting the bill should be examined ! in accordance with the provisions of the Municipal Corporations (Borough Funds) Act, 1872, or taxed by the taxing officer of the Rouse.

We notice the well-known firm of Kelly and Co. are compiling a new edition of their complete Lan- cashire Directory, the price to subscribers being 40s. R. Bidgood, 69, Legh-street, Warrington, is the local agent.—Advt..

-ANOTHER ALARMING LANDSLIP AT NORTHWICH. —During Thursday night eseriouslandslip occurred , behind the Wheat Sheaf Hotel, Northwich, a struc- ture which, about six months ago, had to be lifted 91t. The gable end of the wash-house disappeared into the earth, leaving a hole five yards wide and ten yards deep. The County Bridge over the Weaver, which is only a few yards off, is stated to have sunk two feet.

TILE LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOIL WARRINGTON.— The General Council of the Warrington Liberal As- sociation will meet on Monday evening next, at eight o'clock, in the Committee Room of the Liberal Club, for the purpose of receiving and acting upon Mr. Wm. Crosfield's reply to the unanimous invita- tion given him a month ago tobecome the candidate of the party at the next general election. Whatever the nature of Mr. Crosfield's reply may be, the gravity of the present political situation makes it so absolutely necessary that the Liberals of War- rington should be prepared for any emergency, that the importance of the business to be transacted will command the attendance of every member of the Council who can possibly be present. SERIOUS MAP ACCIDENT AT SANKEY BRIDGES.— On Wednesday evening a serious trap accident oc- curred opposite the chemical works at Sankey Bridges. Mrs. A. Parkes, of the Central Hotel, Widnes, who was accompanied by her Stepson and two children, was driving in a trap, when the horse became frightened at another horse that was back- ing in front of it. It plunged, throwing the occu- pants out of the conveyance. The lady was run over, sustaining a fracture of the ankle, and both children were cut about the head and face, and severely shaken. The alarmed horse, after running a distance, turned round, and would have passed over those thrown out of the trap, who were on the road, had not some people who had come up dragged them out of the way. Mrs. Parkes was taken to Widnes in a passing cab.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Thursday afternoon under the presidency of Mr. T. S. Timmis. Present—The Revs. Fathers Clarke and Finezan ; Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Bradshaw, Deacon, Imison, Glover, Robinson, and Danby (clerk).

WORE IN COMMITTEE. The District Education Committee reported that during February there were 93 applications for the payment of school fees and 280 persons appeared before them for con- travention of the Education Act. Fees were recommended to be paid in 90 cases, and 37 persons were convicted by the magistrates and one boy sent to an industrial school. On the recommendation et the committee, the salary of Mr. H. Davies, attendance officer, who had completed nine years' service, WAS increased according to the scale of the Board. On the recommendation of the School Management Com- mittee. the resignation of Mr. R. Gibson, assistant master, West Bank Scbol, was accepted; and Mr. James H. Brown was appointed certificated assistant master. senior boys' de- partment, West Bank School. Accounts amounting to £434 103 5d were passed for payment on the suggestion of the Finance Committee, who also reported that the school fees for February were as follow i—Simm's Cross £7O 4s ioa, Warrington-road £3l 17, id, West Bank £59 us THE TRAINING OF FEMALE PUPIL TEACHERS.

Mr. Cilover had given notice that he would ask the chair- man of the School Management Committee what was being done to remedy the present defective mode of teaching female pupil teachers. He observed that at the January meeting the Board were unanimous that a better system should be adopted.—Father Finegan replied tuat it was un- wise to supersede the present system until they saw the re• eults of the examinations which take place next month. They had had no means of ascertaining whether the sys- tem was defective or not, because last year they were ex- amined after on!y six months preparation, when it wes u.inal that there should be 12 months. preparation. At the same time he did not defend the system. He himself pre- ferred the old system. The committee had done nothing in the matter and did not intend to do so until the resalts of the examination were known.

div.head: ALLEGITIGN AGAINST THE CLERK.
div.p: ALLEGITIGN AGAINST THE CLERK.

Father Finegan drew attention to a paragraph which had appeared in a local newspaper, with regard to the difference that had existed between the School Management Commit- tee and the clerk. The revel. Father had received informa- tion that the clerk attempted to get the report of the dis- cussion at the last meeting suppressed, that he had given the information for the paragraph which appeared, and that one reporter had been offered a consideration to supprees the discussion in the newspapers.—The Clerk replied that immediately after the 'aet meeting of the Board the reporters were talking about the discussion, and inquired what all the disturbance was about. He told them that he. without the consent of the committee, had diverted a sta- tionery order, hoping to make a saving of between £5 and £lO, but that the committee had reported to the Board that that saving was 'met borne out. He never dictated that paragraph, and did not know it was going to appear. He denied absolutely that a "consideration" was offered for the seppres,ion of the discussion.—Two reporters said the Clerk's statement was quite true, but a third said he was offered a "consideration," but it was not by the Clerk, nor by anybody connected with the School Board.—Mr. Danby said he knew nothing about the offered bribe in any shape or forme7Father Finegan was not satisfied, and said unless the matter was settled satisfactorily he should ask for the whole of the proceedings to be made public. The charge against the Clerk in the first instance was not with diverting a stationery order, but with suppressing letters, and answering them without consulting the committee. In justice to the committee the whole question must be thrashed out, and he would give notice of a motion that would enable this to be done.—Tbe proceedings then concluded.

RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT RUNCORN. Talc INCREASED ASSESSMENTS. The annual nutting of the ratepayers of Runcorn took place on Thursday evening in Bethesda Schoolroom. There was a poor attendance. Mr. W. Handley was voted to the chair.

Messrs. W. Brookes and C. Cooke Were appointed auditors of the accounts of the Burial Board, and it was decided to hold.the meeting to receive their report on the 15th April. It was resolved that the following names of gentlemen qualified to act as overseers be submitted to the magistra- tes :—Messrs. W Handley, W. Whittaker, S. Taylor, E. Imison, W. Hankinson, and D. H. Jones. 'lle two first named gentlemen have filled the office for a number of years, and their abilities and services were referred to in highly Enlogistic terms. Mr.J. Simpson was appointed assessor of taxes, and Mr. W Sutton, the assistant overseer, collector of assessed • taxes. The Chairman made a statement of the finances of the overseers. He said the past year was commenced with a balance in hand of £562 Is 3d. The spring rate was levied at tenpence in the .C, and it produced £2,016 193 41; the autumn rate was levied at ninepecce in the X, and produced £1,861 15s 10d. For bank interest they hadreceived £1 6d, making the total capital £4,442 2s sd. This sum had been expended in the following manner :—Paid to the Guardian?, £2,783; School Board, £600; Burial Board, £220; registra- tion of voters under the new Franchise Act, £4O 14s 101; assistant overseer's salary, office expenses, and sundriee, £268 23 41; balance, £530 53 3d. At the beginning of the year the rateable value was £50,989, and it now stood at £51,938. Comparing the payments with those of last year, the following results were shown. The sum of £265 was paid to the Guardians less than in the preceding year. The Burial Board had received £lOO more, and the School Board aso more. The cost of the registration of voters had been increased but not at a rate commensurate with the amount of work performed. The number of voters had been increased Nom 424 to 2,400, but although this was six times the number, the cost had only been three times as much as the previous year. He understood there had been some soreness felt at certain old properties in the town having been increased during the past year. and he took that opportunity of ex- plaining how it had arisen. It was certainly not due to the action of the overseers. The Guardians of the Union for some years had felt that the basis for connty rating was un- equal, and they commenced an agitation some years ago which had only borne practical fruit that year, the result being that a new county basis was prepared by the Justices showing an increased ratable value of something like £ll,OOO for county purposes over the poor rate valuation. The Guardians felt that they could not stand this increase, and appealed against it. Mr. H. Linaker and himself repre- sented the Union in the appeal, and they pointed out rhe great difference between the two assessments. The Justices met them with this reply: "Our valuation is right and yours is wrong." On behalf of the Guardians they said that they felt sure their own valuation was right, as they obtained it from actual rents paid. This led to explana- tions, and the deputation found that the magistrates took their valuation at the highest they could get. If the pro- perty tax assessment was the highest they took that, and if the poor rate assessment was the highest they tuk that, and thus they got the £ll,OOO increase.. (Leughte-.) The magistrates said that in order to convince them that they were right they would order a copy of the property tax assessment to be sent to them, and in due time that document was received, when it was found there were certain townships very much lower than they were assessed to the poor rate. Rureorn being one of these. In fact, Run- corn was about £3,000 lower, and that was the way the as- sesments wcre got at. Ultimately the matter was com- promised by the Runcorn valuation being increased by the sum of £l,OOl. No doubt in individual cases there had been some hardship, but if such cases were taken before the Assessment Committee they would get the redress they de- served. After this explanation the public would under- stand 801116 of the difficulties which the overseers had had to cool:told with, and over which they had had no control. • A vote of thanks was passed to the chairman, on the moa. tion of Mr. D. Bisbrown, seceded by Mr. Moss.

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

_— WARRINGTON BOROUGH. POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess and Mr. John Fairclough. AN UNFEELING FATNEst.—John Worthington, a baker, was sent to prison for three months, with hard labour, for deserting his wife and four children. Last year prisoner served a similar term of imprisonment for the same offence, and the cost to the ratepayers in supporting hie family amounts to £56 When apprehended, he was working at Walton, near Liverpool. DESERTION.—John Langley, charged with being a deser- ter from her Majesty's South Lancashire Regiment, stationed at Orford Barracks, was remanded to await an escort. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- _

man Davies and Catincillor Greening. HARD LlNES.—William Durkia was charged with neglect- ing to maintain his two children, who had become charge- able to the Union. Mr. Shearer said that prisoner had more children than he could keep, Aid prisoner, whoss wife is dead, said that he had got work at Widnes and would pro- vide a home for them when he was able. The magistrates adjourned the case for a month for defendant to -carry out his promise. THEFT OF RAWITS. William Connor, fish hawker, James-street, and John Duane, bricksetter's labourer. Heath- side, were charged with stealing three rabbits from a stall in the market, belonging to William Lawless, 4, Corporation- street. The theft was committed on Saturday evening, both prisoners having evidently been under the influ- ence of drink. They were each sent to prison to undergo _ _

two months' hard labour. MISCELLANEOUS.—George Hopkins was fined 5s and costs for being drunk in Buttermarket-street on the previ- ous evening.—John Murphy was summoned by his wife for assaulting her on the 6th inst, but the magistrates disrAissed the case at the request of the wife,, who wished to forgive her husband.—Mary Coyne and Catherine Connolly were each fined Ns and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road.—John Glynn, who appeared in answer to an adjourned summons charging him with keeping locig4rs without having his house registered, was dismissed with a caution. TUESDIY.—Bcfore Councillor Broadbent and Mr. R.
Garnett.

THE BEGGING Nulsmia4-.—James Smith, a stranger, was I charged with begging on the previous evening. Mr.Broad- bent remarked that there saemed to be a good deal of beg- ging going on at present, and Chief Constable Hunt said that the sour) kitchens were rather inviting to the float- ing population. Prisoner was discharged with a repri- mand.—John Dooley, for begging in Church-street, on the previous evening, was sent to prison for seven days. DELNICENNESS.—John Daley, a soldier, who received a good character, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Sankev-street, on the previous evening; he was dis- missed.—William Roberts, for being drunk and disorderly at Market-gate, on the previous evening, was fined ss, includ- ing costs. BEATING A WOMAN.—Edward Griffin, forge labourer, was charged with assaulting Mary Knockton, fustian cutter, a young woman, on Saturday. Prisoner knocked her down and kicked her severely. It was thought that his motive was that complainant some time ago informed the police that some men were about to rob a drunken person, and that prisoner was one of the men. He was sent to prison for a month. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Pickmere and Councillor
Greening.

REMANDED ON SUSPICION.—WiII. Simpson, a youth, was charged with offering in pledge a child's skirt, respecting the possession of which he was not able to give a satisfac- tory explanation.—He was remanded for inquiries to be made. DRUNIKENNESS.—Margaret Beatty was charged with be- ing drunk in Queen-street on the previous evening. She was found on the doorstep, and had to be locked up for safety.—The Bench reprimanded the prisoner, and allowed her to go THIIRSDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess and Major Litton.

BAD CHARACTERS.—MichaeI Gallagher and Thomas Garritty, young men, were brought up on suspicion charged with loitering with intent to commit a felony. They re- ceived a very bad character, having frequently been in trouble, and were each sent to prison for two months with hard labour.—lncldentally, the Chief Constable remarked that robberies of late had been very frequent, and men- tioned that on Saturday night the League Hall was broken into and £3 10s in cash was; stolen. FRlDA.Y.—Before Mr. John White, Mr. R. Garnett, and
Dr. Gornall.
DRUNKENNESS.— Michael Livesey and James Gwynne were charged with drunkenness, and were ordered to pay is each.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. Mospes.—Before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. F. H. Gossage. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence the following were fined : Patrick Tarleton, John Fes, William Egan. John Keogh, Catherine McNamara, Martin Quinn, and George Mitchell. A NOISY APPLETON WOMAN.—For shouting and making a great disturbance at Appleton on the 13th inst, Elizabeth Walsh was bound over to keep the peace for three months in the usual sureties.

div.head: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.

MONDAY.—Before Mr. Jas. Reynolds, Rev. E. A. P. Camp-1 bell, and Capt. C. W. Haalehurst. CIIIININIES ON FlRE.—Henry Heaton was fined ad and costs 9s 61, for permitting the chimney of his dwelling- house to be on fire.—James Turnbull, Albert-terrace, was dealt with in a similar fashion for a like offence. OBSTRUCTING CHURCH-STREET. John Williams and Joseph Henry Santley, youths, were charged with having on Sunday night, the seventh March, obstructed Church-street by loitering on the footpath there.—P.S. Neild and P.C. Smith proved the case, and each defendant was fined is, and costs IN 6d. UNREGISTERED LODGING HOUSE. Catherine Morris, was charged under a warrant with keeping an unregistered lodging-house on the 28th May. Mr. W. H. Linaker ap- peared on behalf of the Commissioners, and the case was proved by Mr. Percival, inspector of nuisances. A fine of 103, and costs £1 Os Bd, or a month's imprisonment waa imposed. DRIVING WITHOUT REINS —For this offence, committed at Newton, John Craig and George Edge were each fined is, and costs 9s ad. ASSAULT.—Kate Crogan pleaded guilty to having on the 18th March assaulted Mary Nelson, and she was fined ss, and costs Os ad or seven days. A RUNAWAY.—Thomas Morris, a boy, was charged with absconding frcm the Stockport Industrial School, and he was ordered to be handed over to the school authorities.
P RESCOT- THE DISTRESS IN PRESCOT UNION.

Owing to the depression in the watchmaking trade many of the families of Prescot are in a very distressed state, and a relief committee has been formed. The first meeting of the committee was held on Saturday, several ministers and other gentlemen being present. After a discussion respect- ing the best means of relieving the distress, a list was pre- pared and a large number of relief tickets given to the clergy for distribution. On Monday afternoon a meeting of the Prescot Board of Guardians, the members of which, at the last meeting of the Board, resolved themselves into a committee to fully consider the question of the distress Prevalent in the union, was held at Whiston Work- house. Mr. John Weatherbarrew presided, and there were about seventeen members present, in- cluding Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, J.P., ex-officio. The Clerk (Mr. Hartley) explained what was suggested by the Local Government Board as the best means to adopt to relieve distress without stigmatising the unemployed as paupers In districts in which exceptional distress pre- vailed, the Local Government Board recommended that the Guardians should confer with the local authorities, and en- deavour to arrange with the latter ,for the execution of works on which unskilled labour might be immediately em- ployed. In reply to a question, the Clerk said there was no exceptional distress in the Union more than when he wrote in February to the Local Government Board about the Prescot watchmakers, and explained that hard labour would render them unfit to follow their own trade afterwarde. In fact, he explained that they had not applied for relief, although they were in a very distressed condition.—Mr.Newsome said he felt mire there was a necessity for relief works being commenced.—Mr. Tyrer thought the fact that a large number of men were on the streets might to some extent be explained by the fact that Monday, in some !Niles and occupations, was treated as a holiday.—The Chairman said there had been a deputation from Widnes on the last Board day, and it was said they were invited to come. By whom were they invited ? The Rev. T. Finegan said he did not know.—The Chairman said he had made inquiries, which led him to think that they re- presented men who did not care about work.—Another Guar- di an remarked that the sample they saw was sufficient to

FOOTBALL. Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played .on Saturday must be sent tc thebead office. Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
I

play now being la the visitors' 26, where Barnes drew first I blood for Warrington' by a very good attempt at goal, a minor resulting. Nothing came from the kick out. Far- rell having a free kit* next acceded to him, nothing being gained. The visitors' forwards now tried to equalise the soore, but Massey stopped their career by a timely kick to touch. This brought tic the ire of home forwards, who replied by taking the ball back again, Plumpton, however, showed by his play that he was quite worthy of his posi- . . _ .

ton, saving by a fits pant to half way. Speakman now transferred to Barnes, who threaded his way through tbe thick of his opponents, finishing up by dropping o goal, deafening cheers rending the air, bats dying about in all directions. The visitors' forwards now seemed to lose
heart, another minor shortly afterwards resulting, after some fine forward play on behalf of Ashton, Hayes, and _ _ _

Davies. For some time play was very even until Massey seconded Speakman's effort, taking the oval to the 25, the visitors by a combined dribble removing to centre. Gilbert next showed up by a run and passed to Barnes, who gained ground. Widnes now seemed to have a chance of scoring, but failed to take it, their passing at this point being wretched. Half-time was now called, the ball in neutral ground. After regaling themselves with lemons, etc., ends were exchanged, Fair. Turner putting the ball in motion for home team, the same player tackling •Purvia before any return could be made. The Warrington forwards led off with a danger us dribble, Rigby, Dillon, Heyes, and Povey, showing well up. Smith now broke away front the pack, being collared by Buxton in the hems 23. :A general stampede now took place, the grand stand, which was literally packed with spectators, giving way, fortunately ne one being very seriously hurt. This stopped any play for some time, and great praise is due to the members of the club, and also to the members of the constabulary, for the able manner in which they kept the excited spectators from crowding round it. Turner commenced hostilities again by a good kick, again collaring before a return eould be made. Some excellent scrimmages were the next feature, the home team slightly gaining, eventually Bingham gained ground by a good kick to touch. The backs had now each a turn, Buxton returning a kick and Plumpton stopping a rush. Good forward play was the next feature on the part of the visitors' team, Smith Purvin, and Corns being conspicuous., Farrell and Harding also improved matters by a good piece of passing, Massey doing the needful in the way of checking their progress. The home forwards led by E. Dillon, Heyes, and Ashton, now replied by a rush to the line, Heyes al- most scoring, the danger being removed by a good kick from Plumpton. Gilbert now tried his goal kicking powers, his drop being nearly successful. Not much came of Far- rell's kick-eff, the home forwards being too much on the alert. Ashton and Tamer were new chiefly instrumental in taking the ball to the 25, Plumpton once more relieving his side. For five or ten minutes both sides strove for the mastery, eventually Speakman got hold, and by a piece of good play, got < ver after going through the thick of the Widnes ranks, but the place was not improved upon by the same player. Ashton Stopped the kick out, and up to time nothing further was scored nor anything very interesting took place. The referee galling time, Warrington were de- clared winners by 1 goal, 1 try, and 4 minors, to nil., after a splendid contested game. Cheer after cheer went up for the winners, but when the teams got to the 'bus Tommy Barnes, the hero of the day, was missing, being collared before he could get off the field, and carried shoul- der high through the streets to the dressing-room. Singling out individual play, Fair. Turner's form (according to Widnes idea) was fit for any county, his play and tackl- ing on Saturday last being perfect. Harry Ashton worked exceedingly well in the scrimmage, also dribbling finely. the above two players being the best forwards on the field. Heyes on Saturday last played a splendid game, and if he continues in this form no doubt an international cap will be offered to him. The brothers Dillon, Rigby, and Povey also showed well in the dribble, in fact all the forwards played a good honest game. Speakman and Gilbert com- pletely non-plussed their opposing half backs, the former seeming to mesmerise the Widnes team by his tactics. The two wing three-quarter backs played a good game, but little Tommy was the hero of the match, dodging, passing, and dropping at goal with great success. Buxton was one of the unemployed." Plumpton deserves especial praise for his play on behalf of Widnes. Harding, Bingham, Farrell, and smith seconding him, but with no success attached to their efforts. Warrington: Full back, Buxton ; three- quarter backs, Jolley, Barnes, and Massey; half backs, Gilbert awl Speakman; forwards. Davies, Ashton (cap- tain), wr, Dillon, Fairfield Turner, Frank Turner, Povey, Rigby, E. Dillen, and Heyes. Widnes : Full back, Plump- ton ; three-quarter backs, Harding, Bingham, Pennington ; half backs, Farrell (captain), Ridyard ; forwards, Smith, Purvin, Hardman, Gandy, Corns, Goulding, J. Bingham, Meggher, and Hughes.

ASSOCIATION RULES. PRBSCOT V. LIVERPOOL GYMNASIUM (A TEAM).—This match was played on Saturday, on the around of the former, the Gymnasium winning by 5 goals to 2. EARLESTOWN V. CHESTBR.—The return match between these clubs was played at Chester on Saturday afternoon. The result was a victory for Chester by two goals to One.

_ T. HELENS AMATEURS V. WIIISTOIT ASSOCIATION.— The Amateurs journeyed to Whiston on Saturday :to meet the club of that district, when, after a very hard and well. fought game, they obtained the victory over the home team by four goals to three. EAELESTOWN OLYMPIC 'T. EARLESTOWN ROTERS.—This return match was played on Saturday on the ground of the latter, and an exciting game resulted in a draw, four goals each. Sideleley (Farlestoivn Association) assisted the Rovers, while Percival (Sankey Refiners) played for the Olympians. Mr. J. James was referee. STUNSHAW CROSS WANDERERS V. OOLBORNE.—PIayed at Gol borne on Saturday before a large number of specta- tors. From the first the game was a very fast one, and the play very even. At half-time the score was in favour of Golborne by one goal to nil. The visitors ultimately won a pleasant game by three goals to one. About five minutes before the finish G. Clough met with a slight accident, hav- ing to leave the field. Go'borne team :—W. Jenkineon, goal; H. Davies, G. Clough, full backs; J. Clark, J. Dick- inson, W. Unsworth, half-backs; R. Morris, A. Allen, right wing; T. Kay, J. Flynn, left wing; J. Lowe, centre. LIVERPOOL CuP COMPETITION.—SEMI-FINAL.—BOOTLE T. HAYDOCIC.— Considerable interest was evinced in the meeting of the teams at Stanley (Liverpool) on Saturday afternoon, especially as Haydock had shown form above the average during the season; and thete was consequently an excellent attendance. Play during the first ten minutes was somewhat akin to a scramble ; but afterwards Bootle settled down and held the upper hand, winning by four goals to nil. Teams :—Bootle: G. Galbraith, goal ; T. Veitch and W. Veitch, backs; R. Devlin, T. Gibson, and F'. Woods, half backs; W. Routledge, T. Morris, W. Roberts, Eyton-Jones, and H. Anderson, forwards. Hay- dock: Taylor, goal; Hatton and Baines, backs; Wedg- wood, Carter, and Allen, half backs; Twist, Harrison, S 13arriscn, Moran, and Blackie, forwards. Referee, Mr. S Ormerod (Accrington). WIGAN CUP.—FINAL TIE.—EXTRtORDINARY SCENE.— About 2,000 spectators assembled at Wigan, on Saturday, to witness the final tie of of the competition for the Wigan and District Challenge Cup, which had been announced to be played between Wigan and Ilindley. A long delay was occasioned owing to the Hindley men objecting to the um- pires selected by the Association, and then the Westhough- ton team broke on to the ground in their shirt sleeves, as- serting their right to play on the protest which arose out of the match Wigan v.Westkoughton the previous week, and stating that the committee of the competition had bungled over the matter, first disqualifying Westhoughton and then deciding to reconsider the matter. A scene of confusion followed. The Wigan Chief Constable came on to the ground, and a conference was held in mid-field. The referee blew his whistle, but the malcontents refused to budge. Just after four o'clock the ball was kicked off, Westhough- ton and Wigan men combining and kicking indiscrimin- ately. The event was unprecedented in the whole annals of football. The game was stopped, and another impromptu discussion held. Then the Westhoughtonites retreated, and a re-start was effected. Spectators hooted all round for no apparent cause, and there was no real essay at a match, though Wigan claimed to have won by 2 goals to 0. In the end the spectators took possession of the ball, and the match ended.

POISONED FOXES IN CHESHIRE. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. I James Reynolds and Captain C. W. Haelehurst, Geo. Percival and John Percival, farmers of Park Side Farm, Aston-by-Sutton, were summoned to answer a charge of having knowingly and wilfully set or placed or caused to. be placed on land in his occupation cer- tain flesh or meat, to wit, a sheen s paunch which was mixed with, steeped in. or impregnated with certain poison or some poisonous ingredient so as to render the said meat poisonous and calculated to destroy life contrary to section 2 of the Poisoned Flesh Protection Act, 1864. Mr. Percy Davies, solicitor, Warrington, appeared on behalf of Wm. Henry Howe, gamekeeper in the employ of Mr. A. C. Talbot, of Aston Hall, who had laid the information. Mr. A. E. Fletcher, solicitor, of Northwich, defended, and pleaded not guilty.—Mr. H. Linaker, agent to the Aston estate, was present.—The allegation was that on the 29th January Howe was was out shooting with a party of gentlemen, when in a cabbage field occupied by the defendants he found a potato hamper, turned bottom upwards, and with an iron hurdle on the top. Upon removing these a sheep's paunch was exposed to view. He replaced the hamper and hurdle. Next day Jno. Bodwialr, an underkeeper, and a boy named Joseph Thompson were in the same neighbourhood with a valuable spaniel dog. The dog licked a portion of the meat which was protruding from the hamper and shortly afterwards died in convulsions. Its tongue and gums were black, and there was every appearance of poisoning. Within a few hundred yards of the same spot the dead bodies of two foxes were found, and the tongues and gums of these animals were also black. Howe scraped from the sheep's paunch a sugary substance which had that morning been submitted to Mr. A. J. Haddock, A.1.C., chemist at the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Co.'s works, and he pronounced it to be strychnine. Howe made a claim for compensation for the loss of his dog, but the defendants said be must take his own course. Howe and the boy Thompson gave evidence of an admission made by John Percival when accused of using poison. They alleged that he stated "It's the first time I have used the stuff and it shall be the last." Howe said the defendant's sheep dog, which he had been accused of shooting, bad also been poisoned.— After the evidence for the prosecution had been given Mr. Fletcher submitted that there was no ease against George Percival.—The Bench concurred, and dis- missed the charge against that defendant. —Mr. Flet- cher said the sole object of Howe was to obtain from Messrs. Percival compensation for his dog. He had given notice of action in the County Court, and it was practically admitted that it was not for the pur- pose of punishing the defendants that this prosecu- tion was undertaken, but for the purpose of creating additional evidence wherewith to bolster up tiffs. County Court proceedings. He contended that under the A.ct of Parliament any poisonous substance, as it was alleged in the present case, must be exposed and obviously intended to catch any animal whieh might be straying in that direction. It was perfectly clear that in this case there had been no exposure, and he held that there was no evidence showing that Messrs Percival had laid or caused to be laid any poison John Percival instructed him to indignantly deny that the alleged conversation had taken place.—Wm. Wylde, a shepherd in the employ of Messrs. Percival was called, and stated that it was his custom to kill sheep in the field when there was anything the mat- ter with them. It was also customary to leave the paunches in the field. He killed a sheep in the cab bage field a day or two before the 29th January, and placed the paunch under a hamper, so that the other sheep could not get at it. He never saw it after- wards and had no instructions to put poison upon it. —George Percival deposed that neither he nor his brother had ever given instructions to anyone in their employ to lay poison down. Poison had never been used on their farm except for vermin.—Mr. Reynolds said the Bench were of opinion that if poison had been laid down the defendants knew nothing of it, and the case would therefore be dismissed.
