WAVETITREB V. Sr. RBLENS.—These clubs met en the 13th inst., at Wavertree, to contest the first round of the cup, and after a hard fought game St. Helens scored five and Wavertree three minor points. According to the rules the teams had to meet again, and Saturday last was the ap- pointed time; and after a fast spell of play victory just rested with the St. Helens club. At the call of time an extra twenty minutes' play was decided en by the referee, during which the game was fast and furious. The only result was a try to the visitors, which Hairelden endeavoured to convert into a goal. At the close of play the game was called—SL Helens, one goal, a try, and two minor points; Wavertree, one goal and three minor points. For their re- spective sides, Hoyle,Woeodward, Chatham, Peters, Tickle, James, and Pennington especially distinguished themselves. The visitors were the stroegest in the pack, while the vil- lagers showed well in the open. Teams :—Wavertree: F. Hoyle, back; T. Woodward, P. Morton, and A. " Chat- ham," three-quarter backs; J. M. Spedding and C. F. Dodd, half backs; G. Grierson, T. Singleton, E. Bes- zint, R. Wilcock, J. Morton, Parry, T. Greenfield, Parr, and W. Peters (captain), forwards. St. Helens : A. Tickle. back ; IL Pennington, E. Foreman, and W. Haselden, three-quarter backs; H. Varley (captain), and A. Borth- wick, half backs; C. Anders, T. Pennington, J. Halton, T. Finney, R. Twist, D. McLaughlin, James, J. Barnett, and T. Rogers, forwards. Sr. HELENS RECREATION V. LiTHERLAND.—Tbese teams met at Litherland, on Saturday, in the second round of the contest, and a capital game ended in favour of the Recrea- tion by one try and two minor points to two minor points. Litherland have objected to the try on the ground of in- formality. Teams :—St. Helens Recreation : W. E. Tay- lor, back; R. Langley, John Hankinson, and J. Gregson, three-quarter backs; J. Pilkington and T. Green, half backs ; W. Parr (captain), W. Cook, J. Pyke, James Hankinson, W. Dean, H. Ashton, J. Gaskell, A. Smith, and H. Gregson, forwards. Litherland : J. Webster, back.; D. Banks, H. Johnstone, and J. Helms, threttequarter backs; T. Larkin and G. Hayworth, half backs; J. Holme, T. McManus, J. Murphey, W. :Murphey, R. Harding, E. Fyles, J. Potts, J. Ridcherson, and J. Larkin, forwards. WALTON T. Sr. Ilnuers.—On Wednesday, on the Bootle ground, Marsh-lane, these clubs met to play off their tie in the second round of the competition. The weather was beautifully fine, and the attendance fairly large, and very enthusiastic.- The St. Helens team was exactly the same ILS defeated Wavertree last Saturday in the first round, and showed to much bett2r advantage than Walton, who were weak forward. The game was well contested, but it was ,clearly shown from the start that the Saints were too quick and smart for their heavier opponents, the latter bsing 'beaten by twelve points to two, viz., a goal and four minor points to two minor points. The winners will play War- rington on Saturday in the third round. RUNCORN v. LEIGH.

The Runcorn first fifteen journeyed to Leigh on Satur- day to compete against the football team of that town in the second round of the Challenge Cup competition of the West Lancashire and Border Towns Union, Although Leigh boasted of an unbeaten record for this season, the Runcorn team anticipated an easy victory over their corn- paratively unknown opponents, but in the end the Cheshire lads had themselves a narrow escape of defeat. When the ball was kicked off shortly after four o'clock nearly three thousand spectators, to which Runcorn contributed a com- paratively small proportion, lined the enclosure, and from start to finish made it knewn which way their sympathies lay by vociferous shouts and groans. As regards weight the teams were prettily equally balanced, but in passing and general skill Runcarn had considerably the pull over their sturdy opponents. The ground, however, was very soft and slippery, and in some places water to the depth of several inches covered the ground, making a really effective game impossible. Leigh kicked off, and some give and take play ensued, bat within five minutes of the commencement the home team, by a capital combined rush, forced the ball over the visitors' line, and Lonsdale secured a try, which. however' was not improved upon. Runcorn were still pressed, but Lunt and Speakman afforded some relief, and the ball was gradually worked iuto Leigh terrritory, and a touchdown was conceded. Leigh now looked dangerous, but from a scrimmage H. Hughes made a good dodgy run, and landed a try; Lewis kicked a neat goal. Packed scrimmages were the order of the day, but the superior passing of Runcorn began to tell, and Speakman was given , a nice chance to drop a goal, through a pass by the Run- earn captain, but he stumbled on the slippery ground and missed the leather. Play was transferred to the Runcorn half, but the Leigh territory was invaded by Lunt, who made a splendid run, being pushed into touch in the Leigh 25, and shortly afterwards the whistle sounded half-time. On re- suming, Leigh played up with great determination, and were ultimately rewarded by a rather lucky try. The attempt at ' goal failed. The scoring of the teams was now almost equal, land the greatest excitement prevailed, which was added to by the fact that play was of a rough description, and blood was flowing from more than one Runcorn player. A neat I pass enabled Johnson to secure a meritorious try, but Lewis l did not add the premier point. Speakman shortly after- wards crossed the line, but was ruled back on the ground at a forward pass. Pendlebury of the home team commenced a dribble, which ought to have been easily stopped by Woods who, however' stumbled. Johnson overtook the dribbler and attempted to kick the ball dead, but failed, and Pendlebury dropped upon it, and scored a try, which was converted into a goal. The game then stood Leigh 17 points, Runcorn 14, and there only remained ten minutes to play, but just before the call of time, Runcorn forced Leigh to touch down, and thus escaped defeat. An extra fifteen minutes was played, and the superior stamina and skill of the visitors told wonderfully hi this short time. They made "rings round" their opponents and a try was quickly credited to Wright. Lewis kicked the ball beautifully over the bar, but a Leigh player alleged that the ball struck his fingers as it was going up, and the referee only allowed the try. From a line-out the ball was passed to Speakman, who was collared on the line, but speedily scrimmaging the ball, he carried it over the line, and being closely followed by Johnson, that player secured a try. A protest was made that the ball was passed forward, and the referee stating he was unable to give a decision, as he could not see the play from his position, the Runcorn captain persisted in kicking the ball, and Lewis notched a goal. The Leigh men now refused to play, and the referee kicked off on their behalf, and Wright was just planting a try when the whistle was blown for time, and the referee would not allow the point. The game now stood—Runcorn 31 points, Leigh 17. Leigh, however, protested against 12 of the points, and the subject came before the committee of the Union during the even- ing at Liverpool. They decided that as the referee had net seen the points, the game should be a draw, and played off at Runcorn during the week. The Runcorn team was as follows back, T. Woods; three-quarter backs, E. Lunt, H. C. Speakman, and T. Johnson; half backs, H. Hughes and H. Andrews; for- wards, W. Hughes, W. Wright, J. Lewis, J. Gatley, J. Clarke. J. Barnes, F. J. Joule, G.Wainwright, and W Faulk- ner. Umpires: Messrs. R. Hughes and George Black. Referee: Mr. F. H. Hibbert, Chorley. The spectators were very boisterous, and on more than one occasion during play threatened the referee with vio- lence whilst disputed points were under discussion. One man shook his fist in his face, and said he would "knock his head off." Mr. Hibbert was heard afterwards to say that he would not referee at Leigh again for £5O. WARRINGTON V. WIDNES.

2ND ROUND OF CUP TIE (W.L.B.T.U.)—Warrington on Saturday presented a very animated appearance. Ther reason being that Warrington had to meet the well-known Widnes Club to see who should prove victors for the above trophy. The draw took place a fortnight ago at the Goat Hotel. Speculation since that time being pretty rife on the affair, the home supporters strongly fancying the boys in white, and Widnes were pretty confident that their club would not have its colours lowered. Going along Bridge- street about half-past one were numbers who seemed anxious to be in time to secure a good place, whilst an hour later, I especially after the Widnes supporters arrived, the route from the Central to the field was literally packed with people. The visitors' players stopped at the Griffin (the head quarters of the Warrington Club) and were soon ready for the field of action. The time for kicking off was adver- tised for 3-30, and at the time stated Widnes bounded over the wall into the field of play and were greeted with a mighty cheer from the 10,000 spectators assembled round the enclosure. The home team immediately followed, also coming in for a renewed cheer, and rif,ht well they looked in their clean white singlets, Fair. Turner being taken in turn for an International, County., or " Half County " (as Buxton calls it) man, his badge lookipg very neat. The weather was in every way favourable, and this accounts for the large concourse of people assembled, some whom perhaps could not afford to pay availing themselves of the chimneys of the adjoining houses in order to witness the proceedings. The ground was rather soft, thus hindering fast play to some extent. All the preliminaries being settled Farrell kicked off on be- half of the visitors, Gilbert returning to centre, Harding re- plying to the home 25. For a short time Widnes seemed to have the best of it, which raised the hopes of the visitors' supporters. Rigby was the first to shine by a bit of loose being aided by Speakman and Fair. Turner, but Bing- ham stopped the rush before dangerous. Good scrimmages were next the order of the day until Massey had a chance, but preferred to punt to touch. Fair. Turner at the end of the line showed prominently in the collaring department, at this period frustrating the passes of the Widnes backs. A good rush was now stopped by Bingham. Barnes now gained a lot of ground by a good kick along the line, the same player shortly afterwards passing smartly to Jolley, who got in a smart run. For a short time from now the home team looked as if they were giving an exhibition of the passing game, Massey, Barnes, Speakman, and Jolley being tli‘e parties engaged. This gained a lot of ground, the

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The second round of the Cup Ties brought the Warring- ton and Widnes teams together on Saturday at Warrington. It was the most important watch in the competition, and many observations were made that the winners of this tie would pull off the cup. There can be no doubt but it was a crucial snatch, and was looked upon throughout the union with a vast amount of interest. As the time arrived specula- tion was rather brisk, Warrington being the favourites for money. When Farrell showed the way into the enclosure the team were vociferously cheered, and on the appearance of the "Primrose and Blue," decked in their fine white jerseys, a tremendous shout greeted them. Losing the toss Farrell had to face the wind. The first ten minutes the visitors were in the ascendancy, but afterwards the stamina—now so chief a characteristic in their play—of the Warringtonians, asserted their superiority throughout. The Chemicals were never in the hunt, their united efforts were continually repelling attacks, and standing on the de- fensive. They made a few rushes, but were only spasmodic dying away very rapidly. The backs had many opportunities. but the tackling of their opponents was too effective. The forwards had plenty of power, and used their feet very cleverly at times, and had there been more combination. would have given a vast amount of trouble. J. H. Smith was the shining light, and along with Corns, Perrin, Hard- man, and Gonlden, worked very hard. Plumpton made a grand back, his:kicking and tickling saved his side many times from danger. Of the othe others, Harding, Farrell, and Ridyard were very prominent. The display of the victors was undoubtedly a grand one, and to nil an organisa- tion of the front rank as 'Widnes, the performance is a re- markable one. The team worked splendidly together, under- derstood one another in their passing, which was clean, and plenty of length with It. The most striking feature in their play was the determined manner in which the forwards worked, like veritable Trojans, packing smartly and holding the scrimmage, and then letting out the oval for the half backs. Speakman was in rare form, and the victory achieved on Saturday was in a great measure brought about by his play, and that of Barnes and the forwards. St. Helens qualify for the third round by beating Walton on Wednesday, and will meet Warrington on Saturday. The following additional results of the West Lancashire Cup competition were officially announced at a..lneeting of the committee, held at the Goat Hotel, Liverpool, on Saturday evening :

- KAY'S COMPOUND, a demulcent anodyne expectorant, for Coughs at d Colds. Bold by all Chemists, 91d, Is, Is lid, Es 9d.— Advt. Twelve destitute Syrians have been landed at Liver- pool, and are now being maintained at the cost of the rate- payers. The Rev. John Guttridge, United Methodist Free Church minister, died at his residence, Plymouth Grove, en Mon- day. He was 67 years of age. TRAGEDY AT BRIGHTON.—At Brighton on Thursday afternoon a man named Metcalf, landlord of the Lion Inn, St. James's-street, shot his wife. The customers in the bar hearing the discharge rushed upstairs and found the woman in a pool of blood on the landing near her bedroom, baying been shot in three places. Metcalf was discovered dead in the upper room, having shot himself through the head with a revolver. It is stated the man had been in financial difficulties and was that day to have transferred the business to his wife'f father, a Mr. Williams, and some family disagreement had arisen. Mrs. Metcalf died about a quarter-past five on Thursday evening. As the result of further inquiries, it has been ascertained that the man was 32 and the woman 26 years of age. They had been married about two years, lived very unhappily, and had twice separated.

WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB. A special general meeting of the members of this club was held at the White Bell Inn, Horsemarket- street, Warrington, on Wednesday evening, when the chair was occupied by Mr. John Marsh, the president.—The minutes of a committee meeting recommended "That it is expedient to impose im- port duties upon corn, sugar, and manufactured goods from foreign countries, but not upon articles from OUT colonies."—Mr. THOMAS STELFOX proposed as au amendment that the minutes be passed with the exception to the recommendation referred to. He spoke strongly in favour of free trade, especi- ally in land and minerals.—Mr. JOHN DARBYSHME seconded the amendment, and remarked that the remarks of Mr. Stelfox had his entire sympathy. —The CHAIRMAN said that the manufactured arti- cles that came into this country amounted in value to millions each year, and if that money went into the pockets of the artisans, it would be better both for them and the farmers, for whenever trade was brisk farmers could demand prices for their pro- duce.—After a little further discussion the amend- ment, on being put to the meeting, was lost, and the minutes were carried in their entirety.—The SECRETARY (Mr. J. L. Stelfox) said that he had re- ceived from Mr. Brunner, M.P. for the Northwich DiviSion, the copies of five bills which were now before Parliament, dealing with agricultural in- terests. Three of these bills seemed to be of im- portance. One was for the better regulation of canal and - railway traffic, one a bill to amend the law relating to the recovery of tithe rent charge, and the third was the Game Laws Amentment Bill. He (the secre- t tary) suggested that a resolution should be passed ,expressing approval of the principles of these bills, and asking the various members of Parliament for ' this naighbourhood to do their utmost to support their passage through the House of Commons.—Mr. JOHN DARBYSHIRE thought it would be better to leave the consideration of such a resolution over till they had had time to consider the contents of the bills.—The SECRETARY, however, pointed out that before another meeting of the club could be held the bills would have been dealt with by the House of Commons.—Mr. THOMAS STELFOX then moved that a request be sent from that club to the various members of Parliament of the neighbour- hood to support the bills, and this proposal was agreed to by a considerable majority.—The next business of the agenda paper was "To hear a paper on the history and agricultural value of the best natural grasses for permanent pasture, by Robert Tait, Esq."—The SECRETARY, however, mentioned that he had received a letter from Mr. Tait stating that owing to illness he was unable to attend, but requesting him (the secretaro) to read his paper which he forwarded. The paper, which was a use- ful and interesting one, was then read by the sec- retary, and was illustrated by specimens of various sorts of grasses which Mr. Tait had also forwarded. The paper was afterwards favourably commented upon, and a vote of thanks passed to Mr. Tait.

THE DISTRESS IN WARRINGTON. The weekly meeting of the Distress Committee was held on Tuesday afternoon in the Mayor's Par- lour, Town Hall. There were present the Mayer (Alderman Harrison) presiding, the Revs. J. Yonge, W. R. Parry, E. C. E. Carleton, J. Drummond; Major Litton ; Messrs. P. Monks (hon. sec.), J. Greening, J. White, 3. Smethurst, S. Davies, and R. Garnett. COMMITTEE'S REPORT. Mr. Moxizs read the report of the executive sub-committee, which stated that during the week there had been 323 applications : 153 of these were renewals, leaving 168 new cases to be dealt with. The number of cases visited were 225, and 45 of these were refused. The number of cases (heads) relieved for the week ending Sunday ,was 12415. The accounts for payment were as follows :—for food and wages. £6l 9s ; for cloth- ing, £l9 58 Ix ; total, ..-CBO 45 ri. The committee were of opinion that the time had now arrived for re- vising all the cases receiving relief, as the improve- ment in the weather will enable a large number of agricultural labourers to get employment. The building trades would also be getting into work and should lessen the narmber of applicants, and they after that work begin to should reduce the number of recipients.—On the motion of the Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON, seconded by the Rev. J. YONGE, the report was adopted. THE REY. E. C. E. CAELETON AND "THE EXAMINEE."

The Rev. E. C. E. CaaLrrox said he wishcd to draw the attention of the committee to a passage in a letter which appeared in. a local paper. He then drew a copy of last week's " Examiner " from his pocket and read the following passage from a letter signed " Clifford Dix," viz. :—" Worse than all this eyell, the trade deppression is made to minister to the bad, brutal desire of the church to gain adherents. Money subscribed by the philanthropic is guided, wherever possible, into channels leading to the passive support of the Church and State." He (Hr. Carleton) thought all of them knew that statement was simply a vilifica- tion and false, and no one would believe it for a mo- ment, but he did think a paper that was rightly con- ducted did not allow statements of that kind to appear under an anonymous signature. He had seen some very extraordinary things in that paper from time to time under anonymous signatures, but with regard to the passage he had just read he did not know whether they (the committee) would think it right to ask the editor for the name of the writer, or as him for an apology, because when an editor ad- mitted things of that kind under a fictitious name he made himself responsible.—The Rev. J. YONGE did not think that committee ought to discuss the principles upon which editors should conduct their new,,papers. He had always been under the impression that editors 1 did not hold themselves responsible for the opinions of 1 their correspondents.—The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON I thought that when a statement was made affecting a matter which the public took a great interest in, and 1 affecting a fund of that kind, no editor had the right to admit it into his columns in the way that had been. —Mr. MoNss asked where they would end if they be- gan to take notice of anonymous correspondents P—The Rev. E. 0. E. CARLETON considered they ought to ex- press their opinion as to the way in which the organ referred to was conducted, because it 'affected public opinion to some extent. They had not often an occa- sion to catch these things, but when they bad he thought they ought to do it.—Mr. GARNETT did not think it was a matter they should discuss them—The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON said it was a charge against the administration of that fund. As a matter of fact he did not even dispense their own private charity in that way. They were giving dinners to 30 or 40 children and they did this without asking questions of any of them.—Mr. GREENING thought the/ might rest very easy on that subject. He had not any such view as to Church and State.—The MAYOR said the very fact that such gentlemen as Mr. Monks and Mr. Greening were on the sub-committee was a sufficient refutation of such absurd statements. —Attention was then turned to other business and they let matter drop. THE LAST RELIEF FUND. The Rev. J. YONGB asked if there was a balance left over from the last distress fund. Ms impression was that there had been.—Mr. ::),LBTIEURST was ako of this opinion. Mr. Monks, he said, had been member of the ;former committee.—Mr. MoNiLs could not say from memory whether or not there had been a balance left over, but if there had he thought it would have been handed over to the Infirmary.

A SHIPWRE CKED CREW.—The steamer Newpelton, be- longing to Newcastle, brought to the Tyne on Thursday, from Brest, the captain and 15 of the crew of the ste.mer Premier, of Middlesbrough, which has been stranded near Brest. _ -

SINoULaie TRAM ACCIDENT.—The No. 3 car belong-. log to the St. Helens and District framways Company left the Red Lion, Bridge-street, at ten o'clock on Monday morning, for Prescot. While proceeding up Liverpool-road the front axle broke, and it was found anpossible to proceed any further. The few passengers in the car dismounted, and the car was subsequently dragged to the terminus for repairs. The car traffic in Ormskirk-street was blocked for a short time. ST. HELENS HARRIERS AT ROBY.—A special invitation having been given to the members of this club by the presi- dent, Mr. G. H. Pilkington, to run over to his residence, Wheathill House, near Huyton, on Satutday, his kind invi- tation induced a fairly good number to put in an appear- ance for the chase. The run was a very enjoyable one through Barrowfield, Longbarrow-road, Knowsley Park, the Hazles, and 'futon. The hares and pack were received by Mr. Pilkington and party in a most hospitable manner. The harriers then took actoss country to the Stanley Arms Hotel, Roby, where with friends, numbering about 30, they sat down to an excellent spread, very generously provided by the president. A convivial meeting was held, several toasts being given, the one of the evening "The health of the esteemed president," was ably proposed by J. S. Mather (bon, sec.)

WITH AN EYE TO BUSIIIESS.—A musical young lady says that a composer may very properly make overtures. COURTSHIP AND MARRIAGE.—A novel in three chapters. Chap. L Maid one. Chap. 11. Maid won. The most delicate individual in the world, should he tread upon a lady's train, is liable to become a robe bust man. A Cork paper is responsible for the following erratum: "The words printed 'pigs' and cows' in Mr. Parker's letter on the land question, which appeared in yesterday's issue, should have been 'pro's' and 'con's." "No," said a physician, "Dr. B. is not a partner of mine. We often consult together, and attend each other's patients in case of absence; but we are in no sense partner.. "I see," was the reply; "he is what you might call simply an accomplice." At a recent popular assembly in Paris a speaker patheti- cally inquired, "Why don't the great men of France bestir themselves? Why do they remain cold and unmoved at ice the calamities ef our country ?" "Because they are cast in bronze !' shouted a sarcestic voice in the gallery. A lively party of officers at mess voted a dozen of cham- pagne to whoever should best imitate the voice or ways of .an animal. After sundry neighs, brays, grunts, crows, and squeaks, a competitor in his turn was silent for five minutes, when he observed, "I was a fish !" He won the prize; and, if there is anything in proverbs, he probably swallowed It! OF FIRM FEELING—! conversation between a married man and a confirmed old bachelor: "Do you know that it is a most lamentable thing that you are not married ?" "Why ?" "Because you are leading such a lonely, selfishlife. Suppose some one should .be obliged to break into your room some morning and find you dead." "Well, it might hurt his feelings, but I'm sure it would not injure mine in the least." In his youth the late Samuel Phelps, the actor, used to play in a humble amateur company, and was foolish enough, Mr. J. Coleman tells us, to invite Jerrold, then a printer in the same office with him, to witness the performance. Phelps asked for his opinion. "Have you really made up your misd to chuck up the shop and go on this wild goose . chase ?" said Jerrold. "I have," replied Phelps. " Very well," Jerrold continued.; " don't say afterwards I didn't warn you." "Warn me!" exclaimed Phelps. "Do you mean to say that I shall never make an actor ?" "No. I diln't mean to say anything of the kind. You'll make an actor; but," snarled Jerrold, " you'll make a deuced bad one. When you've learned to move like a man and speak like a. Christian, and got rid of your Devonian dialect— when you've had ten years' practice—if you're not starved to death in the interval—you'll succeed, if you've luck, in getting thirty bob a week in some second-rate country theatre. And now go to the deuce your own way! Good morning !" THE WRONG MEN.—" Excuse me," he said, as he hailed It a getitleman in the corridor of the City Hall, "but will you lend me your eye-glassee a moment ?" He put them on - his nose to read a letter, and returned them with : " Thanks ! Have you the correct time? All! Ten-thirty !" He set his watch and confidently inquired: "Haven't any tobacco about you, eh 9" He was handed a box, and after helping himself to a liberal share, he remarked : "I want to mail a letter in the Lox here, but I find I have no postage stamps. If you—" He was handed a stamp. When he had licked it on ad mailed his letter, he said: "I'm going up Michigan Avenue to Twelfth-street. Do you happen to have a couple of street car tickets ?" " Sir ! This is too much !" exclaimed the other. "I can stand about so much, but after that—" " There! There! Beg your pardon! How did I know you drew the line on street car tickets? No offence—none in the least. I'll take your name and make a memorandum of where your generosity ceases mad this thing shan't happen again. I mistook you for a gentleman who draws the line on paying for the coupe, when I ask myself up to Lis house to supper." IRISH NATIONALIST MEETING AT

EARLE STO WN. On Saturday afternoon a meeting of Irish Nation- alists, under the the awpices of the Earlestown branch of the Irish National League, was held in the Co- operative Hall, El-le-street. The announcement that Mr. J. F. X. O'Brien, M.P. for South Mayo, would address the meeting occasioned considerable in- terest, and the room was well filled by local Irishmen, but Mr. O'Brien was unable to be present. The pro— ceedings, notwithstanding, were of a very enthusiastic and unanimous character. Dr. O'Keeffe, of Widnes, occupied the chair, and he was supported on the plat- form by Messrs. Moore 0. Farrell (Chester), P. J. Boylan (St. Helens), William O'Malley (Liverpool), M. Enright and M. Hackett (St. Helens), P. J. King (Liverpool), organiser of the district, T. Forster, .3...0hn Keegan, P. Jennings, M. Toahey (Earlestown),

See. The CHAIRMAN gave a lengthy address in explanation ef the objects of the meeting. He referred to the history of Ireland from an early period, and urged upon Irishmen the importanee of joining the Irish National League, and thereby support their leader, Mr. Parnell, and help to secure the ends for which he and his fellow members were working. Mr. P. J. BOYLAN (St. Helens) then moved, "That this meeting having the fullest confidence in Mr. Parnell, the distinguished leader of the Irish people ,*pledges itself to aid him by every legitimate means in his efforts to secure for Ireland complete legislative independence." After an allu- sion to the past government of Ireland, Mr. Boylan spoke of landlordism, and said it was now being dragged down. Par- nell and his followers had striven for one platform, and that one platform was to gain legislative indepeedence for Ire- land. (Cheers.) It rested with the Irish people in this country; in America, and in Australia whether Parnell and his friends had to succeed in gaining that independence for their country. The meeting pledged itself to support Mr. Parnell in his efforts, and judging of successes in the past. in spite of obstacles, in spite of Churchill and Chamberlain, if the reports were true they would gain from the Grand Old Man Home Rule for Ireland. (Cheers and a voice: "Gladstone for ever.") In spite of the most horrible oppo- olden that could be put against any people trying to gain their freedom they had overcome all obstacles in the pest, and it rested with the people whether they should go on to the end and reach the goal for which they had been striving for so many years. No one could doubt from what Mr. Parnell.had done in the past he would continue to work perseveringly until he had gained his ends, and that the gallant phalanx of 1886 would gain for Ireland that inde- pendence of which she was robbed a few hundred years agei (Cheers.) The Irish Parliamentary party had shown them- selves worthy of the confidence of the Irish people at home and abroad, and there should be no difficulty for the Irish- men of Earlestown to pass the resolution unanimously, and thereby show Mr. Parnell their willingness to support him in every possible way they could. (Cheers.) Mr. N. ENRIGHT (St. Helens), in seconding the resolution, observed that this was a practical age, as the age of shams bad gone, and proceeded to say that Mr. Parnell as a states- man ranked equal to Lord Salisbury or Mr. Gleclet-ine, if he was not their superior—(a Voice : " He is their superior," and applauEe)—because he said what he wanted, and what he would do, and he did it. When he said he would obtaini legislative independence for Ireland they might depend upon it, with God's help, he weuld obtain it. (Applauee.), Irishmen in Earlestown and elsewhere were better respected to-day than ever they were before, because of that gallant band of 1886, led on by Mr. Parnell, who bad demanded , their rights; a band unconquerable, no matter what com- bination of forces was brought to bear against it, a body of men to whom Irishmen looked up with love and admiration, and a body upon whom the eyes of the civilised world were fixed. (Cheers.) Another reason was that body was backed up by an united people by their pence, sympathies, and best wishes all over the world. In order to assist Mr. Par- nell and his friends he urged upon them the lessons of earnestness and thoroughness, and the importance of regis- tration. He observed that if the voters in that division at the last general election had voted against Mr. Cross, the probability was he would have been thrown out—(" yes ") —and if the whole of the Irish voters in England and Scot- land on that occasion bad not done their duty, their suc- cess en that occasion would not have been half so thorough. (Applause.) In speaking of discipline he alluded to the bt. Helens election, and said no one could be a greater favourite in St. Helens than Colonel Gamble, against whom the Tories brought out a complete stranger—a MAR called Mr. Seton- Karr—and the chances were hundred to one Colonel Gam- ble would go in. The Irishmen themselves would have preferred Colonel Gamble to the other man, but that made no difference to them ; they waited• for their orders, they followed those orders, and went for Mr. Seton-Karr. He strongly condemned any Irishman who was a Liberal or a Tory now that they had an Irish party, and said he must either by a knave or a fool if they did not follow their leader and party, whose motto was "Ireland and the Irish." (Applause.) Neither English party would do any good for Ireland if they could help it, and he appealed to all present to strengthen their cause by joining the local branch of the National League. Mr. M. 0. FARRELL (Chester) supported the resolution. He explained that Mr. O'Brien was unable to attend, as, owing to domestic concerns, he had to go off to Mayo on the pre- vious Thursday evening. He said the present was the most critical period for Ireland for the last 80 years, and in the immediate future Mr. Gladstone would announce what measure he was prepared to advocate for Ireland. He urged them to impress on the English working-men that they desired nothing to the disadvantage of England or English working-men, but what would probably help to ele- vate and raise them and make them happy and comfortable. They bore Englishmen no particular enmity, but they I simply fought for the liberties of Ireland and a complete legislative independence. They were not fighting particu- larly against Englishmen, but they were fighting against tyranny and to the death they would fight against it. (Ap- plause.) Passing in review the history of Ireland, he said coercion act after coercion act had been passed until God alone knew how any Irishmen or Irishwomen remained iN the land. They knew what Mr. Parmell and his friends were working for, and it was for the Irish people to assist them by working and uniting together and voting at elections. Their's was a peaceable movement, but it was a determined and resolute movement. Looking at the ruined homesteads and the depopulated country they thought some determined effort must be made to fix their countrymen in the soil of Ireland, and every Irishman would offer up his life and shed his last drop of blood rather than the former state of things should continue. (Applause.) They were determined to have their rights and liberties, and they bore in mind the words of the immortal Goldsmith "Princes and lords may flourish or may fade, A breath can make them, as a braath bath made, But a bald peamntry, their country's pride, When once destroy'd can never be supplied." (Applause.) Their leader was bringing them surely and rapidly to a successful conclusion ; he was leading them to their old Ireland, where they would make it the pride and gem of the sea. (Cheers) The resolution was carried with acclamation. The CHAIRMAN then announced that the following letter had been received from Dr. Donnellan, of St. Helens : " St. Helens, 19th March, 1886. Dear Sir,—l regret I can- not be with you to-morrow. I trust your meeting may prove to be a great success. Meetings like yours benefit the Irish people here and the peopie in Ireland, and I believe do much to inform English opinion. Register year voters and consolidate your strength. Wishing you every •uccees, I remain yours faithfully, P. DONNELLAN." Mr. M. DORAN then proposed :—" That in order to prove the earnestness of our desire to win for our dear country her rights and liberties, we, the Irishmen of Earlestown and district, hereby promise to join and support the local branch of the National League, and that we also undertake to exert ourselves to prove to our English neighbours that instead of the concessions of Home Rule to Ireland being an injustice to England, is calculated to induce peace and friendliness, and be of natural benefit to the two peoples." He urged that Englishmen perfectly well knew what the Irish people wanted, and said that ought all to follow the advice of Mr. Parnell and disregard English public opinion, and pay no heed to it, but look up to Ireland, to their own rights and what they wanted. (Applause.) He defined Home Rule as the right of Irish men to govern themselves in their own land, and it was nothing improper they were insisting upon. They had struggled for that right for 86 years, and they had now grounded their arms, waiting for the present peace to be broken. They were told by their leaders to wait and see what Mr. Gladstone would bring forward, but they would not grab at anything he might throw out. They had struggled through worst times than the present, and they would struggle until they obtained their rights. He strongly urged the claims of the National League to the support of all Irishmen, and pointed out the benefits they would derive, both to themselves and their cause, by becoming Mem- bers. Mr. O'Renes (Liverpool) seconded the motion, and said he was perfectly satisfi d Irishmen cnly wiehed to have an opportunity of joining the League to take their part in the organisation which would be the best possible sup- port to Mr. Parnell and best calculated to advance the cause they all had so much at heart. (Applause.) At the last general election it was a matter of pride to find that the Irish elections of Earlestown nobly responded to the call of Mr. Parnell to forget their own personal feelings, and the services of the Liberal party in the past, and also to forget the hostility and venom displayed by the Tory party, and support the Conservative candidate. The result showed the Irish electors did their duty on that occasion, and he was certain there would be the same response when it was required in the future. (Applause.) Mr. P. J. KING (Liverpool) supperted the resolution in a stirring address, in the course of which he said the present Irish Parliamentary parts' were determined to persevere until they gained the rights they claimed, and done away with the injustices at present existing. (Applausa) He urged them to join the League, and have a share in gain- ing the legislative independence of their country. He im- pressed upon them the importance of seeing to the proper registration of their voters, reed remarked that now one of the greatest living statesmen of the age was about to grant an act of justice to Ireland they should not do a single thing that could in any way be construed favourable to his and their enemiee. (Applause.) He pointed out the im- portance of a strong organisation, and said in that division if they so minded they could at the next election kick out the Tory representative, and put in a good faithful, honest follower of the great statesman wise now ruled the destinies of this great empire. (A voice: "They could that," and cheers.) By joining the League they would help to make their loved isle a nation once again, and when they bad

THE SAVAGE ATTACK ON A. WIFE. At Warringten Borough Court, on Monday, before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and other magis- trates, John Broderick, tanner's labourer, living in Silver-square, was placed in the dock, and charged on remand with assaulting his wife Ellen, on the night of Saturday, the 13th inst., with intent to marder her. Mr. J. L. Whittle, deputy town clerk, prosecuted, and narrated the circumstances of the ease, which were given in our last issue. Briefly, they weie to the efeet that on the 13th of March prisoner went home from work at about one o'clock and had dinner. Hav- ing given his wife 188, he went out and did not return to tea. In the evening, at about half-past ten, Mre. Broderick and her little boy went out to make some purchases, and prisoner met them in Horsemarket- street. They went to the Corporation Inn, where the husband and wife had each a glass of beer. On their return home the wife said, "Where have you been to-day " and prisoner at once asseulted her. He knocked her down, kicked her several times on the head and other parts of the body, and then fetched a , spade from the scullery, with whieh he struck his wife a blow on the head. She said, "Johany, don't murder ' me," and prisoner replied, " I'll kill you." Prisoner, in aiming a second blow with the spade, caught the child, which was in its mother's arms, across the back. Evidence was given by Mrs. Broderick and the son, Michael Broderick, corroborative of Mr. Whittles opening statement, and Dr. Starkey Smith then described the nature of the injuries received by Mrs. Broderick. • When he visited the house, witness said, the woman had her head bandaged, and was suffering from great loss of blood. There was a large stain of blood in one corner of the house. On the left side of the upper part of Mrs. Broderick's forehead there was an incised w.amd about three-quarters of an inch in length, the chin was swollen and bruised, and there was a wound on the crest of the left hip bone. There were also discolourations on the thighs, legs, and arms. There was a mark across the right shoulder blade of the child about six inches in length. —Prisoner said to the magistrates that he was drunk on the night in question, and knew nothing of what had occurred. He alleged that 1418 wife was also drunk—The magistrates committed him for trial, and he was removed in custody.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

, LONDON. THURSDAY. )i It would be difficult to cite a parallel of the state of affairs at the present moment existing in politics. Both Houses of Parliament meet day by day, sitting through the usual hours, getting through the ordin- ary amount of work, and now and then astonishing the world by some unexpected division. But this is only the lever de ridease—the third Or fourth rate piece played before the curtain rises on the princi- pal drama. Everybody is "waiting to hear from Mr. Gladstone "in a much more real Ivey than,when the Conservatives were in office, they waited to hear from Mr. Smith." The delay to which a term has now been put is reeognised as inevitable. At the same time it paralyses action in other directions, and politics are practically in a state of stagnation, and will remain so till Mr. Gladstone's proposals are before the House. To-morrow a Cabinet Council is to be held, at which it may be anticipated a discussion will be taken with respect to course of procedure. The suggestion that the Land Purchase portion of the scheme should be dropped, or at least postponed, while Home Rule is pushed forward, has been very eagerly accepted. Wise men will await Mr. Glad- stone's explanation of his scheme before making up their minds to condemn it. But there is something in the proposition that British credit shall be pledged for the advantage of the Irish landlord which grates upon the ear. It is amongst Liberals, and above all with the active fighting brigade of Radicals, that opposition to this scheme is chiefly felt. There is a disposition to trust Mr. Gladstone, which will, I believe, be justified in the result. Still this notion of throwing even the contingency of fresh burdens upon the taxpayer is not liked, and any prospect of averting it is welcomed. It is a very curious thing that in the space of three months, and before any action has been taken or any plan submitted the relative positions of the Land Question and Home Rule have been reversed. I remember very well how when Mr. Gladstone assumed office and his policy was discussed, it was said, "Let him deal first with the Land Question, come gradually to Home Rule, and all will be well." Within the current month the opinion has been held that the settlement of the Irish Land Purchase ques- tion would suffice for the present session, and that Home Rule would be postponed till next year. Home Rule wa4 the bugbear. Every one was frightened of it, and anxious to deal first with what was regarded as the lesser evil. Now the public mind has become so familiarised with the notion of Home Rule that it is generally accepted as a matter of course, whilst the Land Question has suddenly become the difficulty of the situation. What is said now, and I believe with truth, is that if Mr. Gladstone insists upon going forward with the Land Bill he will find his Ministry wrecked, whereas if he will drop the Land Question he is safe to carry Home Rule. There would be in this arrangement a certain dramaticjustice that attracts the mind. Mr. Gladstone in his characteristic de- sire to see justice done to all classes has cared first for the landlords, who have not many other people to say a good word for them, and hasdesired before handing over Ireland to a popular government, to secure the interests of the owners of land. But he has met with no corresponding response. The land- lords, as represented by the Conservative party, will be glad to get anything they can, but they will not help Mr. Gladstone in his effort to secure it for them. They have stood aside, doing their best to damage Mr. Gladstone, and notoriously prepared to oppose him tooth and nail in Parliament. This is a fatal short-sighted policy, and if it results in Mr. Gladstone's withdrawing hispropositions conceived in the interests of the landlords, and devoting him- self entirely to the more popular question, there are few who would be found to mingle their tears with those of the disappointed landlords. The escapade of the poor lunatic soldier who yesterday threw a petition into the carriage of the Queen is likely to have serious-public results. The Queen, after lone abnegation of the regular public duties of a Sovereign, had been:brought to regard a return to them as possible. But this incident has, it is said, sLaken her resolve. For many years she has regarded with carious distrust anything like personal contact with her loyal subjects. Infinite pains are taken in her railway journeys to keep her people at arm's length. The shock she received yes- terday is not calculated to reassure her of their harinlessness. The decision of the election judge at Barrow adds a fresh interest to the inquiries still pending, and increases the apprehension with which those imme- diately concerned watch the result. Mr. Dun- can is very heavily hit, for, being found guilty of illegal practices, he is ostracised from Parliamen- tary life for a period of years. It is regarded as a certainty that the Ipswich election will also be voided; but in this case the consequences will not be so severe. Mr. Collings and Mr. West are not charged with personal participation in illegal prac- tices. The consequence will be that, whilst they may be unseated and prohibited from offering them- selves for re-election, they are not incapacitated from sitting tor other constituencies if they can find them.

Mr. J. B. Gough, the temperance lecturer, man- aged in the course of a long and honourable life not only to do much public good but to acquire a com- fortable little income. His will, which has just been enablet him not only handsomely to provide for his wife who survives him, but to give substan- tial legacies to many members of his family, and to present comfortable cheques to various public socie- ties, chiefly missionary and temperance. Mr. Gough was a native of Sandgate, in Sent, and I fancy ' there was some expectation that if he had money to dispose of in this way he would not forget his native town. But all his benefactions are reserved 1 for the home of his adoption. Sandgate, neverthe- less, keeps his memory green. Walking along the one street which comprises the extent of this quaint little watering place the pedestrian comes upon a building standing flush with the street, upon a stow of which is deeply carved an inscription recording how "this foundation stone was laid by John B. Gough when leaving Sandgate for America" ever so many years ago. There is a lull in the sale of shilling dreadfuls. Some uncommonly bad ones have crept in the mani- fold series, and people have grown disgusted or at least suspicious of the whole affair, but at their best the sale of these cheap editions never came near -what ishabitually touched by popular French novels. I. am reading now .a well known French novel which is marked as belonging to the five hundred and for- ty-ninth edition, This is enough to make the mouth water of an English novelist, who, if he reaches a third edition, believes himself on the way to rival Thaekeray or Dickens. The French novel, though cheap enough considering the admirable type and paper used, is not put forth at a catchpenny price. Three francs, fifty cents, equal to something like two and ninepence in English money, is the price; and in France, as far as I know, there is not prevalent our English custom of selling books at twenty-five per cent, off the marked price. Having nothing corresponding with our Mudie, the French buy their books, and when they discover a desirable novel they buy it up to the five hundred and fiftieth edition, which even at a moderate selling price is a fortune for someone—the author I hope. The Saturday of this week and the Sunday which follows it constitute what artists call picture days. Every studio about Kensington or St. John's Wood is made bright and gay. Florists realise the demand for cut flowers, and lay in the necessary stock, and yet in consequence of the demand the price invari- ably goes up. The days are marked in the round of London social events. Properly speaking the Royal Academicians should have their doors closed. They have another week to finish their work, and they have two picture days of their own when they can receive their friends and show off their masterpieces. But the public are exacting, and the Academicians are compliant. They know well that a picture looks nowhere to such advantage as in the room in which it was painted. The lights are sure to be all right. No other man's stronger force kills their modest Work, and so the crowd that are visit- ing. the outsiders come in to visit the B.A.'s; for well those acconallished artists know that the true difficulty at the present moment is not to pai.nt pictures but to sell them. These visits are amusing siren to those who know nothing about art. . There are hints to be got for men as to house ture, and for ladies as to the more engrossing interest of dress. The artist's wife is sure to be got up tastefully and richly. Her husband will have designed his drew, or at least modified it, to suit his better. informed ideas. I.lpos tures look best in his own studio, and hie • e looka best there too. She always knows it, and sometimes win admit it. So you go the round from studio to studio, meet the same people over and over again, till at length you get to be quite accomplished in paying the highest praise to the pictures that least deserve it. It is benevolent .an fashionable to do so.
Mr.diners has suggested April Ist as a convenient date for him to receive the deputation on mining royal- ties.

div.head: Pttris to the (Editor.
div.p: Pttris to the (Editor.
REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF LORDS.

the recent division in the House of Commons nn Mr. Labouchere's resolut.on be a warning to the House of Lords, to either reform themselves or prepare to be re- formed? This is a question that must interest all Liberal politicians at this time. One hears daily in political con- versation that should Mr. Gladstone succeed in passing his measures of justice to Ireland, through the House of Com- mons, they will undoubtedly be shelved by the Tory major- :lcy in the Upper Chamber. Is this statement to be credited? Are the peers so blind to their own interests? Have they tforgotfen the warning of danger to the Upper 'Chamber as at present constituted, shown by the irrita- tion of the country, when they threatened and delayed the Reform Bill of the last Parliament? Surely not. Bat whether they have learnt wisdom or not, must we, I would ask, always submit to this state of things—that all reforms of the future (if introduced by the Liberall p trty), after being passed through the House of Commons (the elected repretentatives of the people) are to be threatened and delayed by this unreformed House of Peers? I believe the country would answer this question in a very decided manner, should the opportunity ba afforded them. Then why delay? In my opinion, it is high time the con- stituencies should consider this question, and Warrington amongst their number; for in the meantime we send a member to St. Stephen's to support by his vote the principle of hereditary legislators hav- ing the power to veto the voice of the people. At the next Parliamentary election the Liberal candidate should be questioned on this matter. He should under- stand that nothing less than substantial reform of the House of Peers will tatisfy the people, and that this reform must include the abolition of the hereditary principle in legisla- tion. That Warrington electors will press this at the next election and obtain Sir Gilbert's pledge to suppdrt this much needed reform, whenever it is again introduced in the House of Commons, or make way for some one else who will, is the ardent wish of yours. ac., Warrington, March 19th, 1586. AN ELECTOR.

div.head: HAPPY ENGLAND.
div.p: HAPPY ENGLAND.

Sir,—lt is by no means an uncommon thing to hear some of our well-to-do parsons, and individuals of the " upper ten." speak to us of the countless blessings we, as working- men of England, enjoy. Some of them would have the poor man believe that he has bat to ask in order to receive, and that his position in fact is the envy of his less-favoured foreign brethren. If such talk as this was addressed to the ears of the rich, then I could well understand the truth of it. But to my thinking the arift of all this is an attempt to make the poor men contented with his poverty, and to keep him from booking over the fence that separates him from his opulent oppressors. But those would-be social guides, be they parsons or dukes, who think that they will succeed in this attempt, have yet a chapter to letrn of the laws which conttol human nature. They say " facts are bard things," and it is especially so in this ctse. Are there not at this moment in "Happy England" teas of thousands of honest working-men that are only saved from starvation by charity? Ay, and in order that some of our Poor Law Guardians should not be imposed upon, the poor have to die on the roadside or on the street, to prove that they were deserving cases for charity. But perhaps I may be charged with drawing too black a picture, and some of your readers tu ty feel inclined t 3 ask. Is there not a brighter side? To such I reply yes, No bright; it is this awful co itrast between the spectre of wretched want on the one hand, and wanton waste and luxury on the other that makes this picture look so pain- ful. The same God that made the sea to shine upon all alike never intended that there should be so great a gulf between one class and another. I don't say that we shall ever be able in this country to do away with class distinc- tion to such an extent as to bring all to one social level ; but I do think that we want a radical redistribution in land and capital, and the sooner the better our leading men grasp the situation.

It is useless to expect any reform touching such a ques- tion from Whigs, Tories, or so-called Liberals, for no sooner do either taste the sweets of office than they at once turn their backs upon all the fair promises they made the coun- try at the hustings. The Whigs become Tories and the Liberals become Whigs, and in this way the country is gul- led, As for the professed Tories, we doa't expect anything from them ; they as a rule are true to their convictions to preserve old institutions, however bad they may be. I am aware that depression in trade has much to do with the existing distress; but this is to my thinking only a natural result of something radically wrong further back; and until the breach which now separates one class from another is made narrower, the millions will continue to be on the brink of starvation.—l remain, tkc.. PLEBEIAN.

div.head: ST. BARNABIS' CHURCH, WARRINGTON.
div.p: ST. BARNABIS' CHURCH, WARRINGTON.

Sir,—The question of Church Reform, giving the Bishop or the congregations more power over the clergy, makes slow progress, and in the meantime we are daily presented with evidence that the aims and actions of certain of the clergy are not identical with the true interests of the parishes over which they preside. Without entering into the larger question of disestablish- ment, which the intolerance of a section of the clergy is aiding to develops., I would draw attention to affairs at the above church. Coming from a Yorkshire village, nearly two years ago, the vicar found an earnest and efficient band of workers stimulated to greater activity by the fact that the parish was made a separate ene, but a short time served to see the principal of these alienated from the church. A bazaar was started with a good object, but it met with very questionable success, the principle up)n which such bazaars are generally conducted being to a large extent ignored, and the treat- ment of those who did the lion's share of the work was the reverse of what they were entitled to expect. Another bazaar, nearly twelve monthe afterwards, was even less suc- cessful, and this in "view of the well-known prosperity of other church bazaars.

The churchwardens long connected with the church have left, and those now in office are, it is rumoured, waiting the relief that the Easter vestry meeting will bring. The choir has been in a most unsettled state, while the teach- ing staff in the Sunday schoola has been weakened by the frequent defection of teachers. All this is ascribed, rightly or wrongly, to the attitude of the vicar, who appears to altogether mistake the character of Lancashire people. The congregation, despite a populous parish, is much below the average, and it has sensibiy declined in numbers during the past two years, though it must be observed that the parish itselt has grown considerably in that period. • The attempt to raise funds for the erection of schools is always entitled to appreciation, Sand the vicar deserves the credit that is due to him in connection with the new schools in St. Barnabas parish. It is said, however, that there is no committee appointed to manage the day school affairs. For a short time there has been a curate employed in this large and increasing parish, but this gentleman's connec- tion with the church has suddenly ceased, the circumstances singularly resembling sotne of the incidents described in B tttleton Rectory." . _

It would be deplorable if affAirs at this church were to come down to the level of those at Earlestown ; but the remedy is obvious, and it would be well for the vicar to r e- fleet that he who lives in the hearts of his parishioners is the only.true type of a clergyman. I send this in the public interest, and in the hope that it will do some public good. I have never been connected with St. Barnabas' Church, but I take an interest in al' that pertains to the parish. Warrington, March 11, 18.86.

div.head: OBSERVER.
div.p: OBSERVER.

TSB DISTRESS IN WARRING-TON.----THE MAYOR'S WEEKLY- REPORT. have the honour to report that the ladies' sowing class has met every day during the week, in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, where they have been engaged with unabated zeal cutting out, making up, and distribut- ing clothing to the poor women and children, and a few very old men whose respective cases bad been previously inquired into. The following garments have been made and given away :—Three dresses, 138 skirts, 90 under gar- ments, six jackets, 3 large shawls, 9 boys' suite, 8 boys' shirts, 5 men's shirts, 24 children's frocks, and under clothing. 2 complete outfits to enable girls to go out to ser- vice, 20 pairs of clogs, and also coals in quantities of lcwt each to the aged poor, and where sickness was known to exist. It is almost impossible to over estimate the value of the ladies' services in this department of true charity. They have, and are working with the diligence, energy, and practical skill of paid needlewomen, and their only and highest reward is the cone .iousness of so much well doing in mitigation of human suffering. The following shows the relief given in bread, SOUP., and coals.:— B.turday. 20th ...... 465 men and women, 1,383 children. Balance In band .......... £341 15 i The following sums have been contributed to the Ladies' Sewing Committee for the purchase of mate- rials for clothes, &c.l—Lord Winmarleigb., £10; Mrs. Sylvanus Reynolds, 103 for clogs ; a friend, per Miss Clara J. Harvey, ss; small slims collected by Miss H. Brown and Miss S. Yarding, £1 ,fis all proceeds of concert by the children of St. Mary' e IVission, Bank Quay, us 3P for clogs. It is also my duty to report that the Sub-relief Committee, at a meeting held on Wednesday evening. resolved to recommend the General Relief Committee, at, their nest weekly meeting to be held in the Mayor's parlour, on Tuesday, 30th inst., that, owing to the favourable . °lunge in the weather, a considerable number of those who have been receiving relief, such as agricultural labourers, bricklayers' labourers, and other out-door workers, being now presumably enabled to obtain work at their respective occupations, should after this week be struck off the "re- -lief list"; and that after Sunday, the 28th instl the distribu- tion of soup should be discontinued altogether, aed that the inquiry officers should be empowered (in lieu thereof) to distribute tickets for bread, &c., to the most needy and deserving who are, or may become applicants, so as to ens- bl e them to obtain the bread, &c., at the shops where they had been in the habit of dealing in more prosperous times. This arrangement, the Sub-Committee thinks, will also be acceptable to the small shopkeepers, who have suffered, by reason of the bread having been mainly purchased from the , large shops. As these proposed departures are very import- at nes, it is to be hoped there will be a large attendance of
e P

the subscribers to the Relief Fund and members of the General Relief Committee on Tuesday next, so as to en- sure a full and free discussion of the Sub-Relief Committee's recommendations, as well as to consider the desirability of organising a Permanent Warrington Relief Committee, the main object of which should be to affori help to the poor and deserving, as well as to expose and punish the iispos- ` ten—Yours faithfully. J. HARRISON, Mayor. Treasurer of the Distress Tani. Town Hail, Warrington, 26th March, 1886.

OUR PUBLIC LIBRARY. Sir,—l was pleased to see your able articles on the sub- ject of our public Library. lam glad to see the matter placed in another light, and the legality of a charge for taking books away questioned. I believe, sir, that von are quite right in your view. It seems a most singular thin; that the ratepayers should pay rates to support a Library. and that those only who can afford to have a Library of their own should, exclusively, have the benefit of a rate- supported one. I was struck with the list of guests at the recent re-open- ing ceremony. Although a public institution, I laile4 to see the names of any working-men on the list; only the names of those well-off in the town. This is only of a , piece with the rest of the business. Now, sir, with your kind iadulgence, I will give you one or two of my views as to the desirability of making the Library absolutely free. We live in an age of compulsory education. Children of the poorest parents are compelled to go to school until they have passed a certain standard—the object being to raise the standard of educatian and intelligence of the whole mass of the people. This is all very well as far as it goes. But suppose a boy goes to school until he is thirteen and then is drafted off to work. After finishing his daily labour, how is be to occupy his time? His parents are poor and if the lad acquires a taste for reading he has no means of gratifying his taste at home, ler his parents have their hands full—they certainly have no sur- plus cash with which to bay books. A hundred to one they think the lad has been better done by than ever they were, and to maintain him so long at school has been a burden to them. For want of books to read, the lad runs about the streets after finishing his work, and in far too many cases , his education is little better than thrown away. Why not give him a chance? Let him have books to read: let him have the means of cultivating the taste he may have ac- quired for reading at school. The lot of poor people is very hard. " Their's is a life of labour and restraint. Their prospects are dreary in the extreme. They have to toil from morning till night, and from one week's end to another—all for a little coarse food and homely raiment ; " and, indeed, often have occasion to be exceedingly.grateful. to get work at all, however poor the recompense may be. Their chances of rising in the world are very limited. In but few cases can they hope to passess many of the things that people in higher stations prize so hizhly—position. property, fine houses, &c.—laut at least they may hope to possess intel- lectual pleasures of the highest order. Sir John Lubbock in his charming essay en "The plea.

sores of reading" expresses his belief that the scholars of the future will be working-men. Professional and com- mercial men find that the severe strain of competition en- ' tails such exhaustion of their mental powers that they will be compelled for the sake of their health to take physical I exercise after finishing their daily occupation. The work- ing-man gets sufficient physical exercise in following his calling, and he can therefore devote more time to literary pursuits. Lord Macauley found his greatest happiness in books. Although he possessed wealth and fame, rank and talents, and all that these can secure, yet they were as no- thing to him compared to the seciety of his beloved books. Working-men who possess neither wealth nor fame, rank, nor talents, may yet share with him the enjoyment to be derived from books. Instead of working men spending their leisure hours in the way so many of them do, hew much more ennobling it would be to pass them in the com- pany of books? "Behold in these what leisure hours demand, _ Amusement and true knowledge hand in hand." By all means let the Mayor be requisitioned to call a town's meeting on the subject. He is a gentleman of such decided literary tastes himself, that lam sure he cannot but sympathise with such a proposal.—Yours truly, Church-street, Warrington. JOHN GANDY.

div.head: CANCER AND ITS PROPER TREATMENT.
div.p: CANCER AND ITS PROPER TREATMENT.

Sir,—lt is unquestionably admittel by the great hulk of men that he who said "one touch of nature makes the world kin" never spoke truer words, never spoke words that were more expressive of a wide-sphered experience. It is equally tree that the man who has passed through much suffering is thereby fitted for the humane work of sympathising with those who are suffering. Experience is a subtle vital chain that links men to one another. The most of people have had the vivid consciousness in their heart of that pent up feeling of sympathy struggling for expression. My reason for troubling you with a letter is sympathy with the suffer- ing, and well nigh hopeless, pure and simple. William Earl, plumber, residing at 12, Cromwell-street, Millfield B, Sunderland, is a man who has reached the meridian of life. He unfortunately was a victim of cancer in the tocgue, and was under the medical care of several medical gentlemen in Sunderland. For these medical gentlemen Mr. Earl has the profoundest respect. At this present time he believes those gentlemen did their very best to alleviate his pain and suf- fering. The first medical gentleman under whose care Mr. Earl placed himself never gave his diagnosis, yet evidently treated the wound as if he believed it was of a serious character, inasmuch as he several times cauterized the affected part with a view to burning out the diseased por- tion, but the cauterizing, although it inflicted an intense pain, ended as it was from the nature of things doomed to end, in a signal failure. The disease increased. Mr. Earl naturally becoming alarmed from an instinctive dread that it was no ordinary sore he was suf- fering from, decided to change his medical ad- viser. He was then told he was suffering from cancer in the tongue, and certainly this must for ever re- main an untold experience what it is to a sensitive nature to hear from the doctor such a diagnosis. This medical gentleman adopted a different mode of treatment. Instead of cauterizing he lanced the diseased part. After each lancing the place grew rapidly worse, which was a per- fectly natural result, as the cancerous diathesis can find no better nucleus than the free surface of a new incision he the lance. Here it was proposed to cut away the diseased portion of the tongue. Under this cutting process two-thirds of the tongue must have been cut, as more than one-half of the member was seized over the surface, and a portion of the healthy must necessarily have been cut to form a healthy cicatrix. Mr. Earl did not see his way clear to submit to this operation, and at this juncture fortunately he heard of Dr. Turnbull, 1, Woodside, 8., Sunderland, who is an M.D., LL.D., and a specialist as a cancer doctor, and just at the nick of time Mr. Earl presented himself to the doctor. There was then a large induration of the toague, fully the size of an ordinary walnut, and two small holes adjacent to the induration. These were yielding a slightly brown coloured pus, with an offensive odour. The tongue was very much enlarged and swollen in the extreme. It was next te impossible for the patient to eat his food, or to articulate a single word. The tongue, in short, was too large for the mouth. He at once placed himself under the doctor's judicious medical treatment. The doctor imme- diately applied his antiseptic, deodorizing and healing tinctures. Meanwhile, putting his patient under what is known as the epidermatic process, and which is not the least important part of the doctor's treatment. He also treated the patient constitutionally. with.a view of dealing with what the doctor considers the predisposing cause. From this; treatment a cursory observer may see how rational the doctor's system is, ap- plying antiseptic tinctures at the part locally affected, and eliminating from the blood the morbific matter, whilst by purely vegetable medicines he grapples with the diathesis deposited in the blood. The doctor being a man of sixty years of age, and of a long varied experience. and a keen observer, is very wary about stating he can make a cure when sufferers seek his advice. He promised Mr. Earl nothing beyond assuring him he would.do everythieg which lay in his power to do for him. After a few dressings the doctor saw the disease was inclined to yield to his treat- ment, and at the end of eleven or twelve weeks the result justified the hope that it would do so. Lyisited Mr. Earl's home, and had a personal interview with him, purposely to see for myself the result of the treatment, and facts are " chields that winna ding." Mr. Earl showed me his tongue, which has now a perfectly natural healthy-surface. He told me all that he felt of it was a peculiar sensation when par- taking of his food, as if he were drinking tea uncomfortably hot. After seeing this cure, whether it be permanent or only temporary, I felt as if I could not resist the impulse expres- sive of my unlimited confidence in and appreciation of the doctor's treatment, and thus determined to ascertain if you wculd kindly favour me by publishing a letter in your valu- able paper. Mr. Earl will have the greatest pleasure of giving the fullest particulars of his ease to any suffering man or woman. But this is only one out of a-vast number where the doctor has had signal moms after other able and humane medical men have failed. We may assert, without fear of contradiction, that Dr. Turnbull cures sixty per cent. of his cancerous patients, and from my own experience of the doctor's system. I shrink not to aver that he could care 80 pee cent., if only cancerous patients could be prevailed upon to come to the doctor at an early stage of the disease. The worst cases and the cases th&,'t beffle the elector most are the eases that have been treated by the knife, and yet withal the doctor's signal ability and aptness in &Ming with this virus of a disease, there are some of his medical brethren that seem fearfully wall-eyed and unwilling ec rive honour where honour is dee. With- in the last six months a lady patient, of whom all hopes of recovery were abandoned, placed herself under the doctor. Her ;position in life, happily for her, enabled her to command the highest media authority and skill. She at length placed terself under Or. Turnbull. She, whilst under the doctor, made a decided improvement. Instead of this suc- cess securing the good ,feeling of the medical faculty, as an outsider would have naturallv supposed it would have done, it seemed to evoke the jea,:ensy, the wrath, and the bitter spleen of one of those men who profess to be willing to spend, and be spent, to benefit humanity that is an heir to a thousand ills. Pr. Turnbull 's character, like his skill, is above legitimate cuspicion, and for any man who claims to belong to society to be guilty of seeking to impugn an honest man's motivea, and blasting his reputation, malign- ing his character, and robbing him of his heart and destroy- ing him of his usefulness in the human family, can only de- serve every honest man's Censure, whether he sees eye to eye with Dr. Turnbull or not. The insertion of this letter will greatly oblige, yours, &c., J. H. GUY, Congregational Minister, February 17th, Perry Cottage, Nayland, Colchester. 1388.
