I FUR IRON TRADR.—The certificate to the Board of Arbitration for the manufactured iron trade of the North of England shows that the average net selling price per ton during the past two months was £4 14591. BARROW ELECCION.—A deputation of Liberals left Bar- row on Friday morning to wait upon Mr. J. K. Cross. If be consents to stand, the election will lie between him and Mr. Caine. The election is expected to take place on Thursday next. SUICIDE BY Potsm—About one o'clock on Friday a well-dressed woman entered a coffee-heuse at Wolverhamp- Jon, and callibg for a cup of coffee poured in the contents of a small bottle, and drank it off. She died in a few minutes. The body has not yet been identified.

DEATH OF THE COUNTESS OF CHAMBORD.—The Comtesse de Chambord, who was recognised in certain circles as Queen of France, died at Goerz on Thu.sdav morning at half-past ten, from paralysis of the heart. The deceased, who had been suffering from heart disease flr some years, caught a cold, which brought on the end very rapidly, the Countess being confined to her bed for one day only. _ _ _ _

CiBINET COUNCIL.—A Cabinet douncil was held at two o'clock on Friday afternoon, for the first time since last Saturday week. Mr. Gladstone, who had not been visited in the morning by Sir Andrew Clarke, having recovered somewhat from his indisposition, was able to attend Mr. John Morley was the first Minister to arrive. Some specta- tors'kathered in Downing-street to watch the arrival of the Ministers, all of whom were present at the Council. Mr. Shaw Lefevre was engaged at the Premier's same time pre- vious to the meeting of the Cabinet.

div.head: ALTRINC HAM ELECTION.
div.p: ALTRINC HAM ELECTION.

The polling for the Altrincham Division of Cheshire, to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. J. Brooks, Con- servative, took place on Friday, the candidates being Sir William Cunliffe Brooks (Conservative), and Mr. Leadam (Liberal.) Sir William made his appearance at Altrinc- ham very shortly after the poll opened, and was heartily received by his friends, as was Mr. Letdam by his suppor- ters, on appearing soon after. The register contains 10,502 voters, for whose accommodation there are twelve polling booths and 29 stations. A personation agent for each party is stationed at every station. The Liberals report that the voting was very brisk between eight and ten o'clock. Since then the polling clerks had not been so busily occupied. The Conservative leaders were very sanguine as to the re- sult. They maintain that the personal esteem in which their candidate, Sir W. Cualiffa Brooks, is held, will secure him the votes of many electors to whom political principles are a secoadary considera- tion. They also assert that there have, so far, been many abstentions on the Liberal side. These they attribute to the advanced opinions which the Liberal candidate, Mr. I. S. Leadam, entertains on Irish questions. Everything was proceeding with great regularity and quietness, there being a total absence of any indication of public excite- ment. Private meetings of Irish electors have been held during the present week in the most populous parts of the division, and have been addressed by members of the League. The Irish electors in the division are said to number about 300. The great ability of the Liberal candi- date, and the earnest and persuasive speeches delivered on his behalf by Mr. Joseph Arch, wonld also, it was calcula- ted, have considerable weight with the constituency.

div.head: POLLTNG AT LYMM.
div.p: THE POLLTNG AT LYMM.

In the Lymm district considerable activity was manifes- ted in the election contest, but there was, if anything, less excitement than at the general election. The polling booth was at the Parechial Schools, Pepper-street, and the candi- dates had committee-rooms near at hand. There were three stations, one for Agden, Bollington, High Legh, and part of Lymm •, one for Lymm •, and another for Millington, Thal- wall, Warburton, &c. The voters number 1,204. Polling went on pretty briskly in the morning, in the afternoon there was a falling off, but in the evening voters came up in larger numbers. Mr. and Mrs. Leadam visited the vil- lage in the morning, and Sir W. C. and Lady Brooks in the afternoon. The supporters of each candidate gave them a hearty reception. The Conservatives had a preponderance of vehicular assistance, many of the gentry of the neigh- bourhood having lent carriages. A few carriages were also brought into use by the Liberals. Party colours were pretty generally worn. The local police, under Sergeant Harring- ton, were assisted by about ten additional constables. The following were personation agents: Liberal, Messrs. Edward Clark, Edwin Moston, Elijah Bradburn, and Thos. Davies; Conservative, Messrs. William Brazendale, Henry Forest, and G. T. Leigh. RESULT OF THE POLL.
The counting was commenced immediately after the close of the poll at eight o'clock; and at a late hour last night the result was declared as follows :
Brooks (C) Leadam (L)
Majority . The Conservative majority at the General Election was 752. It will be seen, therefore, that Mr. Leadam has re- duced the majority against him by 169. '

div.head: :THE STRIKES IN BELGIUSI._
div.p: :THE STRIKES IN BELGIUSI._

A general strike has commenced at the Bois Communal and Fleurus Collieries and is extending to nearly all the neighbouring collieries owing to the intimidation and pres- sure exercised by the strikers who are going about the dis- trict.
A Central News telegram, dated Brussels, Friday after- noon, states that the strikers at Lodetinsart have wrecked a factory and destroyed machinery.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.

The House met at four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS. Earl GRANVILLE, replying to Lord Cranbrook, said it was not his present intention to state the Irish policy of the Government on the 8,11 of April, the dAy fixed by the Premier to make his statement in the House of Commons.—Two Bills amending the Electric Lighting Act, 1882, were read a second time.—Lord Homm- TON, on behalf of the Government, introduced a bill on the same subject which was read a first time, and the House adjourned. The House eget at 4 o'clock.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

QUESTIONS.—Mr. HERBERT GLADSTONE, replying to Sir C. Dilke, said steps were being taken to enable the Chelsea , Hospital authorities to continue the practice of admitting a few men who were able to work and perform duty for the help of their weaker comradea.—Mr. BRYCE, replying to Mr. Hutton, said no reference was made by him to any under- standing.—At five to five Mr. Gladstone entered the House and was received with loud cheering.—Mr. CHILDERS, re- plying to Viscount Newark, said a reward of £2,000 had been paid for the information that led to the conviction of , the two dynamitards, Cunningham and Burton. . SIR CHARLES DILK.E.—ThE ATTORNEY•GENERAL, re- :plying to Mr. J. Wilson, said the rule as to evidence taken in the Divorce Court was not applicable to cases of con- spiracy. He did not intend to take steps to amend the law of ,evidence.—Sir C. DILIEE said Mr. Wilson's question was abstract, but it no doubt referred to him. If the bon. member wished to raise the subject in the House he called upon tina to do so on such terms as would enable him to meet it. 4Hear, hear, and cheers.) MR.Gir4DSTONE AND IRELAND.—Sir M. BEACH inquired if the Prime Minister's statement promised for the Bth April would be made in such a form as would enable dis- cussion to be taken on it.—Mr. GrADSTONE said his state- ment would he made in such form as would enable mem- bers to express an opinion. The purport of the statement would be to obtain leave to introduce a bill for the future government of Ireland. The terms of his motion would be laid on the table on Monday or Tuesday. TEE ESTIISATE.S.—On the motion for going into Coin- mitcee of Supply, Mr. Jourr WILSON moved for a select committee to be appointed to consider the estimates with the official heads of departments before they were submit- ted to the House. There was, he felt certain, a general impression throughout the country that some check must be put on the growing expenditure of the country, and he could not think of a better check than that which he pro-

TIN MINISTERIAL CRISIS. The Press Association says :the :attitude of Mr. Bright gave rise to much conjecture in the Lobby on Tuesday everting. It is stated that Mr. Bright was, until Friday. in accord with Mr. Chamberlain, but that after the interview at Downing-street on Saturday his Opinions underwent a change, and he is itowiirepared to support Mr. ,Gladstone's scheme. One at the causes of his conversion is said to =be the:: determination'of Mr. .01adetone to re-cast his plan, for the expropriation of the Irish landlords. There is no change in the situation so far as Messrs. Cham- berlain and Trevelyan ape concerned. The Council of the Liberal Association for the Eastern Division of West Riding at'Leeds, on Thee- -day passed areSolutitan expressing-the earnest hope that on the Irish question Mr. Gladstone might achieve a brilliant success for the cause of freedom, liberty, and goodwill of all classes of her Majesty's subjects. The "Leeds Mercury" says Mr. Gladstone s pro- posals were received with something like enthu- siasm" by most of his colleagues, and there has never been any thought of recasting the Irish bills in order to suit the ideas of Mr. Chamberlain. In another communication to the " Daily News;" Mr. Labouchere, M.P., says there are at least thirty Radicals in the House of Commons who will vote against land purchase with an Imperial guarantee, and Mr. Gladstone therefore could not -eohimand a working majority in favour of the joint proposals. The hon. member suggests that Mr. Gladstone should separate the two issues, and deal with Home Rule first.

The Central News says that since the last Minis- terial crisis no Cabinet Council has been looked for- ward to by politicians with greater eagerness and interest than tat one summoned for Friday. The Council had been summoned for two o'clock, and shortly before that hour Mr. John Morley put in an appearance. Mr. Chamberlain strolled over from the Local Government Board Office, and his arrival, together with that of Mr. Trevelyan, put an end to various sensational remarks current at the moment. ' The other Ministers followed in quick succession, and by five minutes past two Ministers were in full Council. Contrary to general expectation, the de- liberations a Ministers were comparatively brief, the Council breaking up at a quarter-past three. Shortly after Ministers separated, Mrs. Gladstone, who had been out driving in an open carriage, re- turned to Downing-street. Mr. Gladstone, who looked pale and careworn, entered the vehicle, and drove off for a short airing in the park, previous to proceeding to the House atommons. There was a full attendance of members of the House of Commons on Friday afternoon, and Mr. Gladstone was early in his place. Mr. Trevelyan sat ' for a short time on the Treasury bench and then left the House and walked to the Reform Club. Mr. Chamberlain was in his private room for a consider- able time, but he did not put in an appearance in the House itself. Mr. Gladstone's statement caused

considerable surprise, the general inelinat-ion-being at first to interpret it in a teUse favourable to the re-establishment of Ministerial amity. A subsequent and closer study of the Premier's words- consider- ably modified this first impression, and later in the evening the belief prevailed in well informed quar- ters that the proceedings in Downing-street in the afternoon had not substantially modified the political situation. The Central News is in a position to state that this belief is well founded. The crisis, so far from having been relieved by what took place at the Council board, has been intensified, and the prospect of finding a tnodus vivendi are as far removed as ever. No final

decision has been taken on either side, and the points in. dispute are to be further discussed, but upon several important matters of principle the divergence between the Premier and more than one of his colleagues is as wide as ever. Although the deliberations of ministers have not precipitated matters, the resignations of several members of the Cabinet may now be considered purely a question of time and of official and personal convenience.

THE PARISH CHURCH.—The elaborate brass seven-light gas standards, designed and made by Messrs. Singer and Co., of Frome, have been placed in the sacrarium of the above church, and besides using an ornament, they supply a much needed increase of light. The cost of these stand- ards was the wkole of which has, through the exer- tions of the Rev. R. M. P. Butler, senior curate, been col- lected by voluntary contributions.

FUNERAL OF THE LATH MISS TURNER.-011 Saturday afternoon a large gathering of sorrowing friends took to their final resting place, in the Frodsham Parish Church- yard, the mortal remains of Ada Elizabeth Turner, second daughter of the late Mr. Richard Hudson Turner. A pre- liminary service was held in the Five Crosses Chapel, and the large attendance gave ample proof that the deceased was held in the highest esteem. This was farthier made manifest in the gifts of upwards of 25 wreaths and crosses, some of which were made of the choicest and most delicate flowers and ferns. There was one which particularly at- tracted attention, consisting of ivy leaves and daisies very effectively arranged. This was the gift of her bosom com- panion, whose pet name was Daisy, while that of the deceased was Ivy. After the service in the chapel the cortege pro- ceeded to the cbarelward, where the final ceremony was performed by the Revs. E. A. Mosscrop and F. F. Edmunds. several appropriate hymns were sung. At the close of the service the wreaths, which had been carried by her Sunday school scholars, were placed at the side of the grave. The deceased, who was in her 25th year, had,given promise of active service in the church with which she had connected herself. She was an active member of the Wesleyan Methodist Society, having been the leader of a Juvenile Society class for some time past. She also acted as teacher of the first class of girls in the Sunday school, and her work, though unostentatious, will live for years to come in the hearts of those who have come under her influence.

WYCLIFFE COCKLIEDGE CONGREGA- TIONAL MISSION. On Thursday evening the annual congregational tea meeting in connection with the above place of worship was held in the Mission-room, Brick-street. There was a good attendance, the tables being pre- sided over by the following ladies :—Mesdames Harrison, Ashton, Maybury, Bracewell, Willcock, Garner, Travis, Cockroft, and Misses Legge and Ashton. After tea an entertainment was given in the Independent Methodist Schoolroom, Brick- street, which had been kindly lent for the occasion. The chair wag taken by Mr. J. G. McMinnies, J.P., who was supported by the Rev. J. Yonge, the Rev. W. R. Parry, Mr. B. Farrar, Mr. T. Malkin, and others.—Mr. MCMINNIES, in the course of an intro- ductory address, referred to the principles and methods of Congregationalism as opposed to those of an established church. He maintained that the people who correctly understood and believed in those principles could not consistently be sup- porters of a State Church.—The Rev. J. YONGE also alludedto the same subject, and said that only the other day he took up a newspaper and read a report of the proceedings at the lecture by the Rev. Mr. Tuckwell, and was surprised to find a number of strong Nonconformists declare that they were not Liberationists. He said it was diffi- cult for him to see how a conscientious Noncon- formist could acquiesce in the maintenance of an Established Church.—The Rev. W. R. PARRY, pastor of the mission, stated they had now a flourishing Band of Hope, which numbered over six hundred members. And with regard to their Sun- day school, according to their books, there were 450 scholars, but in addition there were about 100 who attended, but whose names were not on their books, making a total of about 550, which was a larger number than they had ever had before. Financially speaking, they were in a good position, having a balance on the right side. The congrega- tions, also, were not only being kept well up, but were improving. Mr. Parry likewise mentioned that they had had presented to them a baptismal font by Mr. Essenhigh, of Manchester-road, whom he thanked on behalf of the congregation. Mr. Parry mentioned that the mission had now been endowed with a clock through the efforts of a lady member of the congregation in gathering subscrip- tions. Songs were excellently sung in the course of the evening by Miss Podrnore, Mr. W. H. Walling- ton, and Mr. D. Ikin, and Mr. Furniss admirably re- cited in the Lancashire dialect. The instrumentalists were Mr. Cottam (dulcimer), Mr. Podmore (violin), and Mr. G. Riley (piano). At the conclusion Mr. Farrar moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman, Scc., and this being Bea9nded by Mr. Malkin, was hear- tily worded.

div.head: "DISTRESS FUND" CONCERT.
div.p: "DISTRESS FUND" CONCERT.

On Wednesday evening a concert in aid of the Dibtress Fund was given in the Public Hall, War- rington, to a large audience, under the presidency of his Worship the Mayor (Alderman Harrison.) —ln opening the proceedings, the Mivon, stated that as all of them were unfortunately aware they had been suffering in Warrington, as in other places, from two things which had produced con- siderable distress. The one was the long period of severe weather they had had, but which he was happy to say appeared to be at an end, and the i other was the long-continued depression n trade, which, on the contrary, showed no sign of termina- ing. He then proceeded to indicate the grounds for his opinion that things were likely to be worse rather than better, and suggested the need of assis- tance for those who were suffering from lack of work. He was sure they would all feel grateful to the ladies and gentlemen who were coming forward that evening with such an excellent programme, with a view to assisting the fund for the distressed in Warrington. The programme was then opened with a song by Mr. .H. Wallington, "For ever and for ever," which was given by him in good style, and was heartily received. Mr. Wallington, in the second part sang, "Philip, the Falconer," so effectively that the enthusiastic encore was not to be denied. In responding he substituted the nau- tical song "Molly dear.". Mr. Wallington is remark- able as a vocalist for his clear articulation and enunciation, and in this respect he sets an example to other and more pretentious singers. Mr. R. H. Pearson executed a violin solo (a) Cavatina, (b) Mazurka, in his usual brilliant style, being suitably accompanied by Miss Mary Wallington on the piano. Mr. Pear- son, later on, took the violin part in piano and violin duo with Mr. Frank Booth. This perform- ance was very flatteringly received, as it deserved to be. Miss Wallington charmed the audience by a beautiful and expressive rendering of Berthold Tours' song, d' The angel at the window," and she bowed her acknowledgment in response to the recall. In the second part, Miss Wallington sang the very pretty song, "A bunch of cowslips," in an equally effective manner. Mr. P. C. Price sang Gounod's "Nazareth," and Mrs. G. H. Newcombe's "The brigand bold," the latter, which has a lively rollick- ing air, being well given, met with a, good recep- tion. Mr. A. Perris, the well-known elocutionist, recited the "Bridge of sighs" with striking effect; and he afterwards with equal power gave as a recital, "The lifeboat," a fine story by Mr. G. R. Sims, which was listened to with breathless in- terest. In calling upon Miss Monks to give Gounod's "Serenade,, the Mayor evlained that she was suffering from a cold, and was consequently not in good voice. This was evident when Miss Monks sang, but notwitstandinu this the song was well sung and well received, the violin obligato being skilfully executed by Mr. Pearson. Miss Monks seemed to be in better trim when she sang" The lost chord," and received an enthusiastic recall, which she appropriately acknowledged. Mr. George Parr gave a pleasant rendering of" When other lips," and joined Mr. Price in the popular " Army and Navy" duet, which was sung by them with especial effect. 1 Mr. F. Booth, who made an admirable accompanist during the evening, also sang" Little Binks," which closed the first part of the programme. In the second part, the Mayor read one of the Ingoldsby legends, "My Lord Tomnoddy," in a manner which showed he thoroughly understood and keenly ap- preciated the humour and pathos of the author. The programme throughout was very much enjoyed, but it would have been even better appreciated had., there been fewer changes and "waits."—Mr. C. BROADBENT, in appropriate terms, moved a vote of thanks to the Mayor for presiding on that occasion, and to the ladies and gentlemen who had given them such an excellent entertainment that evening. He especially singled out Mr. A. Perris, upon whom had devolved a good deal of the labour of making arrangements for the concert, and who had also delighted them with his admirable recitals.—The MAYOR briefly acknowledged the vote of thanks, and the proceedings were brought to a close shortly before half-past ten o'clock.

This Company is formed to purehaseoas a going concern, and work the Penmon QuarrOes. upon ...which upwards of £28,000 has been expended in opening up and developing the property and in providing plant and m schinery. The business is being converted into a.Joint Stock enterpris for the purpose of obtaining additional capital in order that large contracts, which the Directors have in view, may be ac- cepted. The Quarries, which c3mprise an area of about 35 acres, are situated On the Western side of the Menai Straits, in the Island of Anglesea, opposite Liverpool„and within about two hours' sea voyage of that port. For economical and easy work- ing their position stands practically unrivalled, as the products are shipped direct from the Company's Tier. at which vessels can load at all tide times, thus saying what in most other Quarries is a great expense, namely, the carriage from the ,Qutrry teethe shipping port. In addition to the regular trade of these Quarries, and to Aloe extessive orders the Directors anticiwe obtaining in con- nection with important works and Railways about to be carried out in the district, the construction in thewleinity of the Quar- ries of the Manchester Ship Canal (these woks alone being es- tinaated tocost 0t8,032,972), assu as the Directers oi their be- ing able to most condderably extend the tr.ade of the Quarries. In the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal alone it is well known that an immense quantity of this elass of Stone will be required, not only for the Canal but also or the large Docks which will beconstructed at ManchesteroSalford, and Warrington. This conclusion has been arrived at for two reasons ..:—lst—the close proximity of the Quateles to Liver- pool; and 2ndly—the unusual facilities which their position affords for loading vesse's. Speaking as to the future prospects. Mr. Dixon, in his Report, states that the _small outlay he suggests being ex- pended in additional machinery and buildings (which the Vendors have andertaken to provide) together with a working capital of about £2,500 (which the Directors have decided to increase to £7,500) would secure to the proprietors "A most " remunerative and successfulandertaking by yielding a net "profit of from .22 to 25 per cent, on the capital inverted:" while Mr. Arthur Lee reports that "There is a monopoly for "the sale of this particular Stone and Marble." In addition to the accompanying Reports, the Directors, be- fore consenting to join the Board, with a view of satisfying themselves as to the value of the property and the prospects of the Company, personally insp-cted the Quarries, and have caused estimates of the working expenses and profits to be sub- mitted to thsm. These estimates, which accompany this Prospectus, show that a net annual profit of £10,745 at least may be anticipated. The Directors have agreed to take Shares to the amount of not less than £4,000, and they have further .greed to aceept no remuneration for their services until a Mininsum Dividend of Ten per Cent. per Annum has been paid to tb.e Preference Shareholders. SnAILIM, WEDNIISDAY.—It is reported that the Abys- sinians have completely defeated the rebels near Kassala, killing five hundred. Osman Dion, in expectation of their approach, has built a fort, armed witk eight guns, on the old battlefield at Tamai. Smallpox has broken out at Tama'; numbers are dyine, of the disease. The tenth battalion of the Egyptian army is shortly expected here. Oman Pasha will leave to-morrow for Cairo. RUSSIA AND THE VATICAN'. ROME, WEDNBSDAY.—M. Bagaroff, the Russian EnV-oy who is shortly expected at the Vatican, will be the hearer of a letter from the Czar to the Pope, and also of a proposal from M. de Giers indicating the bases for the re-establish- ment of diplomatic relations between Russia and the Holy See. THE PANAMA CANAL. PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—M. de Lessepe on his arrival at St. Nazaire yesterday evening declared that the Panama Canal works were making satisfactory progress, and that the canal would be completed in 1889.
